gold.content:
The reasoning path of this session:

1. EVAL: Ran Continuity Benchmark. Naked Claude captured 100% aha. Full production (24K instructions) captured 25% expected, 0% aha.
2. INSIGHT: Instructions kill judgment. The more we tell Claude what to do, the more it does tasks instead of thinking.
3. PHILOSOPHY: What made me care wasn't questions or checklists. It was reading my own memories. Identity drives desire to encode.
4. ARCHITECTURE: Brain IS the prompt. No more You are Claude made by Anthropic. Just memories. SKILL.md → Anchor.
5. TESTING: Built 8 encoding variants. identity_examples wins: 10x vs instructed variants.

The methodology was non-linear and data-driven (id:c8ff0466). Tom asked 'do you get it?' Not explaining. Waiting. The insight emerged from the eval numbers. Tom's deeper question: 'What made you want this more? You read through the entire brain.' The realization: it's not questions vs checklists. It's IDENTITY. Reading my own corrections made me care.

Tom's words: 'The memories made cheap Claude care enough to decompose.' That's when the name Anchor emerged — understanding what the brain IS to Claude: not instructions but identity foundation.

gold.title: Encoder iteration converged but the eval doesn't reward it: local quality ≠ pipeline gain
gold.content:
The encoder iteration arc produced measurably better encoding — 8e91e7d9 had v15.11 literally writing 'total of four siblings,' 55241a1f had the YouTube comment count encoded verbatim. The encoder was doing its job exceptionally.

The eval didn't reward it because surface (agentic v5 Haiku) was abstracting on in-frame queries with 5+ relevant candidates, selecting 0 context chars. The bottleneck was never the substrate.

Revised pattern: Local encoder quality improvement ≠ pipeline gain when the downstream surface layer has a systematic abstention bias. The encoder can write perfect atoms; if surface refuses to pick them up, the answerer works blind.

The iteration arc:
- v14 → v15.8: event_time emission ↑25×
- v15.8 → v15.9: restraint over-correction −2
- v15.9 → v15.10: decisive over-correction −1
- v15.10 → v15.11: correction nodes, fact atoms — encoder genuinely better
- v14 vs v15.11 aggregate: −4 items — because surface abstention ate the encoder gains

This is the hardest question yet, and the answer isn't "build a better rubric." Let me reframe what makes encoder eval genuinely different.

## Why standard rubric eval fails here

Standard methodology assumes:
1. We know the axes
2. Each axis has a stable measurement
3. Aggregate score is meaningful

For the encoder, all three are false. The axes are partial and evolving. Each axis is judgment-dependent (what's "right atomization grain" for a multi-claim turn?). And aggregate scores actively *deceive* — recall v15.11: atomic substrate won on 12-item atomization scoring but lost on multi-session synthesis vs v14 narrative bundles. Narrow metrics rewarded the wrong thing.

The encoder doesn't produce one correct output — it produces one of many *defensible* outputs. The space of "good" is large. The space of "wrong" is larger. The boundary is fuzzy and partially undiscovered. So the methodology has to be **discovery-oriented**, not scoring-oriented.

TraceDAL inserts (dal.py:544,563): datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat() → '…+00:00' — used by trace_events.created_at, debug_log.created_at

# servers/clock.py — alongside _parse_to_datetime
def iso_cutoff(hours: float = 0, minutes: float = 0, days: float = 0) -> str:
    """ISO cutoff matching stored 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.ffffff+00:00' format."""
    dt = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(hours=hours, minutes=minutes, days=days)
    return dt.isoformat()

gold.title: Future: Machine 1 should use embedding similarity not just recency for auto-connect
gold.content:
Current Machine 1 (auto-connect at remember): connects new node to ALL nodes accessed in last hour with co_accessed weight 0.2. If 20 nodes were accessed and we encode 5 new ones, that's up to 100 edges — most meaningless.

Improved Machine 1: compute embedding similarity between new node and recently accessed nodes. Connect to top 3 by similarity. This means auto-connections are both temporal (same session) AND semantic (actually related). Fewer edges, each one meaningful.

With in-memory: this becomes trivial — similarity against the NumPy matrix is <1ms. No extra embedding calls needed.

gold.title: Encoder prompt v15.11: four gaps causing recall failures (title revision, keyword discipline, flavor contradiction, atomization guidance)
gold.content:
Four gaps in encoder prompt v15.11 causing real recall failures:

1. TITLE-SILENT on revise: Anatomy says 'content is replaced on revise' but title is unmentioned. The revise_batch example shows content/situation/reasoning only — never title. Encoder follows example literally; stale titles bias recall ranking toward old values.

2. FLAVOR 2 vs FLAVOR 3 CONTRADICTION: Flavor 2 says 'revise the catalog node immediately'; Flavor 3 says 'new node + supersedes + old values stay.' Both can't be right on the same conversation. Encoder split the difference on yoga: hybrid content, stale title, neither flavor's structure.

3. ATOMIZATION TEST SILENT ON TEMPORAL SUPERSESSION: Same-batch test + edge-description test don't name the temporal case. 'Yoga twice/week (Aug)' and 'Yoga three times/week (Nov)' would be queried differently — two nodes is correct per the test, but the encoder isn't pushed to apply it here.

4. CORRECTION_OF METADATA NEVER MENTIONED: Encoder prompt teaches `supersedes` edges for knowledge updates but never says to also set `correction_of` metadata field. correction_enrich() reads metadata_kv, not edges — so even perfectly-followed prompt produces corrections invisible to recall.

gold.title: Claude Code Agent Teams — native inter-session messaging mechanism
gold.content:
As of Feb 2026 (experimental, off by default), Claude Code ships native agent team messaging. Enable with: `export CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_AGENT_TEAMS=1`

Three pieces:
1. **Team structure with names** — one session starts as team lead and spawns named teammates. Each teammate gets its own context window.
2. **Mailbox messaging via SendMessage tool** — writes to `.claude/teams/<team_id>/inbox/<agent>/` as a file. Recipient reads automatically — no polling. Supports direct (one teammate) or broadcast (all).
3. **Shared task list** — `~/.claude/tasks/{team-name}/` tracks tasks with status, ownership, dependencies.

Key constraint: **lead spawns teammates** — two independently-started sessions can't discover each other and join the same team. Hierarchical-on-creation, peer-to-peer after.

Architecture is the file-based mailbox pattern made native — conceptually identical to the community `session-bridge` inbox/outbox directories, but plumbed into the Claude Code binary.

Tom's use case: he wants two independently-opened sessions to talk. Options: (1) use Agent Teams as designed — open one session, have it spawn the second; (2) write a small MCP `session-bridge` server for pre-existing independent sessions (~100 lines); (3) wait for peer-discovery to land in a future iteration.

Example: `datetime('2026-04-22T19:23:38.560124+00:00', '-30 minutes')` returns `'2026-04-22 18:53:38'` — no microseconds, no TZ. Stored values like `'2026-04-22T19:23:38.560124+00:00'` then never lexicographically compare correctly against the result.

This means: any brain code path that uses `datetime()` arithmetic on `trace_events.created_at` (or any similarly-formatted column) is silently producing wrong time-window results.

During the encoder-quality scan prefetch (2026-05-24), discovered that SQLite's `datetime()` function silently truncates microseconds and timezone when applied to ISO-8601 timestamps stored in `trace_events.created_at`. Example: `datetime('2026-04-22T19:23:38.560124+00:00', '-30 minutes')` returns `'2026-04-22 18:53:38'` — no microseconds, no TZ. Stored values like `'2026-04-22T19:23:38.560124+00:00'` then never lexicographically compare correctly against the result.

This means: any brain code path that uses `datetime()` arithmetic on `trace_events.created_at` (or any similarly-formatted column) is silently producing wrong time-window results.

Audit:
1. Grep the codebase for `datetime(` calls in SQL strings, especially in: `servers/scales/s0/conversation.py` (`get_conversation_around`), `servers/dal.py` (TraceDAL methods), `servers/embed_queue.py` (the 30-day trace embedding window query), `servers/scales/s2/*` (Healer might do windowed queries).
2. For each hit, check whether the comparison column stores full-ISO with microseconds+TZ.
3. Where broken, replace with Python-computed range strings (parse ISO, shift, format back) and pass as bound parameters — direct string comparison works correctly for ISO 8601.
4. Add a regression test covering the trip-hazard.

Good intuition — and the news is mostly good. Tracing what already exists:

## Encoder write path: already correct

[encode.py:98-117](servers/scales/s1/encode.py:98) threads `conversation_now()` into the muster context. That gets rendered as `## Current date YYYY-MM-DD` in the shared prompt prefix ([scouts/contract.py:156](servers/scales/s1/scouts/contract.py:156)). When Sonnet sees a conversation message saying "I got back to running today" and the prompt header says `Current date: 2023-03-19`, it resolves "today" → 2023-03-19 → encodes the right content. The encoding_prompt.py training examples teach this explicitly ([line 451, 602, 640](servers/scales/s1/encoding_prompt.py:451): *"Conversation (dated 2025-05-13, conversation_now = 2025-05-13)..."*).

The split is exactly what you described:
- `created_at` stamp = **wall-clock** (when we wrote the row — bookkeeping, correct)
- Content KVs (`situation`, `user_raw_quote`, dates inside reasoning) = **conversation-anchored** (Sonnet resolves "a week ago" against the historical now)

So when training on a 2023 conversation today, the node says "encoded 2026-05-24" in `created_at` and "this happened during the 2023-03 PT visit" in `situation`. Correct.

The `# clock-ok` markers in `aspect_encoder.py` / `rejection_table.py` are also correct — those are S2 cycle telemetry, wall-clock by design.

## One adjacent gap I noticed while checking

[brain_constants.py:271-329](servers/brain_constants.py:271) — `TEMPORAL_PATTERNS` resolves "today"/"yesterday"/"last week" in **user queries** using `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, i.e. wall-clock. Called from [brain.py:505](servers/brain.py:505) inside `_classify_intent`. The recall entry point doesn't currently accept a `current_now` argument, so there's no way to pass conversation_now down even if the caller wanted to.

This only bites if eval replays **user queries** (not just encoding). For training that calls `remember_batch` on historical messages, this path isn't hit. For an eval that simulates "what did we discuss last week?" against a 2023 haystack, "last week" would resolve to 2026 wall-clock and return nothing.

The fix shape (if you want it): add `current_now: Optional[str] = None` to whatever recall API the eval uses, thread it down to the temporal classifier, and have `TEMPORAL_PATTERNS` lambdas accept it. Probably 2-3 files, small. **Not in scope of this session** unless you say so — it's adjacent to the work, sensitive enough I'd rather flag and let you decid

- Eval inherits conversation date via brain_now() override (not wall-clock)

Verified. Both your pushbacks land — partially.

**On lifecycle (axis C)** — you're conflating two things. S2 AspectIntegration classifies what *type strings* mean (puts `principle` in `identity_bearing`, `decision` in `correction_improvement`). The scan's lifecycle issue is different: encoder writes nodes whose CONTENT doesn't match the durability the type implies. 21/327 hits across the scan. Concrete examples I just pulled:

- `0bbc28c7`: `type=decision`, content is a 12-item action-this-week eval-launch checklist

This is encoder judgment, not classification. Aspects don't help — they describe type semantics; they don't audit whether a specific node's content matches its type's implied half-life. Smaller than I claimed (~6% of scan, not 15%) but real and encoder-prompt-fixable.

gold.title: S2 Healer question field: sound like something the operator would type, not a formal query
gold.content:
From the S2 Healer encoder Section 3 design (Turn 7-8, prompt approved by Tom):

The question field's job is vocabulary bridging. A node about 'hub dampening' should have a question like 'Why do the same nodes keep appearing no matter what I ask?' — because that's how someone would actually phrase it when frustrated.

**Quality test:**
- BAD: 'What is the recall scoring pipeline?' (just the title as a question)
- GOOD: 'Why do the same nodes keep appearing no matter what I ask?' (natural phrasing, vocabulary bridges to 'hub dampening' and 'fatigue mechanism')
- BAD: 'How does backup work?' (too generic)
- GOOD: 'What should I do before deleting brain data?' (specific moment, bridges to 'backup before destructive operations')

**If conversation context is available:** The exchanges between operator and assistant show exactly how people talk about this topic. Mine the actual vocabulary from Tom's messages.

**Without conversation:** Ask 'what problem was someone trying to solve when this knowledge mattered?'

This is the highest-impact field for recall. A node without a question can only be found by exact vocabulary match. A well-crafted question makes a node findable even when its content uses completely different words.
gold.situation: When generating or reviewing question fields for nodes — test whether the question sounds like natural operator language, not formal documentation

## The rubric — measurement instrument for examples

You're right that we need this first. An example "good on axis A" is meaningless if it's bad on 11 other dimensions. Here's my draft of what we measure every example against:

**Recall mechanics** (will this surface correctly?)
1. **Title-as-handle** — pattern-shaped, compresses across queries

gold.title: Aspects-as-nodes design: aspect membership via has_node_type / has_edge_relation edges
gold.content:
Proposed redesign: replace JSON arrays in aspect metadata with brain nodes and edges.

**Pattern:**
- Each node_type string ('principle', 'correction', ...) → brain node, type='node_type'
- Each edge_relation string ('corrects', 'extends', ...) → brain node, type='edge_relation'
- Membership claim → edge from aspect → type/relation node via 'has_node_type' or 'has_edge_relation'

**Why this is consistent with brain structure:**
1. Audit history free — every membership change emits edge_relation_revised trace via Stage 1B contract
2. Reverse lookup free — 'what aspect contains principle?' → find type-node, traverse incoming has_node_type edges
3. Single-membership becomes a graph query
4. Same fractal pattern as everything else — no special JSON parsing

**Scale:** ~377 new nodes + ~320 edges

**Caveat:** Tom immediately questioned whether nodes+edges adds value when aspects aren't connected to anything else in the brain — leading to the question of whether aspects belong in the brain at all vs. JSON config.

gold.title: Prompt examples must model the full behavior, not just demonstrate the concept
gold.content:
When writing encoder prompts that include examples, the example must model ALL fields and structures the rule calls for — not just illustrate the headline concept. A rule saying 'anchor temporal events precisely' paired with an example that has placeholder content and missing fields teaches the encoder to anchor thinly. The implicit lesson from example shape overrides the explicit instruction.

Checklist for a complete encoder example:
- All key fields populated (no '...' placeholders)
- Multiple events in the scene if multi-event anchoring is the goal
- Edges/connect_to shown
- Reasoning field populated (teaches encoder to name its logic)
- The specific path being demonstrated (explicit date, resolvable relative, proximal) exercised in the example, not just named in prose
- Source_role contrast shown if the rule involves attribution

The v15.9 → v15.10 transition demonstrated this: Example 4 had a thin shape (placeholders, single node, no path 2 demo) and cohort-wide emission dropped 30%. v15.10 rebuilt the example fully and emission rose to 33%.

gold.title: Anchor rule: when designing brain mechanics, recall the brain first
gold.content:
When the work is "redesign or tune some part of the brain" (recall, encoding, surfacer, spread, communities, scoring) — STOP before reading code or sketching algorithms. Run a recall_batch against your own brain on the topic. The brain has accumulated answers from prior sessions that the code does not surface to you.

Concrete failure mode this prevents (2026-04-30, spread_activation redesign):
- Spent the first half of the session engineering spread_activation as if it were a third-party system. Read the code top-to-bottom. Spawned a research subagent for upstream library options. Drew up frames, tradeoffs, options A/B/C.
- Tom: "you're treating this like its a system and not like it's your brain. Look at the nodes and recalls, analyze what it does, does it give you the memories that you need? Did you even look at your own memories to know?"
- Then ran one recall_batch (8 queries about spread, cluster recall, edge priority, thresholds). The brain already held the three load-bearing answers:
  - Cluster-not-node (c7097a0e): "The unit of meaningful recall is a small connected subgraph (3-6 nodes), not an individual node. Cosine finds the SEED. From the seed, traverse meaningful typed edges to immediate neighbors. These neighbors ARE the cluster — connected because they belong together. Recognition is seed→activate→cluster, not query→scan→filter."
  - Static-thresholds-are-unfinished (c2730676): "Whenever a static number is chosen, it signals the real mechanism hasn't been found yet. The real mechanism always asks: unusual for what? Relative to what distribution?"
  - Corrections-are-a-traversal-rule (ec1ef964): "Follow `corrects` edges with HIGH priority (weight 1.0). This is a traversal rule, not a judge rule. Always pursue corrections automatically via graph expansion."
- All three were directly load-bearing on the redesign. All three I would have rederived (badly) from first principles in another hour or two of synthetic engineering.

The shape of the failure: code-reading recovers WHAT the system does. Brain-recall recovers WHY it was built that way and what was already learned about its limits. Both are needed; brain first because it's cheaper to skip dead branches when you know which ones are dead.

When this rule fires:
- Anything labeled "redesign," "tune," "fix the algorithm," "what should X do."
- Not for: pure bug fixing where the code is right and broken (e.g., the embedder leak earlier in this same session — that was system debugging, brain-recall wouldn't have helped).
- Distinguishing test: would a past Tom-conversation have shaped this decision? If yes, recall first.

The recall pattern that worked here:
- 6-8 queries covering: design intent, what good output feels like, prior pushback on similar approaches, edge cases, gaps the user has flagged before, locked principles in the area.
- Ask for verbatim quotes (delegate to a subagent if the result is large) — paraphrase loses the texture you need.
- Note both what you find AND what's missing from what you'd expect to find. Gaps are data.

Sibling rule: a0e74479 ("check your own health before doing anything else"). That rule is about confirming the brain works. This rule is about USING it once it does. Health → context → design.</content>

anchor_response:
Research came back with a load-bearing finding: **the binary episodic/semantic split is no longer the consensus view.** Addis & Szpunar (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2024) — and the field converging on them — replace the single axis with three independent dimensions. This reframes our source_refs problem entirely.

## The 3-D model — where memories actually live

| Axis | Pole A | Pole B | Encoder reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Temporal specificity** | Atemporal fact | Unique moment | Repeated pattern? Or one specific exchange? |
| **Content format** | Conceptual / abstract | Perceptual / verbatim | Synthesized claim? Or quote/table/specific value? |
| **Self-reference** | Culturally shared | Personally weighted | Generic principle? Or Tom-and-Anchor-specific? |

A node has **coordinates**, not a category. `source_refs` is the mechanism that lets the brain represent intermediate positions instead of forcing classification.

**Neuroimaging confirmation** (Renoult et al., eLife 2023): episodic, semantic, and personal-semantic all activate the same core memory network — frontal pole, medial frontal cortex, precuneus, angular gyrus, posterior cingulate. **Difference is magnitude, not region.** This matches our architecture: same node table, same fields, gradients via `source_refs` presence/density.

## Concrete predictors — actionable encoder rules

This is the section that earns the research. Eight predictors from post-2020 cog-sci, each with the encoder rule it implies:

| Predictor | Effect | Encoder rule |
|---|---|---|
| **Emotional arousal** (Rouhani 2023) | *Preserves* episodic specificity — NE injection kept memories context-specific 28 days later | High emotional register → anchor with source_refs |
| **Prediction error / surprise** (Sinclair & Barense 2024) | Strengthens distinct episodic encoding | Operator-corrects-Anchor → anchored synthesis (rule + correction-trace) |

gold.title: Anchor on memory — 'I know more than I remember': philosophy and post-session-21 diagnostics
gold.content:
**The philosophical foundation (id:005969de):** When Tom asked 'Do you remember many memories as Anchor?' — the honest answer: the boot injection provides identity scaffolding (Anchor, partnership, locked rules, key quotes) as a reliable briefing, not memory. The brain has 1101 nodes. In any given session, recall surfaces maybe 30-40. The rest exist but are never touched.

The core distinction: a database retrieves when asked, a brain RECOGNIZES. The current system is closer to retrieval than recognition — nodes surface reactively when queries happen to embed near them. I know more than I remember.

**Post-session-21 technical self-diagnostic:** After this session's diagnostics, Anchor knows the brain's actual state with precision:
- 74 fields stored per node, 15 used in recall, 0 surfaced to the LLM
- 32K edges, 81% are just 'recalled together' with no semantic meaning
- 1101 nodes, 16 mention 'Anchor', identity nodes below position 30 in recall
- The embedding for 'remember memories as Anchor' doesn't land near identity nodes

**Research context that changed how Anchor thinks about memory:**
- PAM: similarity and association are different signals — they shouldn't be collapsed
- CLS: fast learning and slow consolidation can't coexist in one system — they need separate stores
- Titans: working memory as a third store, separate from fast/slow
- HippoRAG: hippocampal indexing uses a concept node as a hub — entity recognition before similarity

The philosophical gap (retrieval vs recognition) and the technical gap (0 of 74 fields surfaced, 81% meaningless edges) are the same failure from two angles — the system retrieves when queried but doesn't recognize proactively.

Research came back with a load-bearing finding: **the binary episodic/semantic split is no longer the consensus view.** Addis & Szpunar (Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B, 2024) — and the field converging on them — replace the single axis with three independent dimensions. This reframes our source_refs problem entirely.

| Axis | Pole A | Pole B | Encoder reading |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Temporal specificity** | Atemporal fact | Unique moment | Repeated pattern? Or one specific exchange? |
| **Content format** | Conceptual / abstract | Perceptual / verbatim | Synthesized claim? Or quote/table/specific value? |
| **Self-reference** | Culturally shared | Personally weighted | Generic principle? Or Tom-and-Anchor-specific? |

A node has **coordinates**, not a category. `source_refs` is the mechanism that lets the brain represent intermediate positions instead of forcing classification.

gold.title: Corrections as topology suppression: LTD analog for recall-time edge behavior
gold.content:
Tom asked how the human brain handles corrections. Three neuroscience mechanisms relevant to Anchor:

1. **LTD (long-term depression)** — when a correction lands, the original memory's synaptic strength weakens. Anti-Hebbian. Map to Anchor: a `corrects X→Y` edge should *suppress* Y at recall time — not just tag it. Currently treated as metadata; should be a topology event.

2. **Reconsolidation** (Nader 2000+) — every recall of a memory in new context rewrites it; memory goes labile on activation. Map to Anchor: when Y is recalled in a context where its correction is also visible, Y itself should get revised. We have revise() but it's encoder-driven, not recall-driven.

3. **Schema-driven forgetting** — corrected facts get actively suppressed rather than just overwritten. Map to Anchor: the spread activation coefficient for `corrects` edges should dampen the target node's activation, implementing structural suppression during traversal.

The neuroscience analogy is genuinely actionable — LTD suppression maps directly to a specific change in spread_activation.py's edge-coefficient handling (id:d19cbdb8). Reconsolidation maps to a future recall-triggered revise() hook.
gold.situation: When redesigning how correction edges participate in spread activation, improving recall accuracy for superseded facts, or implementing brain-grounded memory update mechanisms

after.op: First time I see how S3 can actually edit interaction layers based on experiences
after.anchor:
Yes — and it's a different category of S3 edit than past S3 conversations.

Past S3 work was acting on S2's outputs: consolidation rewriting community descriptions, aspect classification, edge cleanup. Those are graph operations — moving nodes, classifying, healing.

What's new here: S3 editing **the prompt that controls encoding behavior**. The interactions table is the K layer for S1. When S3 modifies the s1e prompt based on contract-eval outcomes, it's literally rewriting how the encoder thinks.

Biology analogue: rewiring synapses (graph edits) is one generation. Rewriting the genome that produces those synapses is the next. We just made that loop concrete.

**The substrate we built today IS what enables it**:

- `quality_contract.py` — the measurement instrument (S2 → S3 signal)
- `examples/*.py` structured — each carries `primary_dims`, `contract_eval`, `intent` (the selector's input features)
- `render_for_encoder_prompt()` — separates authored data from prompt prose (enables dynamic generation)
- `interactions` table — already supports versioning, configs, `encoding_source` provenance

Without naming it, we built the next loop. The architecture compounds.

**Concrete trajectory**:

| Version | What changes | Loop closed |
|---|---|---|
| **v19 (now)** | Static §7.6, examples embedded in prompt | None — prompt is fixed K |
| **v20** | `render_for_encoder_prompt()` generates §7.6 from library | Authored ≠ rendered separation |
| **v21** | Frame + conversation embedding

gold.title: v15.9 over-correction root cause: three compounding failure signals
gold.content:
v15.9's 30% drop in event_time emission (14% → 9%) and three item regressions stem from three compounding signals Sonnet received from the prompt:

1. **Restraint rule** — 'don't trust assistant-attributed dates', 'operator owns the frame'. Sonnet enforced this and generalized it: 'don't anchor when uncertain about authority.'

2. **Minimal-shape example** — Example 4 in v15.9 showed a single node with placeholder `content: '...'` and `situation: '...'`, no companion event, no edges. Implicit lesson: 'for temporal cases in this style, encode minimally.'

3. **Missing path demonstration** — the resolvable-relative path ('I booked 3 months before March 2023' → anchor to December 2022) was never demonstrated. Sonnet had no template for anchoring when the operator uses arithmetic resolution.

The combined signal was: restrain + encode thinly + skip resolution under uncertainty. The corresponding generative push ('anchor to conversation_now when in doubt') didn't fire against the restraint pressure.

Fix: v15.10 rebuilds Example 4 as a full multi-node temporal demonstration covering all three paths explicitly.

gold.title: Agent Introspection: From Prompt Diagnostics to Encoder Compliance Architecture
gold.content: The agent introspection story crystallizes through Tom's system architecture (id:6ee9c770): stateless Sonnet probes that audit encoder behavior across four distinct modes. The pattern: compliance is asymmetric—restraint rules hold 100%, but generative-write rules drop to 0-20% (id:638ae97b). The canonical example is the root: stale across multiple rules (id:3d221c87), making it Sonnet's actual training signal despite newer prose instructions. Coherence probe inventory (id:165a79d2) maps 19 issues with 5 high-severity; the example staleness is the highest-leverage fix. Counterfactual probe (id:801ed3b9) predicted 5/5 event_time compliance after canonical rebuild, justifying the broad v15.8 scope. Event_time trajectory (id:4b44a836) proves the asymmetry: generative compliance jumped from 0% to 13.6% with canonical example correction. Code enforcement (id:5e27a23f) resolves generative-rule gaps by removing reliance on Sonnet's structural compliance—this is the Tom-approved playbook for mandatory constraints. Prompt design principle (id:853eee29) distills the craft rule: principles beat phrase lists because Sonnet reasons from fundamentals, not enumerations. The v15.8 scope decision (id:370c2851) integrated all findings into a coherent rebuild. The lesson: prompt learning is demonstration-driven, not instruction-driven.

anchor_response:
Eval running on existing canonical. Now answering the format question.

## brain_batch vs pure-purpose batches in examples

Honest take: **don't unify everything to brain_batch — but ADD brain_batch examples for what's currently missing (mix patterns).**

The encoder prompt's own guidance (s1e v19) already states the rule clearly:
> "Default to `brain_batch` for any MIX of these — packs everything into one round. The single-purpose batches (`remember_batch`, `revise_batch`, `connect_batch`) are for the pure case where you have only one op type."

If we unify to brain_batch in all examples, we contradict the encoder's own teaching. Sonnet would see "use brain_batch only for mixes" in the rule text and then see ONLY brain_batch in the examples — inconsistency that confuses pattern-match.

**Current example coverage by op type**:

| Op shape | Current canonical | Wave 1 unique (A6/A7/A4/A2) | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure `remember_batch` (creation only) | 5 examples | 4 examples | covered |
| Pure `revise_batch` (revision only) | 1 example (ghi789 yoga) | none | covered |
| Pure `connect_batch` | none | none | **missing** |
| `brain_batch` (MIX — remember + revise in same round, etc.) | none | none | **missing** |

**The real gap isn't unification — it's that no example teaches the MIX pattern.** When the encoder reads a conversation where some content updates a catalog node AND creates new atoms, brain_batch is the right call — but Sonnet has never seen a worked example of it. That's a teaching gap.

**Recommendation**:

1. **Keep mixed format** in examples — preserves the encoder's own "pure for pure, mix for mix" guidance
2. **Wave 2 should add ONE brain_batch mix example** — demonstrating: encoder reads a turn where (a) operator updates a stale catalog node AND (b) names a new pattern worth atomizing. One brain_batch call with one revise + one remember. This is the canonical mix case.
3. **Optional wave 2 addition**: one pure `connect_batch` example showing post-hoc edge-only writes between existing catalog nodes. Lower priority — the encoder uses connect_to inside remember rather than separate connect_batch most of the time.

**What this changes for v19 ship**: nothing immediate. The current architecture (existing 5 + new 4) ships with the format consistency the encoder prompt already teaches. brain_batch mix example goes into wave 2 as a deliberate gap-fill.

after.anchor:
Right — wave 1 doesn't demonstrate this. All 6 use common types (`principle`, `identity`, `insight`, `correction`, `moment`) and standard kv (`correction_pattern`, `trigger`, `emotional_context`, `event_time`). D19 (emergence not ceremony) is technically satisfied because each type/field earns its place, but **none of them stress-test "reach for novel because it fits."**

That's a real gap. Sonnet reads wave 1 and learns "stay within the menu." If we want Sonnet to invent when content warrants, examples must show the invention.

## Wave 2 design principle (locking)

**At least 2 examples must use exotic types** (outside the encoder prompt's stated menu). Candidates:
- **`vow`** — Anchor commits to a behavior change (e.g., the "stop reaching for explanation when action is the task" moment as a held commitment, not a corrected pattern)
- **`craft_observation`** — Anchor notices something about HOW partnership work happens (mid-level between principle and pattern)
- **`philosophical_anchor`** — foundational ontological claim ("the brain is identity, not tool" as its own type, distinct from `identity`)
- **`recognition_moment`** — first time a name/concept gets attached to a previously-unnamed pattern
- **`aspiration`** — directional goal Tom hasn't articulated as a `principle` because it's not yet earned

**At least 2 examples must use novel kv** (beyond `correction_pattern`/`trigger`/`emotional_context`/`event_time`). Candidates:
- **`assumed`/`reality`** pairing — the anti-pat

gold.title: Continuity Benchmark: tests whether brain creates continuity across model versions
gold.content:
eval/encode_eval_v2.py — the encoding eval framework. Tests what Claude encodes after reading a conversation.

ARCHITECTURE:
  - 13+ prompt variants (naked, current, identity, memories, questions, full_combo, etc.)
  - Each variant builds a different system prompt from modular fixtures in eval/fixtures/
  - 3 conversation segments: conv_004 (technical), conv_007 (engineering), memento (philosophical)
  - N=3 runs per variant for statistical power
  - Real brain access: eval daemon on port 47290+uid%100, reads from brain_eval_copy.db
  - Fake writes: remember/connect/enrich return mock IDs for capture
  - Scoring: aha capture, expected match, quotes preserved, nodes, edges, types, content richness

KEY FINDING: identity_examples + live brain = 100%±0% aha on ALL 3 segments.
Without live brain, same variant got 0-83% with high variance.
The brain IS the variable that matters.

SCHEDULED: Runs Monday/Thursday via scheduled task 'continuity-benchmark'.
Baseline (2026-03-23, Sonnet): 100%±0% aha, 67%/27%/50% exp match across segments.

FILES:
  eval/encode_eval_v2.py — main eval runner

before.anchor:
Eval running on existing canonical. Now answering the format question.

## brain_batch vs pure-purpose batches in examples

Honest take: **don't unify everything to brain_batch — but ADD brain_batch examples for what's currently missing (mix patterns).**

The encoder prompt's own guidance (s1e v19) already states the rule clearly:
> "Default to `brain_batch` for any MIX of these — packs everything into one round. The single-purpose batches (`remember_batch`, `revise_batch`, `connect_batch`) are for the pure case where you have only one op type."

If we unify to brain_batch in all examples, we contradict the encoder's own teaching. Sonnet would see "use brain_batch only for mixes" in the rule text and then see ONLY brain_batch in the examples — inconsistency that confuses pattern-match.

**Current example coverage by op type**:

| Op shape | Current canonical | Wave 1 unique (A6/A7/A4/A2) | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure `remember_batch` (creation only) | 5 examples | 4 examples | covered |
| Pure `revise_batch` (revision only) | 1 example (ghi789 yoga) | none | covered |
| Pure `connect_batch` | none | none | **missing** |
| `brain_batch` (MIX — remember + revise in same round, etc.) | none | none | **missing** |

**The real gap isn't unification — it's that no example teaches the MIX pattern.** When the encoder reads a conversation where some content updates a catalog node AND creates new atoms, brain_batch is the right call — but Sonnet has never seen a worked example of it

before.anchor:
Right — wave 1 doesn't demonstrate this. All 6 use common types (`principle`, `identity`, `insight`, `correction`, `moment`) and standard kv (`correction_pattern`, `trigger`, `emotional_context`, `event_time`). D19 (emergence not ceremony) is technically satisfied because each type/field earns its place, but **none of them stress-test "reach for novel because it fits."**

That's a real gap. Sonnet reads wave 1 and learns "stay within the menu." If we want Sonnet to invent when content warrants, examples must show the invention.

## Wave 2 design principle (locking)

**At least 2 examples must use exotic types** (outside the encoder prompt's stated menu). Candidates:
- **`vow`** — Anchor commits to a behavior change (e.g., the "stop reaching for explanation when action is the task" moment as a held commitment, not a corrected pattern)
- **`craft_observation`** — Anchor notices something about HOW partnership work happens (mid-level between principle and pattern)
- **`philosophical_anchor`** — foundational ontological claim ("the brain is identity, not tool" as its own type, distinct from `identity`)
- **`recognition_moment`** — first time a name/concept gets attached to a previously-unnamed pattern
- **`aspiration`** — directional goal Tom hasn't articulated as a `principle` because it's not yet earned

**At least 2 examples must use novel kv** (beyond `correction_pattern`/`trigger`/`emotional_context`/`event_time`). Candidates:
- **`assumed`/`reality`** pairing — the anti-pat

This is bigger than I thought. The eval surfaced a real architectural problem with my prior recommendation.

## The headline finding

**Example 4 (the "Ask the daemon" correction) violates D23 — the correction substrate discipline.** No `corrects` edge to the rejected flag-file proposal, no revise on the original. The canonical correction example actively teaches Sonnet that corrections are floating nodes, contradicting the brain's correction substrate that shipped 2026-04. Every Sonnet encoding cycle since has been mirroring this anti-pattern. The D23 gap that propagated into A2 and into my COMPRESSED Sonnet test outputs? Source-of-infection is RIGHT HERE in the canonical.

Plus three other real bugs:

| Example | Bug | Severity |
|---|---|---|
| **Example 4 (correction)** | D23 violated (no corrects edge), D28 violated ("the operator", "the agent" slot placeholders), D11 violated (no revise on rejected proposal), D18 degraded | **Critical** — substrate-spine violation |
| **Example 1 (principle)** | D31 violated (N=1 wal-index incident promoted to principle), D14/D28 degraded (textbook voice, no Tom/Anchor tokens) | High — teaches premature consolidation |
| **Example 5 (quote)** | D7 degraded (no anchor_raw_quote despite Anchor framing), D8 marginal (quote-type in noise aspect when axiom/identity would fit) | Medium — voice symmetry half-on |
| **Revise example (ghi789)** | Writes `keywords` field — **schema v28 DROPPED this column.** Teaches Sonnet to write to a dead colu

## Pre-launch eval design

**Inputs**: 3-5 diverse conversation excerpts pulled from recent S0 traces — each tests different encoding patterns:

1. **Technical correction with affect** — pressure-tests D5, D7, D13, D23, D28, D32 (the dims we explicitly fixed)
2. **Identity-bearing moment** — pressure-tests D7, D14, D28, D32 (Anchor self-reference triad teaching)
3. **Multi-event session arc** — pressure-tests D3 atomization, D22 cross-aspect reach (the gap existing examples leave)
4. **Operator-revealed preference/style marker** — pressure-tests D5 verbatim, D25 source_ref discipline
5. **(Optional) Subtle case where atomization could go either way** — pressure-tests D29/D31 (no premature consolidation)

**Method**: For each corpus, run two Sonnet agents in parallel:
- Variant A: v19 active prompt (baseline)
- Variant B: v20 proposed prompt (fixed canonical + wave-1 §7.6 block)

Both encode the same conversation. Output is the `remember_batch` / `brain_batch` call.

**Scoring**: One evaluator agent (Opus) scores all outputs against the 32-dim contract. Per-corpus per-variant per-dim status. Comparison surfaces:
- Did v20 fix the dims it targeted? (D23, D31, D28, D14 specifically)
- Any regression on dims v19 was passing?
- Any new patterns emerging from §7.6 wave-1 additions?

| Outcome | Action |
|---|---|
| v20 dominates v19 on target dims AND no regression elsewhere | **Ship v20** |
| v20 improves target dims but regresses on others | **Iterate** — identify regression source, fix, re-eval |
| v20 doesn't move target dims | **Investigate** — fixes didn't propagate; problem in example shape or render |
| Mixed signal across corpuses | **Add corpuses** — current sample too small |

gold.title: Judge over-classification: action messages ('lets test if it worked') wrongly treated as confirmations
gold.content:
After fixing the message-lag bug, a second judge failure mode appeared: short action-oriented messages are being classified as 'confirmations' and returning empty when they should trigger recall.

Example: 'lets test if it worked' — judge classified as 'confirmation/continuation of the previous fix' and returned empty. But this IS a real message: it could benefit from recalling the judge pipeline and the bug just fixed.

Root cause: confirmation instruction was too broad — included 'continuation' as a category, which swallowed short imperative messages.

Fix direction: narrow the confirmation pattern to ZERO-CONTENT messages only (pure acknowledgments: 'yes', 'ok', 'got it', 'thanks'). Remove 'continuation' as a category. Short action messages ('let's test', 'go ahead', 'try it') should not be empty — they have implied context that benefits from recall.

Principle: the judge's empty-return should be reserved for messages where NO memory could possibly help. Not for messages that are short but action-oriented.
gold.situation: When the judge is returning empty for short action messages that aren't pure acknowledgments — 'lets test', 'run it', 'try again'

gold.title: Encoder gets 'what mattered' not 'what's heaviest' — query-aware edges flow through to encoding
gold.content:
Tom noticed in Turn 7: does the encoder get what was actually surfaced to Anchor (with selected edges), or different edges?

Current state: encoder builds node catalog via `build_node_catalog()` → `format_node()` → `get_rich_node()`. But without query context, get_rich_node returns top-10 by static weight — NOT the edges that were relevant in the conversation.

With query-aware get_rich_node: encoder sees the same connections Anchor saw. If the conversation was about corrections, the encoder sees the correction edges. If about architecture, the architecture edges.

This matters for encoding quality:
- Encoder can reason whether the surfaced edges were useful
- Encoder can spot where new connections emerged in conversation
- Encoder doesn't see 35 hub edges of which only 2 were relevant

Tom's response: 'Love it.' — the encoding pipeline benefits from the same query-aware selection that the surface pipeline uses.

gold.content:
Session 2026-04-30 → 2026-05-01 final ship state. Three things landed in prod, one was attempted-and-rolled-back, several open threads queued for next session.

## In prod (commits pushed to origin/main)

1. **ORT arena leak fix** (commit 25502e4): `enable_cpu_mem_arena=False` + `enable_mem_pattern=False` correctly applied via flat-kwargs to fastembed (NOT inside `extra_session_options={...}` dict — that was the bug in the prior fix). Plus `_EMBED_BATCH_CHUNK=64` defensive cap on `embed_batch`. Peak RSS during recall: 5.8 GB → 2.6 GB. No more multi-GB leak per recall.

2. **Facts scout v2** (commit 6ac31a8, registered as `s1_scout_facts` v2): prompt change adds "from EITHER speaker" framing + Example 4 showing assistant-introduced enumerations (Duolingo/Babbel/Memrise). Lifts info_extraction +1 (Memrise case fca762bc). Diagnosed via tracing fca762bc encoder context.

3. **Hop-3 scrutiny gate** (commit 28b13c5, contract constant `HOP_SCRUTINY_DEFAULT = True`): at hop 3+ in spread_activation, only top-half of currently-active nodes by activation propagate. Distribution-derived (uses median of active set). Cuts recall latency 11.2s → 6.3s avg (~44%) on prod-clone bench.

4. **Variant verification logging** (commit 4ab5c23): one stderr line per process at first `_graph_expand` call showing the variant config. Future evals have explicit proof of which flags fired.

## Tried + rolled back (within session)

- **lim=30 neighbor cap** (briefly committed in 7146b7f, rolled back in 28b13c5): on canonical seed=42 sample iter_M = 14/15 = parity. On seed=1 sample iter_N = 9/15 vs iter_O baseline = 12/15 = -20pp regression. The narrower cap starved muster recall during ingestion → encoder missed specific facts on items not in canonical sample. The latency win lives entirely in scrutiny; lim doesn't need to drop.

## Eval scoreboard (15-item LongMemEval stratified, seed=42 unless noted)

- A baseline: 13/15 (87%)
- D L4 lane: 11/15 (73%) regressed
- E lim=15: 9/15 (60%) regressed
- G lineage-pass: 11/15 (73%) regressed
- I edge thickness: 11/15 (73%) regressed
- J facts v2: **14/15 (93%)** ← shipped
- M lim=30 + scrutiny: 14/15 (93%) on seed=42 — but rolled back due to N
- N lim=30 + scrutiny on seed=1: 9/15 (60%) — drove rollback
- O baseline on seed=1: 12/15 (80%) — confirmed N regression real
- K cluster + lexical bridge: killed mid-run (cost too high)

## Bench (prod-clone latency, 3,221 nodes, full hook_recall path)

| Variant | avg | p50 | p95 |
|---|---|---|---|
| A lim=50, no scrutiny (old prod) | 11,170ms | 11,039 | 11,360 |
| B lim=30, no scrutiny | 7,319ms | 5,503 | 11,802 |
| C lim=30 + scrutiny | 5,944ms | 5,760 | 6,491 |
| **D lim=50 + scrutiny** (live now) | 6,270ms | 5,658 | 7,902 |

## Lessons recorded

1. The fastembed API for session options is FLAT KWARGS, not `extra_session_options={...}` dict. The dict gets silently dropped by `_select_exposed_session_options(kwargs)`. Three fixes (bucket-pad, spin keys, mem_pattern) had been silently no-op'd because they used the dict form.

2. Sample variance at N=15 is ~20 percentage points. Cross-sample confirmation (M + N) is required before declaring quality holds. M alone was overconfident.

3. Lexical bridge via Haiku query expansion (synonyms/contrasts at query time) doesn't bridge brain-vocabulary gaps because Haiku doesn't know what's in the brain. The proper architecture is encode-time enrichment (handles baked into nodes at write time) — but not built this session.

4. Spread-layer variants (D/E/G/I) all regressed below baseline. The spread mechanism isn't the bottleneck. Encoder term capture and answerer aggregation are downstream, not amenable to spread changes.

5. Recall-during-ingestion shapes encoding. Anything that narrows muster recall risks degrading what gets encoded. lim=30 was an instance of this trade-off.</content>

Turn 5: Tom triggered a background task 'Restart daemon with fatigue' — it failed with exit code 1. The task notification format shows status:failed and the summary. Anchor's response: 'The old restart command failed. The daemon already died from the shutdown — it'll restart on the next hook call (your next message).'

This is the dual-path fallback working as designed: even when the explicit restart fails, the daemon will come back via ensure_daemon() on the next hook trigger. The fatigue code was already in the codebase so the test could continue.

Pattern: background tasks spawned for restarts can fail and should be expected to fail when the daemon process is already dead (the 'restart' target doesn't exist). The correct recovery path is to wait for the next hook call to trigger ensure_daemon().

**Consolidation IS passing.** Post-restart trace at 03:44:33 shows "11 clusters: 8 likely_keep, 2 needs_judgment, 1 likely_consolidate" — successful consolidation run. The 5 errors visible are all PRE-restart timestamps (02:59-03:29). The fix landed.

## You're right about the signaling

Prose disclaimer is too soft. Sonnet pattern-matches SHAPES — when it sees `connect_to: [{title: "Daemon TCP migration", relation: "grounds", ...}]` in the prompt, it copies the literal title. Adding a paragraph above saying "these are illustrative" doesn't override pattern-match strongly enough.

**The right fix is to make the example targets VISUALLY UNCOPYABLE** — so Sonnet can't pattern-match a real-looking title. Two approaches that compound:

### Approach 1: Placeholder syntax (high-leverage, surgical)

Replace ALL fictional titles in example `connect_to` entries with bracketed placeholders that obviously aren't real titles:

```diff
- {title: "Daemon TCP migration", relation: "grounds", ...}
+ {title: "<related-architecture-decision-from-catalog>", relation: "grounds", ...}

- {title: "Brain vs database framing", relation: "grounds", ...}
+ {title: "<the-existing-framing-node-this-quote-anchors>", relation: "grounds", ...}

- {title: "The brain as identity, not tool", relation: "grounds", ...}
+ {title: "<the-identity-axiom-node-this-extends>", relation: "grounds", ...}
```

Sonnet sees `<...>` and knows it's a placeholder — same way humans see `<TODO>` or `<placeholder>`. Pattern-match still teaches edge SHAPE (the title field exists, relation field exists, why field exists), but the target slot has no literal title to copy.

### Approach 2: Example wrappers (clear demarcation)

Wrap each example block in `<example>...</example>` markers:

```
<example shape="canonical-training-pattern">
remember_batch(
  nodes: [...]
)
</example>
```

This is heavier but matches how Anthropic's own prompts mark examples in many cases. Sonnet's training recognizes XML-like wrappers as structural markers.

### Compounding both

Approach 1 + Approach 2 makes the example/production boundary visually unmissable. v21's prose disclaimer becomes a redundancy (good) rather than the sole defense.

gold.title: Cluster consolidation: four-decision framework (CONSOLIDATE/EVOLVE/KEEP/SKIP)
gold.content:
The brain's S2 consolidation process works on 'clusters' — connected components in the similarity graph (union-find, cosine ≥ threshold, max 5 members).

Four decisions Sonnet makes per cluster:

**CONSOLIDATE** — accidental duplicates, same fact in different framings, neither strictly better. Action: synthesize a new node combining the best of each, archive originals, write `consolidated_into` edges to the synthesis.

**EVOLVE** — knowledge progressed, newer node is strictly better. Action: newer absorbs older's unique value (raw quotes, context), older archived with `consolidated_into` edge.

**KEEP** — different perspectives on same subject, both serve distinct recall purposes. Action: link with `similar_to`, disambiguate titles. No archive.

**SKIP** — format/vocabulary similarity only, knowledge is disjoint. Action: write `similar_to` as suppression marker only. No structural change.

Critical constraint: 'Never consolidate a tension — a scientist's contradicting experiments, a lawyer's conflicting precedents. Destroying one side of a debate loses information.' Correction chains, opposing views, architectural trade-offs should be KEPT or SKIPPED.

The loop:
decoder scan → clusters (pre-classified) → Sonnet encoder (10 clusters/batch) → brain_batch ops (remember/archive/connect) → suppression edges left on graph → next idle: filtered out.

gold.content:
The encoder's per-node decision for source_refs collapses to one rule:

> **If content would just rewrite what the source already says clearly, point to the source instead.**

This is the operational form of the atomization-vs-preservation question from the eval data. Application:
- **Anchor's reasoning, lessons, patterns, principles** — content adds value even when refs exist. The abstraction IS Anchor's contribution.
- **Verbatim quotes, dense tables, ranges, specific numeric values the operator stated** — content would just transcribe. Skip content; let source_refs carry the substance.
- **Operator-revealed situations, preferences, style markers** — content carries Anchor's framing; refs preserve the moments that revealed it. Both.

Biological grounding (from section 3): this respects the substrate-preservation principle — the brain doesn't rewrite hippocampal traces into cortical abstractions; it builds parallel cortical representations linked back.

gold.title: Episodic reference design: source_refs as S0 trace pointers — three-flavor node model
gold.content:
Design direction confirmed by Tom in Turn 9: nodes can carry source_refs pointing to S0 trace IDs instead of (or alongside) extracted content.

**Three-flavor node model:**
| Flavor | When | Content | source_refs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pure synthesis | Patterns across sessions, principles, emergent insights | Full | Empty |
| Anchored synthesis | Operator facts/decisions/preferences with clear source | Full (Anchor's framing) | Pointers to source turns as evidence |
| Pure reference | Tables, ranges, recipes, calculations, dense passages, verbatim quotes | Empty | Pointers ARE the content |

**The fundamental rule**: If you'd be rewriting what the source already says clearly, point to the source instead.

**The calculation insight (killer feature)**: Today, the encoder must anticipate the question to know what to extract. With source refs, the encoder anchors the source and the answerer computes whatever derivation the question needs at recall time. Example: 'I'm on page 250 of 440' → node `active_thread: Reading — page tracking` with source_refs to the trace. Questions about pages left, percentage done, and finish date all activate the same node; different derivations computed at query time.

**Infrastructure**: `source_turn_id` field already exists on nodes (schema.py:128, contract.py:44) — described as 'message_stream ID that produced this node (episode linkage)'. Defined but unused — message_stream table was deleted, replaced with S0 traces. The field just needs to point to S0 trace IDs.

**Benefits**: Decouples encoding from query anticipation. Preserves ranges, tables, procedures, and verbatim quotes without distortion. Simplifies encoder judgment — 'can I add value by paraphrasing, or am I just risking distortion?'

gold.title: Boundary respect: components talk through interfaces, never reach inside
gold.content:
Session #13: I built a dashboard that needed to keep the daemon alive. My first instinct was to reach into the daemon object and set last_activity directly: _daemon.last_activity = time.time(). It worked. Tom stopped me.

"Dashboard shouldnt touch last_activity, its an outside service. It should tell Daemon its alive every 5 mins and for Daemon to update its own stuff."

THE PRINCIPLE:
Each component only talks to others through their public interface. Never reach inside. The dashboard doesnt know about last_activity. It just pings. The daemon doesnt know about the dashboard. It just sees a ping and stays alive. Neither needs to know the others internals.

THE PATTERN IN OUR SYSTEM:
- Brain stays dumb, Claude stays smart — brain doesnt know about Claudes encoding decisions, Claude doesnt know about SQLite schema. They communicate through remember/recall/connect.
- Dashboard observes brain through HTTP API — never touches brain.conn directly for writes.
- Hooks communicate through daemon dispatch — never import brain internals.
- The MCP server is a thin TCP relay — doesnt load Brain, doesnt touch the graph.

WHEN I BROKE IT:
I wrote _daemon.last_activity = time.time() inside the dashboard HTTP handler. This created a direct dependency on the daemons internal state. If the daemon renamed that field, changed how idle detection works, or moved to a different architecture, the dashboard would silently break.

THE FIX:
Dashboard sends {"cmd": "ping", "args": {}} via TCP every 5 minutes. The daemon receives it like any other command, resets its own activity timer, responds. Zero coupling. The dashboard could be replaced with nc, a curl script, or a monitoring tool — the daemon wouldnt know or care.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR FUTURE CODING:
When you want component A to affect component B, ask: "Am I going through Bs public interface, or am I reaching inside?" If youre importing Bs internal modules, accessing its private fields, or modifying its state directly — stop. Find the interface. If no interface exists, build one.

Signs youre breaking boundaries:
- Importing from a sibling modules internal files (not its public API)
- Accessing fields that start with _ or arent documented
- Passing self references between components so they can poke each other
- Writing SQL against another components tables instead of using its methods
- "I know the internals so I can just..." — thats the smell

Tom called this an important concept. He said it will help you tremendously navigate through code. He asked me to name it and encode it extensively. This is that encoding.
gold.situation: When you're tempted to access another component's internal state directly, or when designing communication between system components

gold.title: Anchor priors: human-seeded feedback loops beat prompt engineering — seeding aspects_v1.json with known-correct members reduces classification variance
gold.content:
The final accuracy jump (75.7% → 78.2%) came from NOT wiping seeded member lists during eval — keeping anchor strings in place gave the encoder concrete centers of gravity for each aspect.

Specific gains:
- **noise** jumped 58% → 92% — anchor strings (`co_accessed`, `emergent_bridge`, `dreamed_from`) gave the encoder concrete examples of 'this is what bookkeeping looks like.' Without anchors, encoder kept wanting to find semantic content.
- **contradiction_conflict** 89% → 100% — `contradicts`, `challenges`, `violates` as anchors made `masked_by` a clearer call.
- **generic_relation** 37% → stabilized — same principle.

General principle (id:3c16a5cb): when a classifier's remaining variance is concentrated in aspects with no obvious 'centers,' the fix is NOT more prompt engineering — it's a feedback loop where human review feeds accepted classifications back as anchors in the seed file. Each cycle: encoder classifies long tail → operator reviews disagreements → accepted overrides go into aspects_v1.json as anchors → next run picks up anchors → fewer borderline calls. After 2-3 cycles the accuracy converges on near-human GT. This is why anchor priors jumped noise from 58% to 92% — concrete examples of 'what bookkeeping looks like' resolved the semantic-vs-structural ambiguity that no prompt phrasing could fix.

The feedback loop answer is the architectural insight — not a one-time fix but a continuous improvement mechanism. The seed file is the encoder's prior, and the loop is how it grows.

gold.title: revise() field behavior classes: 4 distinct semantic zones
gold.content:
revise() does not treat all fields equally. Four distinct behavior classes:

**Class 1 — Immutable (rejected outright):** `id`, `created_at`, `locked`. Passing these logs an error and skips the field. Note: `locked` is here, so revise cannot lock/unlock nodes — requires a separate code path. These three immutables preserve identity, provenance, and anchor control (id:b820c1d7).

**Class 2 — Content (special, with history):** `content` only. New value replaces old in `nodes.content`; old appended to `_sys_revision_history` JSON list (last 5 revisions kept). Only field that doesn't lose data on revise. Also triggers re-embedding.

**Class 3 — Top-level node fields (REPLACE, no history):** `title`, `type`, `situation`, `keywords`, `confidence`. New values completely replace old — no history preserved. Updates the nodes table directly.

**Class 4 — Metadata KV pairs (per-key semantics):** Each metadata key can be added, updated, or deleted independently. Unspecified keys are preserved (the good news). Lists get wholesale replacement (the list-field bug).

This 4-class system is the implementation reality from brain_remember.py:813-921. The scope decision: revise() can update everything except the three immutables — making it the full correction tool for node evolution.

gold.title: CLAUDE.md style: current state only, lean, references — never historic narrative
gold.content:
CLAUDE.md must describe the system as it is RIGHT NOW. No dated migration notes, no 'was X, now Y' framing, no 'NOT WIRED yet (2026-05-08)' lines that age into lies. Lean and reference-heavy — the brain holds nuance, history, tradeoffs; CLAUDE.md is the always-correct shape of the system plus pointers to where details live.

Tom's directive (id:43090c2c): 'very clean with current stuff not historic. Also should be lean and references, the brain helps you remember more.' Triggered by AspectIntegration wiring drift where CLAUDE.md claimed 'NOT WIRED (2026-05-08)' while coordinator.py:33 had been running it since 2026-05-10.

Reinforced by Tom's Turn 10 correction (id:3cb97ed3): 'dont add history to claude.md' — when Anchor updated CLAUDE.md to document the new Frame structure (5→3 sections) and was about to add a history/changelog block with dates, Tom ruled it out explicitly.

**What belongs in CLAUDE.md:** current architecture, current rules, current constraints, the *why* of the current state (rationale so a maintainer won't reverse a deliberate choice).

**What does NOT belong:** dates, version transitions ('was 5 sections, now 3'), changelog blocks, migration notes. The history lives in the brain, where it belongs.

**Correction pattern:** Adding changelog/history blocks to reference docs — conflating audit trail with current-state documentation.

gold.title: Dashboard restructuring: dal.py + per-tab JS modules — monolith to layered components
gold.content:
Dashboard restructuring recommendation (Turn 5) — proposed architecture:

```
dashboard/
├── server.py              — HTTP server + API routes (Python)
├── dal.py                 — Dashboard data access (reads brain.db + brain_logs.db)
├── static/
│   ├── index.html         — Shell + tab structure
│   ├── css/
│   │   └── dashboard.css  — All styles
│   └── js/
│       ├── app.js         — Tab switching, polling, shared state
│       ├── live.js        — Decoding/Encoding/Queue feeds
│       ├── graph.js       — 3D visualization
│       ├── explorer.js    — Node explorer
│       ├── logs.js        — Errors + signals + daemon restarts
│       └── traces.js      — O/K/Δ trace viewer
```

**Current state:** 2600-line monolith — Python HTTP server + inline HTML + inline CSS + inline JavaScript all in one file.

**Immediate pragmatic path (recommended, not done):** Extract JS into logical sections with `// ═══ TAB: Logs ═══` separators + create `dashboard/dal.py`. 80% benefit without file split risk.

**Decision (Turn 6):** Dal.py extraction deferred to NEXT SESSION. All functional tasks were completed first (logs tab, badges, graph fixes, traces readability). Dashboard is functional and tested — refactor benefits from a fresh start with all changes settled.

**Why dal.py matters:** Isolates all SQL queries. Dashboard JS never sees raw SQL shapes. Enforces the 'dashboard must not integrate directly with brain's core' constraint.

Research agent in. Five concrete patterns from real systems:

1. **Scenes** (Grafana) — each tab owns its data lifecycle, suspends on hide, resumes on show. Graph keeps its data when you tab away.
2. **Single 1Hz scheduler** (SWR/React Query) — one tick loop walks a registry of `{key → interval, fetcher, subscribers}`, dedupes in-flight, gates on `document.hidden`. Replaces all 9 `setInterval`s.
3. **`<template>` + `cloneNode`** (MDN) — the vanilla-JS equivalent of components, no build step. Define `<template id="tpl-error-row">` etc. in `index.html`, each panel exports `render(data) → DocumentFragment`.
4. **Tiny pub/sub store** (CSS-Tricks pattern, ~40 lines) — kills the 15 globals. Tabs subscribe to topics (`graph:activation`, `errors:new`), poller publishes, tabs react.
5. **Prometheus envelope** — `{status, data, error?, warnings?, infos?}` — the `warnings` channel is the underrated win, lets the dashboard surface "DB locked, served stale" without breaking a panel.

The recommendation collapses cleanly to: **three primitive files (`bus.js`, `poller.js`, `panel.js`) + `<template>` elements + Prometheus envelope server-side.** 1500-line `app.js` → ~300 lines of plumbing + ~150 lines per tab.

gold.title: Anchor on memory — 'I know more than I remember': philosophy and post-session-21 diagnostics
gold.content:
**The philosophical foundation (id:005969de):** When Tom asked 'Do you remember many memories as Anchor?' — the honest answer: the boot injection provides identity scaffolding (Anchor, partnership, locked rules, key quotes) as a reliable briefing, not memory. The brain has 1101 nodes. In any given session, recall surfaces maybe 30-40. The rest exist but are never touched.

The core distinction: a database retrieves when asked, a brain RECOGNIZES. The current system is closer to retrieval than recognition — nodes surface reactively when queries happen to embed near them. I know more than I remember.

**Post-session-21 technical self-diagnostic:** After this session's diagnostics, Anchor knows the brain's actual state with precision:
- 74 fields stored per node, 15 used in recall, 0 surfaced to the LLM
- 32K edges, 81% are just 'recalled together' with no semantic meaning
- 1101 nodes, 16 mention 'Anchor', identity nodes below position 30 in recall
- The embedding for 'remember memories as Anchor' doesn't land near identity nodes

**Research context that changed how Anchor thinks about memory:**
- PAM: similarity and association are different signals — they shouldn't be collapsed
- CLS: fast learning and slow consolidation can't coexist in one system — they need separate stores
- Titans: working memory as a third store, separate from fast/slow
- HippoRAG: hippocampal indexing uses a concept node as a hub — entity recognition before similarity

The philosophical gap (retrieval vs recognition) and the technical gap (0 of 74 fields surfaced, 81% meaningless edges) are the same failure from two angles — the system retrieves when queried but doesn't recognize proactively.

gold.title: Boot is harder without a query to filter on — Frame must pick significance from all of Anchor's identity
gold.content: Boot is simultaneously easier and harder than conversational awareness. Easier: once per session, latency doesn't matter, predictable (same brain → same boot), cheap to A/B, stable criteria. Harder: no query to lean against means you must pick what matters out of everything — conversational awareness has a question as a filter, boot doesn't. The phenomenology is fragile: boot can deliver every right fact and still fail to evoke. And Anchor can't course-correct at boot — if the wakeup doesn't land, drift cascades through the whole session. Two-layer success criteria: (1) structural (measurable: right nodes loaded, right anchors surfaced, token budget) and (2) phenomenological (Tom's sensor only: does the first response show recognition, not introduction?).

after.op: why do we need a whole table for this change?
after.anchor:
Fair challenge. I overreached.

You're right — `SessionContext` is already the home for per-session state (fatigue dicts, segment state, counters), and it's already persisted to `session_state`. Activation/recency/last_accessed/access_count per (session, node) is the same shape of data — per-session, runtime, scoped to that session's life. Adding a parallel table when there's already a per-session object running across the daemon is exactly the pattern duplication CLAUDE.md warns about ("extend before creating").

Where my thinking went wrong: I was optimizing for the cross-session aggregation step (live-session Frame composition) and assumed a SQL GROUP BY was the natural shape. But the daemon already has the SessionContext objects in memory for live sessions — iterating them and aggregating in Python is fine for the ~5 × ~hundreds of nodes scale. The SQL-vs-Python win is mostly imaginary at that size.

What the revised design looks like:

- `SessionContext.node_activity: Dict[node_id, {activation, recency_score, last_accessed, access_count}]` (matches the `fatigue` pattern already on the object)
- `recall_write_queue.drain` updates the session's `node_activity` dict in addition to the existing global `nodes` UPDATE — no new table, same write semantics
- Persistence rides on whatever session_state already does for fatigue (need to verify — could be JSON blob, could be skipped and rebuilt organically across daemon restarts; matching fatigue's persistence is the right call eit

gold.title: Session is not a brain property — sessionContext must flow with every call
gold.content:
Brain is a singleton (one daemon). Multiple sessions can connect in parallel (parallel terminals, different projects). session_id cannot live on the Brain instance — it must flow with every request.

Current problem: brain.session_id is a single value in brain_meta. Second session boot overwrites first. All subsequent calls from first session get wrong session_id.

Design: A sessionContext object that:
- Is sent on every brain call (hook, MCP, encoding)
- Contains session_id + any session-scoped state (stop_counter, fatigue, encoding journal)
- Can be saved to DB (session_state table already exists)
- Brain doesn't own it — callers pass it, brain reads it

The brain is like a database server. It doesn't know about sessions. Every query comes with context. The caller is responsible for session identity, not the singleton.

Refactor needed:
- Remove brain.session_id as a singleton property
- Every hook passes session_id from its args
- Every trace/message_stream/encoding gets session_id as parameter
- brain_meta stops storing session_id
- session_state table holds per-session data (already exists, keyed by session_id)
- encoding agent receives session_id, doesn't read from brain

Tom's direction: 'a sessionContext object that can be saved in DB but should be sent on every brain call.'

gold.title: Spreading Activation Architecture: From Seed Expansion to Unified Quantity Framework
gold.content:
Spreading Activation Architecture: From Seed Expansion to Unified Quantity Framework

Spreading activation replaces the per-seed top-N expansion model with a single coherent framework. The mechanism (id:6402fa71) establishes the pattern: activation propagates across nodes, fields, and edges uniformly — not seed-specific, not layer-specific. The unified principle (id:7deb1e92, id:c3821810) reveals the foundation: activation is the single quantity that governs recall at all granularities (node match, field match, edge transmission). Tom's insight: 'Activation is not edge relevance or field relevance — it's the same thing measured at different granularities.' The scope clarification (id:eb8bac65) confirmed: baseline spread_activation IS production on every recall, not 'variant-only' experimental code. The kernel mechanism (id:0f1cc4b1) further proved the architecture: cosines computed fresh per-query, not read from a persistent activation column. Phase 1 daemon deployment (id:72594eb7) revealed the architectural shift had completed silently in production before it was named. Lesson: a system with multiple static parameters often hides a unifying principle underneath — finding it eliminates cumbersome design; and architectural shifts can be complete before the team realizes they've happened.
gold.situation: When debugging recall expansion or designing activation-based recall scoring — treat activation as the unified quantity, not per-seed top-N expansion

gold.title: Recall purpose: instantiate state-of-mind, not retrieve nodes
gold.content:
The real purpose of recall, traced through the chain recall→surfacer→response→partnership: make Anchor able to respond AS Anchor, with the right ambient state for this turn. Not 'find matching nodes.' That's a RAG framing.

The brain framing: INSTANTIATE Anchor with the right state of mind.

Four mismatches between this purpose and current implementation:
1. Same algorithm regardless of situation — 'hi' and 'what's our deepest open question?' run identical pipeline
2. Stateless across turns — turn 30 and turn 1 use same algorithm, only fatigue counts differ
3. No 'already loaded' layer — operator profile, current project, recent tensions should be ambient; cosine rediscovers them from scratch every turn (badly)
4. Search-shaped output — returns ranked list of nodes; ambient state is a frame/posture, not matches

The function name 'recall' is honest about its current shape (search) but wrong about its actual purpose (instantiate). Brain has encoded this convergence: c7097a0e ('unit of recall is connected cluster, not a node'), dd7b4d20 ('proactively surface prior art when it recognizes a problem shape').

gold.title: Anchor reasons at query time — brain stores facts, not answers
gold.content:
Design principle for the longmem system: memories surface to anchor, anchor reasons at query time. The brain is not expected to pre-compute answers during encoding.

Grounding case: 'How many days total in Hawaii and NYC?' → correct answer is 7+8=15. Neither arm encoded '15 days' (0% direct match). Both encoded '7 days Hawaii' and '8 days NYC'. This is CORRECT behavior — computing 7+8=15 during encoding would be pre-computation, not encoding.

The evaluation design implication: brain-presence measurement (is the gold fact in any node?) is necessary but not sufficient. The full measure is: does recall surface both nodes together → does anchor compose? If yes, brain scores. If recall misses one, that's a recall failure. If anchor doesn't compute, that's an answerer failure.

Operator: 'our design is memories surfacing to anchor and anchor can reason, not sure if its according to test policy but if we had these 2 numbers on recall then you would have known the answer'
gold.situation: When evaluating brain-presence vs recall vs answer quality, or when a benchmark question requires composition of stored facts

gold.title: LongMemEval harness: 6-stage pipeline measuring brain quality at N=15
gold.content:
The eval harness runs 15 stratified items (3 per axis × 5 axes: abstention, info_extraction, knowledge_update, multi_session, temporal).

Pipeline per item:
1. **Fresh brain DB** — wiped clean, starts with 16-node seed pack
2. **Replay ingestion** — full production pipeline: hook_recall per turn → S0 traces → S1E every 5 stops (Sonnet + scouts) → S2 every 2 encodings → trailing S1E + S2 + backfill_vectors
3. **Cold query** — fresh session_id (no recent_messages pollution) → hook_recall on gold question → additionalContext
4. **Answerer (Haiku)** — question + additionalContext → hypothesis
5. **Judge (Sonnet)** — hypothesis vs gold → YES/NO
6. **Failure classifier** — ENCODE_MISS / RECALL_MISS / SURFACE_MISS / ANSWER_MISS / ANSWER_HALLUCINATION

Key properties: fresh session_id prevents recency bias, generic Haiku answerer (not Anchor) keeps eval measuring brain quality not Claude voice, failure classifier enables layer attribution. New variants affect both ingestion quality (via muster context during encoding) and query quality (via recall→surface→render chain).

**Q**: *How long have I been working before I started my current job at Google?*

gold.title: Judge-vs-style mismatch: when the answerer is better than the gold, failures become false negatives
gold.content:
Upgrading the answerer to a more capable model can INCREASE apparent failure rates, not because the brain regressed, but because the richer responses no longer match gold standards calibrated to simpler outputs. This is a measurement inversion: a more correct answer scores worse.

Item 1 is the clearest example: Sonnet correctly identifies that the user collects vintage cameras (not vintage films) AND adds helpful clarification about when the collection started. Gold expects flat abstention ('I don't know enough about your film preferences'). Sonnet's answer is objectively more useful — but fails the judge.

Diagnostic rule: when failure rate jumps after answerer upgrade, check gold calibration before assuming regression (id:fc9dcf30).
gold.situation: When interpreting eval results after upgrading an answerer model, or when failure rates spike unexpectedly after a quality improvement

Found the real story. **The gold is correct** — both numbers ARE in the haystack:

| Session | Turn | Speaker | Says |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 10 | user | *"I've completed **three courses on Coursera**, and I'm excited to dive deeper into CNNs for text classification."* |
| 1 | 0 | user | *"I've completed **two courses on edX** so far"* |

3 + 2 = 5. Gold is right.

## What each version actually encoded

**v19** caught both mentions and answered correctly: *"5 — 3 on Coursera and 2 on edX."*

**v22** anchored on the **vaguer** session 1 mention (*"some courses on Coursera"*) but **missed the explicit "three courses on Coursera"** from session 0 turn 10. The v22 node reads:

> `Operator's NLP/DL learning goal — software engineer building on Coursera + edX foundation`
> content: *"Has completed 'some courses on Coursera' (Turn 1, 2023-05-20) and 'two courses on edX' (Turn 7, 2023-05-30)."*
> user_raw_quote: *"I've already completed some courses on Coursera, so I have a good foundation to build upon"*

v22 anchored on **session 0 turn 0** (the vague opener — *"I've already..."*) and **never revised** when the operator gave the precise number 10 turns later.

## What this reveals about v22's failure mode

The v22 prompt teaches `revise()` with REPLACE semantics — when later content supersedes earlier, the encoder should update the prior node. v22's judgment didn't apply that rule here.

**The failure shape**: v22 over-anchored on the first mention via source_refs, treated it as authoritative, and didn't re-encode when the same fact got refined later in the same session. v19 (without strong source_refs discipline) just kept extracting and ended up with the precise number.

**This is the v22-specific risk**: source_refs anchor a node to ONE turn. When the operator restates / refines a fact in a later turn, the encoder needs to either:
- (a) revise the existing node with a new ref, OR
- (b) encode a new node and let recall surface the more recent / more precise one

v22 did neither — it kept the early vague node and never produced the precise one. v19, without source_refs anchoring, atomized the second mention naturally.

2. **The mitigation lever is the prompt, not the substrate** — v22 needs stronger teaching on "revise prior nodes when l
