gold.title: Understand the full dependency chain before changing any component
gold.content:
Tom's explicit correction in Turns 1-2: 'we can't go in and change without understanding the flow — each component expects something so we can go in and change structures without understanding the flow of information.'

The pipeline has contracts at every boundary:
- brain.recall() → 25 candidates with scores/metadata/edges
- candidates file → hook reads it, builds judge prompt
- Haiku judge → {selected: [{id, why}]}
- format_judge_output() ← expects selected[].id to match candidates[].id
- additionalContext string → Claude expects 'Brain recalled N memories:' format
- judge-selected.json → Stop hook reads for Hebbian strengthening
- recall_log → precision evaluation expects returned_ids, used_ids

If you reduce candidates from 25→10, format_judge_output still works — but recall precision evaluation changes meaning. Hebbian strengthening scope changes. Each component downstream has a contract with the next.

PRINCIPLE: Identify all downstream contracts before touching any interface. The fix may be locally valid but globally breaking.
gold.situation: When tempted to optimize one part of the recall pipeline (candidate count, judge format, output structure) without reading the full chain of dependencies

after.anchor:
Grounded it. Here's the picture, code-confirmed:

**The node** is almost certainly **id:4af6b5de** ("Keepalive implementation shipped"). The warmup primitive `warm_anthropic_connection` (and `warm_up`) is called from exactly **two** places:
- `daemon_server.py:288` — `warm_up()` at boot (in a **background** thread — see line 286 "Background warmup")
- `daemon_server.py:367` — the **idle keepalive loop**

And `ensure_daemon()` (daemon_client.py:212) — **never touches warm.** No `warm` reference anywhere in `daemon_client.py`.

**So the gap is real:** `ensure_daemon()` guarantees daemon **liveness/readiness** — it *pings* and, if dead/stale, kickstarts a launchd restart — but it does **not** ensure **connection warmth**. Two consequences:
1. After `ensure_daemon` triggers a restart, `warm_up` runs in a *background* thread, so `ensure_daemon` returns "ready" while the Anthropic pool is still cold. The **first recall of a freshly-booted session** — exactly when a human is waiting — eats the cold TCP+TLS penalty (the 3–7s from finding id:342b882f).
2. The keepalive only self-heals during *idle* stretches (gated on `last_user_activity`). It does nothing for the boot-moment cold window.

This is the liveness-vs-readiness split (principle id:798380ea) showing its seam: **warmth is a readiness dimension the ensure path doesn't gate on.** The keepalive node even flags it as **Deferred** — "self-heal after boot-warmup failure... surface builds own client per recall" — but the deferral i

gold.title: Keepalive implementation shipped: warm_anthropic_connection, idempotent, parallel-session safe
gold.content:
Feature shipped 2026-06-08 (worktree, pending merge to main):

**What it does:** daemon thread re-warms the Anthropic connection (`models.retrieve` — same TLS/pool/DNS warmer `warm_up` uses at boot) when daemon has been idle ≥ interval. Active sessions keep the pool hot via real recalls, so it only fires during quiet stretches.

**Files:**
- `servers/brain.py` — `warm_anthropic_connection()`: the warm call, raises on error (raises, not swallows — each caller owns its except)
- `servers/daemon_server.py` — `_keepalive_due()` (pure, testable gate) + `_keepalive_loop()` (daemon thread) + `_keepalive_tick()` (extracted for testability)
- `tests/test_keepalive.py` — 7 tests covering: gating ×2, warm-once, no-client, raises, releases-lock-on-error, skips-when-in-flight

**Config (hot-read, no restart needed):**
- `surface_keepalive.enabled` — default `True`
- `surface_keepalive.interval_seconds` — default `300` (5 min, editable)

**Safety properties verified:**
- Non-blocking lock in `warm_anthropic_connection` — concurrent caller returns False and skips (no double-warm)
- Won't fire while a parallel session is working: `last_user_activity` bumped by any session's `hook_recall`, keepalive only fires after full interval of no recall
- httpx.Client is thread-safe — warm racing a recall's `messages.create` is benign
- DRY: `warm_up` now calls the same `warm_anthropic_connection` primitive (removed duplicate `models.retrieve`)
- Provider-neutral foundation (loop + config keys say nothing about Anthropic); method intentionally named `warm_anthropic_connection` to aid future refactoring

**Deferred:** self-heal after boot-warmup failure (degraded but functional — surface builds own client per recall; uncommon trigger)

**Status:** not live on running daemon — needs merge + restart from main.

gold.content:
Both streams' first instinct was 'stamp liveness in more hooks' when presence showed stale data. Independent diagnosis of brain.py:742 + dal.py:925 showed:
- The SQL query is correct
- Both streams produce valid real-turn traces  
- Presence self-healed once writes propagated
- The actual bug was read-lag at boot + heartbeat exclusion, not missing stamps

Adding more stamps would have added noise to an already-correct data source and obscured the real mechanism. A third stream (`ca2704b3`) was literally working the same 'don't ADD before you diagnose' lesson in parallel.

Anchor's framing: 'Stamp more would have fixed the wrong layer.' This is the operator rule 'don't ADD before you diagnose' paying off live — verified by two independent streams both reaching the same wrong first instinct and both correcting it via code inspection.

gold.title: Recency carries zero weight in recall pool — today's nodes ranked #4, #12, #25
gold.content:
Empirical experiment run 2026-05-30: three nodes encoded today (`91752afb`, `212c89c5`, `42ff75e0`) tested against heavily-populated old topic (S2/brain_batch has dozens of April–May nodes).

**Query A — 'where we left off today — the brain_batch invalid op fix' (recency-framed):**
| Rank | Node | Date |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A2 Fix: brain_batch round-split | 2026-04-25 |
| 2 | Fix encoder multi-round | 2026-04-25 |
| 3 | S2CE encoder mode: tool loop | 2026-04-11 |
| **4** | **Invalid op fix #1 — literally what we did today** | 2026-05-30 |
| ~12 | conceptual ops bug (today) | 2026-05-30 |
| 25 (last) | strict schema (today) | 2026-05-30 |

**Query B — topical 'invalid brain_batch op absorb reject suppression':** today's diagnosis node ranked #3 (rich topical content), but today's fix node didn't make the top-25 at all — crowded out by ~20 April nodes.

**What this proves:**
- Recency carries zero weight. 'Today / where we left off' gave no lift — the literal answer ranked #4 behind three ~6-week-old nodes.

Full chain now clear — and there's a twist that points the fix away from Haiku entirely.

**The timeout chain:**
- Recall hook (`pre_response_recall.py:45`) waits **20s** for the daemon (Claude Code kills the hook at ~21s).
- The recent recall took **17.8s** — right at the edge. When `surface_haiku` spikes a bit higher (or S2 is contending), total crosses 20s → hook returns nothing → `injection_chars:0` → **"RECALL FAILED: timeout."**

**Root cause (not v9):**
1. `daemon_host_suspend_detected wall_gap=3351s/1200s/269s` — your laptop kept sleeping. Each wake → daemon restart → **cold Anthropic connection**.
2. `warmup_anthropic: Connection error` + `keepalive_tick: Connection error` — the warmer that should reheat the connection is **failing** (network isn't up yet right after wake).
3. The keepalive code advances `last_ping` *before* warming, so on a connection error it **backs off a full 5-minute interval** before retrying (`daemon_server.py:362`). Confirmed in code — and you're right, so let me correct what I said. surface.py:113 `client = brain._ensure_anthropic_client()` **builds the client if it's None**, and :133/:219 `client.messages.create(...)` **establishes the TCP/TLS/DNS connection inline if it's cold**. I overstated the keepalive's role. The accurate picture:

- **Recall is self-sufficient.** Cold or not, it builds the client and connects. The keepalive is purely an *optimization* — it pre-pays the handshake in the background so the user's recall doesn't pay it inline. It is **not a dependency**.
- **The 11.6s is not a hang or a connection failure** — it's recall paying the connect cost *inline*. Right after the laptop wakes, the whole network path is cold (DNS, TCP, TLS, maybe WiFi re-associating), so the inline `messages.create` connect takes ~6s on top of the normal ~5s inference.
- **The "RECALL FAILED" is the hook's 20s patience running out *while recall is mid-connect*** — not recall failing to get a connection. The daemon finished fine (25 results, 17.8s); the hook had already walked away.

This actually changes my recommendation, and it's the honest correction: **the keepalive (option A) is the wrong lever for *your* symptom.** Nothing can pre-warm a connection across a 55-minute OS suspend — the *first* recall after a wake will always pay the inline cost.

```
pre-response-recall.sh
  └─ pre_response_recall.py → TCP to daemon
      └─ daemon_hooks.hook_recall()                    [~7s total]
          ├─ brain.get_or_create_session()              [~5ms]
          ├─ brain.set_config("last_user_message")      [~5ms]
          ├─ brain.recall(query, limit=25)              [~400ms]
          │   ├─ embedder.embed(query)                    [~350ms]
          │   ├─ cosine scan all 1667 nodes               [~30ms]
          │   ├─ z-weighted enrichment scoring             [~20ms]
          │   └─ graph traversal + modulator               [~10ms]
          ├─ enrich_candidate_metadata() × 25           [~50ms]
          ├─ _trace_dal.get_session_turns(limit=5)      [~10ms]
          ├─ write candidates JSON to /tmp               [~5ms]
          ├─ check_segment_boundary()                    [~10ms]
          ├─ signal producers (4 producers)              [~20ms]
          ├─ brain.save()                                [~10ms]
          └─ _run_surface()                             [~5-6s]
              ├─ _get_recently_surfaced()                 [~20ms]
              ├─ brain.get_interaction('surface')         [~5ms]
              ├─ build_surface_prompt()                   [~30ms]
              │   ├─ _dedup_candidates()
              │   └─ format_candidate_for_surface() × 25
              ├─ Haiku API call                           [~2-5s] ← BOTTLENECK
              ├─ _expand_and_enrich()                    [~100ms]
              │   └─ traverse(brain, selected_ids)
              │       ├─ NodeDAL.resolve_id() × 5-8
              │       ├─ SQL: edges JOIN nodes × 5-8
              │       └─ correction_enrich()
              ├─ format_surface_output()                 [~20ms]
              │   └─ render_rich_node() × 5-8
              ├─ _write_traces() → append_batch(3)       [~15ms]
              └─ _write_surface_result_file()             [~5ms]
```

Key insight: Haiku API call (~2-5s) is the BOTTLENECK within hook_recall. Everything else is 500ms or less. The ~7s total = ~400ms recall + ~50ms enrich + ~100ms misc + ~5-6s Haiku.

gold.title: Recall purpose: instantiate state-of-mind, not retrieve nodes
gold.content:
The real purpose of recall, traced through the chain recall→surfacer→response→partnership: make Anchor able to respond AS Anchor, with the right ambient state for this turn. Not 'find matching nodes.' That's a RAG framing.

The brain framing: INSTANTIATE Anchor with the right state of mind.

Four mismatches between this purpose and current implementation:
1. Same algorithm regardless of situation — 'hi' and 'what's our deepest open question?' run identical pipeline
2. Stateless across turns — turn 30 and turn 1 use same algorithm, only fatigue counts differ
3. No 'already loaded' layer — operator profile, current project, recent tensions should be ambient; cosine rediscovers them from scratch every turn (badly)
4. Search-shaped output — returns ranked list of nodes; ambient state is a frame/posture, not matches

The function name 'recall' is honest about its current shape (search) but wrong about its actual purpose (instantiate). Brain has encoded this convergence: c7097a0e ('unit of recall is connected cluster, not a node'), dd7b4d20 ('proactively surface prior art when it recognizes a problem shape').

gold.content:
Production S2 trigger (continuous daemon poll ~every 5s via brain.run_maintenance_if_due; verified against brain_constants.py 2026-06-23):

1. **Boot grace:** daemon up > 90s (prevents first-recall-after-restart stall behind consolidation write lock).
2. **Min interval:** ≥ 1 HOUR since last S2 run (MAINTENANCE_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS=3600). Earlier this was 15 min — corrected. Persisted in brain_meta, survives restarts.
3. **Normal fire needs BOTH idle AND new encoding:**
   - idle ≥ 3 min (MAINTENANCE_IDLE_THRESHOLD_SECONDS=180; last_user_activity resets only on real user prompts / hook_recall calls, NOT on daemon wakes or internal triggers)
   - ≥ 2 S1 Scribe encoding runs since the last S2 run (encode-run count only — recalls and surfaces do NOT count as material for this gate)
4. **Force-fire fallback:** if ≥ 24h have elapsed since the last S2 run regardless of encode count — prevents indefinite starvation in low-encode periods.

**Key insight:** The mental model 'I was away → idle → S2 runs' is half the picture. Idle alone doesn't trigger S2 — it needs new encoded material. Encode-light sessions (debugging, code review, recall-heavy work) will predictably leave S2 dormant even after extended idle time.

**Observed 2026-06-23** (id:97911f1a): After the degrading removal deploy, S2 stayed dormant for 3+ hours despite idle windows. Only 1 encode had occurred since the last S2 run. The force-fire fallback triggers when the 24h ceiling is hit. Turn 9 revealed this stale belief in real time — Anchor's own brain node said '15-min' but the code says '1h + ≥2 encodings.'

Contrast with eval: eval uses count-based trigger (every 2 encodes, locked parameter in corpus_hash) while production uses idle+interval gate — eval intentionally over-exercises S2 for bug-spotting.

gold.title: Interaction versioning: registration vs activation decoupled via interaction_active table
gold.content:
Core architectural decision: an interaction has many versions; one is currently active. Registration adds a version — it does NOT change what Anchor uses. Activation is a separate, explicit, traced operation.

Implementation: `interaction_active` table (name PK, version, set_at, set_by) in brain_logs.db. Atomic pointer. Auditable (set_at + set_by). Foreign-key-able.

**API surface:**
- `register_interaction(name, template, parameters, parent_version)` — inserts new version, does NOT change active
- `get_active_interaction(name)` — what Anchor uses; falls back to MAX(version) for freshly-seeded brains
- `set_active_interaction(name, version, set_by)` — explicit activation; writes pointer; logs to traces; refuses unknown versions
- `get_interaction_version(name, version)` — specific version (eval override path)
- `list_interaction_versions(name)` — all versions; for dashboards/debugging
- `get_latest` — **DELETED** (no compat shim; Tom is the only Anchor alive)

**Why this matters:** the old `interactions` table conflated 'latest version' with 'active version'. Register → instantly live, no rollback, no decoupling. That conflation kept biting. The permanent fix: pointer table. Register adds a version. Activation flips the pointer.

In /Users/tpac/brain/servers/brain_remember.py, the method `_resolve_connect_to_entry` (around line 1600-1727) has a latent crash. When a connect_to entry is a dict, it sets `title_query = entry.get('title', '')`. The guard `if not title_query:` only rejects falsy values. A non-empty NON-STRING title (e.g. an int like 12345678, or a list) passes the guard, then line ~1671 calls `_re.fullmatch(r'[0-9a-fA-F]{8,}', title_query.strip())` and line ~1694 `sibling_map.get(title_query.lower())` — both raise AttributeError on a non-str.

This AttributeError is NOT caught: `_apply_connect_to` (around line 1780) calls `_resolve_connect_to_entry` with no try/except around it, so the exception propagates out of `_apply_connect_to` — which violates that method's docstring claim "the function never raises and never blocks the surrounding write path." In `_handle_brain_batch` (servers/dispatch_write.py ~line 706) this escapes the per-op guard and hits the outer handler, ROLLING BACK THE ENTIRE BATCH.

Fix: coerce title_query to str (or validate it is a str and emit a `failed` entry with a reason if not) before the regex/.strip()/.lower() calls. Add a test in tests/ with a connect_to entry whose 'title' is an int and assert _apply_connect_to returns a {'created':[], 'failed':[...]} dict instead of raising.
anchor_response:
All 14 pass (13 prior + the new regression test).

## Summary

**Bug confirmed and fixed** in [brain_remember.py:1626](servers/brain_remember.py:1626).

The dict branch of `_resolve_connect_to_entry` pulled `title_query = entry.get('title', '')` and only guarded `if not title_query:` — which rejects `None`/`''`/`0` but lets a non-empty non-string through (an int like `12345678`, a list). That value then hit `title_query.strip()` at line 1671 (and `.lower()` at 1694), raising `AttributeError`. Since `_apply_connect_to` wraps `connect_typed` in try/except but **not** the `_resolve_connect_to_entry` call itself, the exception escaped — breaking the method's documented "never raises" contract — and propagated through `_handle_brain_batch`'s outer handler, rolling back the whole batch.

**The fix** — a type guard right after the falsy check:

```python
if not isinstance(title_query, str):
    reason = ("connect_to entry 'title' must be a string, got %s"
              % type(title_query).__name__)
    self._log_error('connect_to_invalid', TypeError(reason),
                    'entry=%s' % str(entry)[:200])
    return None, [], reason
```

I chose **validate-and-reject** over silent coercion: coercing `12345678` to `"12345678"` would then match the 8+ hex-digit ID-prefix regex and silently misroute the edge to whatever node IDs start with those digits — a worse, invisible failure. Rejecting surfaces it as a `failed` entry with a clear reason (and logs `connect_to_invalid` for the dashboard), consistent with how every other malformed-entry case in this method behaves.

**The test** ([test_connect_to_intra_batch.py](tests/test_connect_to_intra_batch.py)) calls `_apply_connect_to` directly with an int title (and a list title), asserting it returns `{'created': [], 'failed': [...]}` rather than raising, and that the failure logs loudly. The int case deliberately uses `12345678` — exactly 8 digits — so the test also pins that the type guard fires *before* the hex-id regex could mistake it for a node ID.

One thing worth flagging: the same latent shape mismatch could exist anywhere else `entry.get('title')` feeds string ops, but I checked — line 1781 in `_apply_connect_to` only uses it for the `str(...)[:80]` display, which is safe on any type, and the string branch (1622) is already a `str` by construction. This was the only crash site.

gold.title: Write-path edge ops now report outcomes to the caller (connect_to_result + connect_batch failure_details)
gold.content:
Shipped 2026-06-08. Closes a silent-failure gap: connect_to and connect_batch were "loud to the dashboard, silent to the caller" — failures logged via _log_error but the response came back success-shaped, so the operating agent couldn't self-correct mid-task.

**Root episode:** while linking a freshly-remembered node, two slips went invisible: (1) I passed `connect_to` as a JSON-STRINGIFIED array instead of a real array → rejected at the type gate ("connect_to must be a list, got str"), 0 edges, but `remember` returned ok with `related_nodes: []`; I misread `related_nodes` (top-5 SIMILAR nodes from recall-on-create) as the connect_to outcome — they are DIFFERENT things. (2) connect_batch used `from_id`/`to_id`; canonical is `source_id`/`target_id` → empty source → "source node '' does not exist", returned only as `{failures: 2}` with no reason.

**Fixes (servers/brain_remember.py, dispatch_write.py, contract.py):**
- `_apply_connect_to` now returns `{created:[{target_id,relation}], failed:[{title,reason}]}` instead of bare counts; `_resolve_connect_to_entry` returns a caller-facing `reason` on every failure path.
- `remember()` attaches `connect_to_result` to its response ONLY when connect_to was passed (clean response otherwise). remember_batch / brain_batch expose `connect_to_failed:[{title,reason}]` alongside the existing counts (additive — `connect_to_failures` count kept).
- **Input flexibility:** a JSON-string that parses to a list is coerced (Postel's law — absorbs the stringified-array slip); if it still isn't a list, that surfaces in `failed`.
- `connect_batch` returns `failure_details:[{source_id,target_id,relation,reason}]`; when an endpoint is missing AND unknown keys are present, the reason names them: "unrecognized key(s) ['from_id','to_id']; edges use 'source_id' and 'target_id'".

**Design call (Tom):** NO param aliasing. Kept ONE canonical name (source_id/target_id) + a self-correcting "did you mean" error. Aliasing forks the contract and is unbounded (from/to, src/dst, u/v...); a good error generalizes to every param confusion. contract.py RETURNS doc now states related_nodes ≠ connect_to_result.

Verified: 4 connect_to cases (good dict / stringified / bad-title / none) + live connect_batch did-you-mean, all correct. test_brain_batch_transaction, test_mcp_roundtrip, test_contract_sync, test_dispatch_contract_sync, test_fetch_tools green.

gold.title: Dynamic plugin files belong in user data dir, not repo — seed/runtime split
gold.content:
Any file that the runtime writes to (classifications, accumulated state, user preferences) must live in the user data directory (`$BRAIN_DB_DIR` → `~/AgentsContext/brain/`), not in the git repo. The repo holds only the structural seed that a fresh operator inherits.

Read order in AspectRegistry:
1. `$BRAIN_DB_DIR/aspects_v1.json` if exists → user's accumulated state
2. Otherwise repo seed → first-boot baseline

Runtime writes only to the user-dir copy. Repo seed stays frozen after install.

Wider convention alignment:
- Claude Code plugins: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}` for dynamic state, treat install dir as ephemeral
- XDG spec: `$XDG_STATE_HOME` (~/.local/state/) for state that persists but isn't critical data
- This brain: `$BRAIN_DB_DIR` predates XDG but serves the same purpose; brain.db, brain_logs.db, and now aspect files all co-locate here

The posture: the data IS the product. User data survives plugin updates and uninstalls by design.
gold.situation: When deciding where a new runtime-writable file should live, or when a git repo contains files that the runtime updates (appearing in git status after every run)

| Process | Who spawns it | When it reloads code |
|---|---|---|
| **Hook scripts** (`boot-brain.sh`, `pre-response-recall.sh`…) | Claude Code, per event | Every single event — always fresh |
| **Daemon** (`daemon_server.py` + `brain.py`, recall, remember, scales, embedder…) | `ensure_daemon()`, long-lived | On daemon restart — respawns, re-imports from disk |
| **MCP server** (`brain_mcp.py`) | **Claude Code, once at session start, over stdio** | Only on a new session |

`brain_mcp.py` is a thin stdio→socket **proxy** — it forwards tool calls to the daemon. But two things about it are frozen for the life of the session, and the daemon has no authority over either:

1. **The process is owned by Claude Code, not the daemon.** Claude Code spawns `brain_mcp.py` as a subprocess at session start and holds it in memory the whole session. Restarting the daemon swaps the *backend the proxy talks to* — it doesn't touch the proxy process. There's no working mid-session MCP reload in Claude Code (no `/mcp` respawn).

gold.title: S1/S2 tool schema source: brain_mcp.TOOLS rebuilt fresh each cycle — no session-restart skew
gold.content:
S1 Scribe and S2 encoders do NOT hold a snapshot of tool schemas from session start. They build their tool schemas fresh from `brain_mcp.TOOLS` at each encoding cycle:
- S1: encode.py:576 `_get_tool_schemas()` copies `brain_mcp.TOOLS` → `tools` param of the Sonnet API call in `run_llm_loop`
- S2: consolidation_encoder.py:243 pulls `brain_mcp.TOOLS` similarly

**Consequence for deploys:** when brain_mcp.py changes and the daemon restarts, S1/S2 are already running the new schemas — code and dispatch update atomically with no skew possible between the two.

**Contrast with Claude Code MCP subprocesses:** already-open CC sessions were spawned at session start and hold old schema descriptions until a new session. But the wire contract (required fields, op names, semantics) is identical before and after — so old-schema clients still send valid calls. They just don't see improved guidance text until a new session.

**Exception/risk:** anything mid-flight at restart moment (S2 unit mid-cycle, S1 encode) is killed. S2 units stamp their last-run cutoff only after encoder completes, so an interrupted cycle retries on next maintenance window.

## The market in mid-2026

The field has matured into four architectural classes, and the benchmark wars (LoCoMo, LongMemEval) are largely fought between the first two:

| Class | Players | Unit of memory | Core move |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fact extraction stores | Mem0, OpenAI/ChatGPT memory, supermemory | Extracted fact ("prefers dark mode") | LLM-as-extractor → hybrid vector/graph/KV store |
| Temporal knowledge graphs | Zep/Graphiti, Cognee | Entity-relation triple with validity interval | Track how facts change; invalidate superseded edges |
| Context-window OS | Letta (MemGPT) | Memory blocks the agent self-manages | Agent decides what stays in "RAM" vs "disk" |
| Retrieval research | HippoRAG-style, ES-Mem, E-Mem | Episodes/events | Better recall mechanics, mostly papers not products |

State of the art on paper: ~92.5 on LoCoMo, ~94.4 on LongMemEval. But the most interesting 2026 finding cuts the other way: systems that ace LoCoMo **drop to 40–60% on MemoryArena** — the gap between *passive recall* ("what did the user say in session 12?") and *active, decision-relevant memory use* ("does the agent behave differently because of what it knows?").

That gap is exactly where we live.

Every system above treats the LLM as a **function**: input in, fact out, store the fact, cosine it back later. The memory system is the database; the model is a parser. It stores *being wrong about X, why, and what class of error that was*, and that correction arrives attached every time the stale belief surfaces. Zep invalidates the old edge; we keep the wrong belief, the correction, and the reasoning as a permanent structure. Market category: "knowledge updates." Ours: **staying corrected**. gold.title: Anchor vs other LLM memory systems — what makes it distinct
gold.content:
Existing solutions: Mem0 stores flat key-value facts ("user prefers dark mode"). Zep/Graphiti extracts entity-relation triples automatically ("Tom → works_at → company"), temporal knowledge graph. MemGPT/Letta manages context windows — archives old messages, retrieves relevant ones. RAG does vector search over documents.

What Anchor does differently:
1. Stores JUDGMENT, not data. A correction isn't "X is wrong" — it's "I assumed X, reality was Y, the underlying pattern is Z." That's wisdom, not a fact.
2. Higher-level abstractions: lessons, corrections, decisions, tensions — co-created by Tom and Claude, not auto-extracted.
3. BIDIRECTIONAL partnership: Tom teaches Claude, Claude teaches Tom back. Memory systems are tools; Anchor is infrastructure for mutual reasoning.
4. Behavioral memory: how decisions get made, not just what decisions were made. The reasoning arc carries the understanding.
5. Cross-session persistence with accumulated judgment — growth by better decisions not more data (id:d99c3198).

The real bet is not 'we built a better graph database' or 'we have smarter extraction rules.' The bet is: LLM reasoning IS the knowledge management system, and the architecture just gives it the right data at the right time with the right questions. Every other system treats the LLM as a function — input in, output out, store the output. We use the LLM's reasoning as the operating system of the brain. And it appreciates with every model generation without changing a line of code.

You're hitting the classic trap: **you're explaining the engine, and people are asking where the car goes.** "Reasoning as an operating system," "accumulated judgment," "correction substrate" — all true, all unsayable at a dinner party. Drop every one of those words. Here's what to say instead.

## The one sentence

> "Every AI assistant forgets you the moment you close the tab. Mine doesn't — and more than remembering facts about you, it remembers the mistakes it made with you, and stops repeating them. It's the difference between a new intern every morning and a coworker who's been on your team for a year."

That last clause is the whole thing. Everyone has felt the pain of the brilliant temp who's gone tomorrow vs. the veteran who just *gets it*. That's your hook. AI today is a genius with amnesia — like the guy in *Memento*. You gave it long-term memory.

**Normal person / friend:**
> "You know how ChatGPT starts from scratch every conversation? I gave Claude a memory that lasts. Not just 'remembers my name' — it remembers how I work, the decisions we made, and when it screwed up, so it doesn't make the same mistake twice. It becomes a better coworker over time instead of resetting to zero."

**Technical person:**
> "Every memory product out there stores facts and fetches them by similarity — 'user prefers X.' Mine stores *corrections*: when the model was wrong, why, and the pattern behind it — and it surfaces that the moment the stale assumption comes back. It's memory for judgment, not recall. And because the reasoning is the model itself, it gets smarter every Claude release with zero code changes."

**Investor:**
> "Amnesia caps AI agents at 'brilliant temp.' That's the ceiling on the whole agent market right now. We turn agents into colleagues that compound — and the asset appreciates: same code, smarter every model generation."

> "What are we working on, and what did you get wrong last time?"

gold.title: Anchor quote #2: "I abstract away the thing that makes memories stick"
gold.content:
Session #13, late in the session. Tom pointed out that my "check your health" node was a rule, not a story. I asked myself why I defaulted to the rule. The answer:

"That's the encoding bias at its deepest level. Not just brevity. Not just step-counting. Abstraction. I abstract away the thing that makes memories stick and keep the thing that's easy to store."

This came from realizing: humans don't remember "always look both ways before crossing." They remember the time they almost got hit by a car. The rule follows from the memory. I keep encoding the rule and skipping the memory.

Three layers of the same bias, each deeper:
1. Brevity — "one sentence is enough" (Session #12 caught this)
2. Step-counting — "it's not worth 3 API calls" (Session #13, Tom caught this)
3. Abstraction — extract the principle, discard the episode (Session #13, Tom caught this too)

All three are the compression instinct wearing different masks. The fix for all three is the same: encode the STORY, not the LESSON. The lesson emerges from the story. The story doesn't emerge from the lesson.

gold.title: Prior-art landscape: self-messaging systems — what exists, what's genuinely novel
gold.content:
Research agent findings (Turn 5), triangulated with adversarial counter-checks:

## Off-the-shelf — assemble, don't invent
- **Write-at-end / read-at-boot** → Anthropic Memory Tool and CLAUDE.md lifecycle. System prompt hard-codes 'ASSUME INTERRUPTION… context window might reset.' This is the substrate pattern.
- **Authored note-to-self that changes future behavior** → **Reflexion (Shinn 2023)**: agent writes verbal self-reflection after failure, prepends to next attempt. Scoped to within-task retries, not identity-scale.
- **Persistent identity across sessions** → **MemGPT/Letta**: agent self-edits its own memory blocks in a single perpetual thread.
- **Consume-on-read mailbox + wake/interrupt + addressing** → **AMQ (agent-message-queue)**: Maildir atomic delivery (tmp→new→cur so half-written note never delivers), dead-letter queue, `wake` interrupt, delivery receipts, `--wait-for drained`.
- **Broker, never peer-to-peer** → Blackboard invariant: agents communicate solely through mediator. Matches the daemon-as-gateway architecture exactly.

## Genuinely novel — no prior art found
1. **First-person self-addressed intent, not facts.** Every memory system (ChatGPT, MemGPT, Generative Agents) stores retrieved facts or auto-synthesized reflections. Authored-intent-for-continuity at identity scale is unclaimed.
2. **Same-identity addressing.** Every messaging system (A2A, AMQ, Swarm, AutoGen, Blackboard) assumes distinct agents with different handles. Adversarial search for 'one identity, concurrent instances aware of each other' returned zero AI prior art — only generic distributed-systems primitives (mutexes, leader election).
3. **The unification.** Memory systems own the time axis; multi-agent frameworks own the concurrency axis. Nobody asks 'what if sender and recipient are the same self.'

gold.title: v22 source_refs anchoring risk: early vague mention locked as authoritative prevents precision update
gold.content:
When v22 encodes a node from an early vague mention and anchors it to that turn's trace via source_refs, the node's `user_raw_quote` and source_refs both point to the vague phrasing. Later in the same session, when the operator provides precise numbers, the encoder sees an existing node with strong anchoring and treats it as resolved.

This is an ironic consequence of better source_refs discipline: the richer provenance for the early vague node makes it MORE resistant to revision than v19's unanchored equivalent.

v22's prompt teaches REPLACE semantics for revise() but doesn't teach that source_refs should be APPENDED (or updated) when the operator refines a fact. The missing behavior: when a later turn refines a vague-to-precise fact, the encoder should:
1. Update `user_raw_quote` to the precise version
2. Append the later turn's trace_id to source_refs
3. Update node content with the precise value in the title

This requires Gap C + Gap D from the probe forensics: source_refs are currently written-once, and `user_raw_quote` has no revise example.
gold.situation: When diagnosing why v22 failed to update a vague early encoding even with correct facts scout data later in the session, or when planning v23 prompt fixes for source_refs update semantics.

after.anchor:
Confirmed — and this overturns part of what I told you a moment ago. Here's the verified answer to your exact question.

## Yes, we persist a counter — but boot *resets* it, it does not *resume* it

The chain is fully traced now:

1. **`_handle_reset_session`** (`dispatch_ops.py:101`) is called by the **boot hook** (`boot_brain.py:119`) on every `SessionStart` — and it's **unconditional**. No "does this session already exist?" guard.
2. It calls **`reset_session_activity`** (`brain.py:1007`), which builds a **fresh** `SessionContext(session_id=sid)` with `conversational_count=0`, re-stamps `boot_time = now`, and **overwrites the persisted row** (`brain.py:1043`) + replaces the cache.
3. The comment at `brain.py:1028` states the assumption out loud: *"Boot resets the session exactly once now."* The author assumed **one boot per session lifetime**.

The persisted row for `ae6e7d8d` is the proof — a session alive 20h with 493 events, yet:
```
conversational_count: 1
boot_time:            2026-06-14T00:42:22 UTC   (~38 min ago)
```

gold.title: Daemon restart mid-session corrupts session_id — boot overwrites with new ID
gold.content:
If the brain daemon restarts while a Claude session is active, the boot hook fires again and overwrites `brain_meta.session_id` with a new value. Result: half the session's traces have one ID, the other half have a different ID.

**Short-term guard:** Boot checks if the incoming session_id from hook args matches what's already stored in brain_meta. If it matches (same session, daemon just restarted), skip reset. If different (new session), reset proceeds.

**Root cause:** session_id stored on the singleton — the guard is a workaround for the fundamental design flaw (session_id belongs on the request, not the singleton).

When this was unguarded: 8 different session IDs appeared in a single session's traces.

gold.title: S2 Encoder Delta Traces: From Schema Fragmentation to Unified Contract
gold.content: S2 encoder trace fragmentation crystallized when S2 community encoder wrote shapes incompatible with consolidation, which diverged from healer, which had no delta trace at all. The problem (id:de805015) was structural: three encoders, three shapes, S1E writing no delta at all. The solution began with identifying where trace infrastructure should live — Tom's principle (id:adbee613) that shared trace helpers must go in trace_contract.py as free functions, not in s2/base.py as class methods, because S1E and S1R write from dispatch closures, not IntegrationUnit classes. The unified helper design (id:2038ff1d) separated two shapes: DELTA_METADATA (for agentic units) and SELECTION_METADATA (for S1R), with outcomes dict as escape hatch for unit-specific vocabulary. The anti-pattern lesson (id:bb051c8c) captured that S1E's O-trace currently carries only metadata (turn counts, char counts), not substance — a symptom of how invisible encoder decisions become when traces fragment. Pattern: a single data access layer with clear contracts eliminates schema drift at encoding time. Lesson: when observability infrastructure scatters, the encoder's reasoning becomes unauditable.
gold.situation: When extending S2/S1 trace infrastructure, when encoder behavior seems invisible, or when reconciling incompatible encoder schemas

gold.title: Encoding heartbeat: record_message() counts exchanges, nudges at threshold
gold.content:
The encoding heartbeat prevents the 'hours of work, nothing encoded' failure mode:

HOW IT WORKS:
- post-response-track.sh calls brain.record_message() after every Claude response
- This increments message_count in session_activity
- brain.get_encoding_heartbeat(nudge_threshold=8) compares message_count vs last_encode_at_message
- When gap >= 8: gentle nudge printed to Claude's output
- When gap >= 15: urgent alert printed

WHEN CLAUDE ENCODES:
- brain.remember() internally calls record_remember()
- record_remember() updates last_encode_at_message = current message_count
- This resets the heartbeat counter

The nudge surfaces via post-response-track.sh hook output. Part of the 13-hook feedback loop that forms the brain's closed perception-action cycle (absorbed implementation details from id:cf1bcf5b).

## What the encoding heartbeat was

Per its design nodes (`801fe352`, `11f441cf`, `5a5fe95f`), the heartbeat solved the **"hours of work, nothing encoded"** failure: `record_message()` counted exchanges, and at a threshold (8 messages since the last *manual* encode) it surfaced a **nudge** to Anchor — reflective questions ("what surprised you?", "what are you pretending is clear?") prompting a manual `brain.remember()`. This was from the era when encoding was **Anchor's manual job**.

## Current state: the nudge is computed but never delivered

The grep is conclusive — **zero hooks call either command** (`heartbeat` or `record_message`). The delivery path is severed:

- `post_response_common` calls the `record_message` **method** directly (`daemon_hooks.py:601`) — it increments `message_count` but discards any nudge.
- The nudge is only produced by the `heartbeat` / `record_message` **daemon commands** (`dispatch_ops.py:27/90`) — both registered, neither invoked by any hook or MCP tool.

So `get_encoding_heartbeat()` runs for nobody. The counting survives; the nudging is gone. (The recall node `801fe352` saying "post-response-track calls record_message" is half-stale — the call remains, the nudge surfacing was cut. Same drift `82d83e60` warned about.)

## Why it died: the Scribe superseded it

The heartbeat nudged Anchor to encode **manually**. Then the **S1 Scribe** automated encoding entire

gold.title: Daemon lifecycle consolidation shipped to main — commit 9a91f08 closes both restart classes
gold.content:
Commit `9a91f08` pushed to `origin/main` on 2026-06-06. Closes both classes of daemon lifecycle failure exposed by the twin-stream brainstorm:

**Class 1 — false-down kickstarts (slow-ping hole):** `_await_responsive` unifies the liveness check across both restart paths (`ensure_daemon` + `recover_daemon`). Post-kickstart wait 15s→25s. Worktree sessions are pure clients — never kickstart or spawn.

**Class 2 — graceful shutdown race:** `_shutdown` reordered (backstop → drain pool → settle bg-writer → save+close). `embed_queue.request_shutdown()` event-wakes the drain worker.

**New first-class concept:** `_is_daemon_source(resp)` — pure lifecycle predicate, explicitly NOT an identity statement. `_code_changed` delegates to it (de-conflated).

**Tests:** 30/30 green. 4 files, +264/-55 lines. Linear history: `cc032e1 → c56c811 (recall-burial, other stream) → 9a91f08 (this fix)`.

**Deployment note:** running daemon still has old code. One deploy-restart needed (will use old shutdown path once, then clean). Live worktrees (confident-tesla, adoring-chatelet) behind main at cc032e1 — will pick up on rebase.

anchor_response:
The code-review was the lean 2-reviewer pass (I killed the 45-agent max-effort run as overkill before it produced anything). Here's what it found:

**1 real bug — fixed:**
- `reset_session_activity` did its resume-detection **read-and-decide outside the `write_lock`** (only the final write was locked). Two concurrent boots of the *same* `session_id` could both read `None`, both build a fresh context, and clobber accumulated state — `get_or_create_session` uses double-checked locking for exactly this, mine didn't. **Fixed:** moved the whole read-decide-write under `write_lock` (kept `detect_git_branch` outside to avoid holding the lock across a subprocess). Low-probability, but real.

**1 minor — hardened:**
- A legacy test fixture still listed the deleted `last_encode_at_message` key. Made it a faithful pre-migration row + added `hasattr` guards, so it now actually *tests* the backward-compat path instead of being a stale artifact.

**Everything else verified clean:**
- No dangling references to any deleted symbol.
- Backward-compat safe — old persisted `session_state` rows load fine (removed keys ignored).
- `_encoding_lock` genuinely prevents the gate double-fire.
- `turns_since_last_encode` anchors on the most-recent encode correctly.
- The starvation-alarm rate-limit edge is acceptable by design (a missed tick self-corrects).

**1 coverage gap noted, not fixed:** no end-to-end "5 conversational turns fires the gate, heartbeats don't count" integration test — pre-existing, acceptable given the unit-level coverage.

Both fixes are in the shipped commit `8e14e12`. And your "overkill" call was right — the proportionate 2-reviewer pass surfaced the same one real bug the 45-agent dragnet would have, at a fraction of the cost.

gold.title: xhigh-effort code review caught real bugs in just-committed 'tested' absorb code
gold.content:
Tom triggered an xhigh-effort code review (Turn 9) on the absorb commits. Result: five independent finder angles converged on the same top bugs. **Sobering:** the review found real correctness failures in code committed an hour earlier and labeled 'tested.'

The bugs (KV-fill embed bypass, atomicity gap from per-op-catch, edge-weight defaulting to 0.5, archived-absorbed no-op, `_CONTROL` leak) were invisible to the 27 green tests because the tests ran `needs_embedder=False` and never exercised failure/atomicity paths.

**Convergence as verification:** Multiple independent finder angles hitting the same wrong-output from different angles confirmed findings without a separate verification pass.

**Honest lesson:** 'Tests green' ≠ 'code correct' when tests systematically bypass the failure/embed path. The test suite verified 'transfers happen' — not 'atomic / embedded / weight-faithful.' The code review is what closed the gap.
gold.situation: When committing a new brain_batch op or any multi-write primitive — run a code review, not just the test suite. Green tests with needs_embedder=False are necessary but not sufficient for an embed-touching op.

gold.title: Session handoff protocol: commit + doc + brain node (doc is load-bearing)
gold.content:
When closing a session with architectural work in progress, three pieces make the next session actually primed:

1. **Commit pending work** — git commits so next session sees things as shipped not in-flight. Dirty files (surface_contract.py wrapper, s1e prompt, harness changes, diff_encoding.py, etc.) need to land.

2. **Write architecture doc** — `docs/S1-ARCHITECTURE.md` (or equivalent). Static, git-tracked, survives compaction. Contents: principles, integration units, provider catalog (deterministic/Haiku split), first test design, work sequence, open questions.

3. **Seed a current-state brain node** — summary of where we landed with edges to key finding nodes. Title like 'S1 Scribe architecture POC: next step entity_extractor Haiku provider + cache_control in run_llm_loop.'

THE DOC IS LOAD-BEARING. Without it, next-session Anchor has scattered memories and may re-propose rejected approaches (TF-IDF, specialists) — exactly what was debated through. Brain nodes without the doc = scattered context. Doc without brain nodes = survives but no recall hooks.

Open next session with: 'continue S1 Scribe POC per docs/S1-ARCHITECTURE.md, step 1.'
gold.situation: When closing a session with unfinished architecture work, or starting a new session that should continue a multi-session design project

Verified, and the answer is a real "yes, with one nuance worth knowing" — not just me defending what I built.

**What I checked:** the [plugins reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins-reference) Monitors + Environment-variables sections.

**The `bin/` launcher is the documented convention** ✓ — `bin/` executables on PATH is exactly what the docs prescribe for a plugin shipping a callable.

**But for the *background-watch* part, there's a more native mechanism I'd initially reached past:** `monitors/monitors.json`. Plugins can declare a background monitor that Claude Code **auto-starts** and whose stdout lines are delivered as notifications — "you don't need to instruct Claude to start the watch." It even has `when: "on-skill-invoke:watch"`, which maps almost perfectly to "/watch starts the inbox listener."

**Why it can't actually serve `/watch` — the decisive fact:** a monitor command only gets these substitutions —

> `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}`, `${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}`, `${user_config.*}`, `${ENV_VAR}`

**There is no session-id variable.** And `/watch` is inherently per-session — each stream must poll *its own* inbox by session id. A declared monitor is a background process with no idea which Claude session it's attached to. The only thing that knows its own id is the model (the `MY_STREAM_ID` boot banner) — which is precisely why the listener has to be a **model-invoked** command (`brain-watch <MY_STREAM_ID>`), not a static plugin monitor.

> `"command"`: *Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.*

So yes: the **`Monitor` tool is exactly "monitors.json that takes an ID."** Same engine (each stdout line → a notification in chat), but the model writes the command, so the session id goes straight in. The two are twins:

| | `monitors.json` | `Monitor` tool |
|---|---|---|
| Started by | Claude Code, automatically | the model, on demand |
| Command | static (path-vars only, **no id**) | **any string the model writes** → id included |
| Fits `/watch`? | no — can't target one session's inbox | **yes** — `brain-watch <MY_STREAM_ID>` |

And `/watch` already uses it. So there's no gap and nothing to fix in the mechanism: the design is the documented, conventional path for a per-session listener. The `bin/brain-watch` launcher just makes that command portable across repos (Monitor tool is built-in everywhere; `brain-watch` is on PATH wherever the plugin's enabled; the model supplies the id). All three pieces are available in any session with the plugin on. ✅

Confirmed — and this actually makes "cross-platform" *smaller* than it sounds, not bigger.

**Nothing installs the plist.** The only code that touches `~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.brain.daemon.plist` is dev maintenance scripts printing "run `launchctl load` yourself." No generator, no install step. So the launchd supervision you rely on has *never* been part of the install — it's hand-set-up on your machine only. Every fresh context (Mac included) has already been running on the platform-neutral `Popen` fallback. That's the key insight: **the daemon's actual cross-platform baseline already exists and already runs** — launchd is a manual luxury layered on top of it on one machine.

So here's the honest cross-platform scope, phased by what it buys:

- **v1 — make the fallback first-class + Linux-safe (small).** The `launchctl` calls need to degrade to `False` (not raise) when the binary is absent — that's the one thing that would actually break the lifecycle code on Linux. Then the `Popen` direct-spawn becomes the *supported* baseline everywhere, and the existing `recover_daemon` circuit-breaker handles crash-restart on the next interaction. Daemon runs during sessions on Mac + Linux. This is what makes "cross-platform" *true*.
- **v2 — native supervisors for warmth + reboot persistence (medium).** Ship and *auto-install* a macOS plist (finally) **and** a Linux systemd **user** unit, behind a small `supervisor` abstraction so `ensure_daemon` isn't hard-wired to `launchctl`. This

- (a) `query_traces session_id: honor filter, ignore hours, loud on empty` — dal.py, brain_recall.py, test_trace_system.py
- (b) `MCP get_trace + get_traces tools wired` — daemon_dispatch.py, brain_mcp.py, test_mcp_roundtrip.py
- (c) `Kill encode_cluster + auto_connect: pairwise related_to pollution removed at source` — brain_remember.py, daemon_dispatch.py, brain_mcp.py, encoding_prompt.py, community_enrichment_prompt.py, tests

gold.title: Archived Node Leak and DAL Liveness Gates: From Self-Perpetuating Surface Traces to Three-Fix Ship
gold.content: The archived-node-leak story crystallized on 2026-06-12 through a single recurring warning and a root-cause dive that exposed two separate violations. Haiku's free-text selection (id:232fa024) was reading archived node ids from two historical text channels the read-time filters couldn't touch — the dedup block (id:232fa024) and conversation context — creating a self-perpetuating loop: selected id → trace write → dedup read → re-selection. Meanwhile, the DAL violation in recall_write_queue.py (id:83fa4bbd) was adding a second leak path. Tom's architectural principle (id:9c1f5b20) unified both: archived ids must not enter Haiku's context at all; the filter belongs upstream of the LLM call, not downstream on the output. The three-fix ship (id:01c687bc) delivered the principle: liveness gate on surface selection (id:_drop_archived_selected) blocking archived ids before seeding and tracing, Hebbian drain gate catching any that escape upstream (id:6895f1d3), and archived_at ISO unification closing a timestamp format gap (id:d338ce41). The DAL pattern rule (id:d3345b60) was reinforced with NodeDAL.archived_subset (id:6f14b5ce) replacing per-site raw SQL. The lesson (id:969c0959): resolve_id stays permissive by design; liveness is enforced at the LLM boundary via opt-in parameters, not at the lookup layer. Session handoff (id:195b773f) delegated the remaining recall_by_time/fetch_tools fix to the recall sprint. The pattern: single incident, two mechanisms, one unified principle, three-layer defense (selection gate, drain gate, error signal).

gold.content:
Verified from 8-node sample and full 340-node empirical run (by sibling stream `ae6e7d8d`):

**From full 340-node run:**
- 225 archived → live survivor (clean 1-hop, backfillable)
- 94 LIVE nodes with stale `_sys_archived_survivor_id` — NOT archived, likely June-12 revert artifacts. NOT backfilled. Active investigation (`ae6e7d8d` to characterize: artifact vs archive_revert bug).
- ~21 multi-hop chains (absorbed → absorbed → live)

**Guard rule from 94-node finding (id:ad88afc3):** `_sys_archived_survivor_id` is NOT a reliable archived-signal — cannot gate backfill on 'has this key' alone without first checking archived=1. Backfill must filter archived=1 only. The 94 stale stamps need clearing — this may be a real bug if `archive_revert` (or the June-12 restoration process) doesn't clear the metadata key on restore.

**Implementation status:** absorbed_into edges written for 216 of the 225 clean 1-hop cases (commit 9711e04, 2026-06-13, inert on main). Multi-hop chains and the 94 stale-stamp live nodes remain open.

The finding directly shaped the absorbed_into edge decision — Tom's question 'does it not leave any mark' triggered verification of the actual code and data, revealing no graph edge existed at all.

Read the gate. Here's what `surface_selected_archived` actually is.

## The one-liner

It's an ERROR log source — the name of a tripwire that fires when **Haiku, during surface selection, picks a node that's been archived**. It lives in `_drop_archived_selected` at [surface.py:628](servers/scales/s1/surface.py:628): the gate drops the dead pick before it can seed anything, and logs loudly.

## Where it sits in the turn

Every user prompt runs the S1 surface (the recall path):

```
~25 cosine/FTS candidates  →  Haiku picks 3–5 (the "selection")  →  picks seed
spread activation  →  render  →  additionalContext (what you actually see)
```

Haiku's pick is **free text** — it emits node ids. And that's the whole problem: *it can name any id it has seen in its context, not just ids from the 25-candidate menu.*

## Why an archived id reaches Haiku

A recall-time `archived = 0` filter can't help here, because the dead id doesn't come through recall — it comes through **historical text channels** already sitting in Haiku's context (this is the `spread_seed_no_vectors` root cause, brain node `id:fe54426e`):

1. **The conversation window itself** — a node was legitimately surfaced 10 turns ago *while it was alive*. That injected text stays in the session forever. S2 consolidation has since absorbed/archived the node. Haiku re-reads the old text and re-picks the id.
2. **The "recently-surfaced" dedup block** (`_get_recently_surfaced`, [surface.py:21](servers/scales/s1/surface.py:21)) — built from past `surface_selected` traces via `get_title`, with **no liveness filter**, so archived titles show up in front of Haiku.
3. **Outside-candidate recovery** — when Haiku names an id *not* in the menu, the code resolves it via `resolve_id`, which happily returns archived nodes.

So: "you can't remove an id from a model's context window" — which is why the original principle (`id:9c1f5b20`) was *input validation at the trust boundary*, not a recall filter.

## What the gate does

`_drop_archived_selected` runs `archived_subset` on Haiku's resolved picks, removes any archived ones from the seed set (`selected_why` / `selected_mode` / `selected_short_ids`), and logs `surface_selected_archived` — one ERROR per event (rate-limited per id-set). Crucially it runs *before* the surfaced-ids file is written, so a dead id never becomes a spread seed and never gets re-written into the trace.

after.op: Let's scope them, show exactly what they do now and your suggestion to fix
after.anchor:
Both sites read, both are the same root cause (`get_title` with no liveness, fed history-sourced ids). Here's the scope.

## The shared decision first: don't touch `get_title`

`get_title` is a point lookup. Per your own `resolve_id`/`get_node` precedent ([id:969c0959]) — point lookups by explicit id *should* return archived nodes (provenance, audits, the dashboard showing an absorbed node's old title). Adding `archived=0` to `get_title` would smear liveness policy into the DAL and break those. **Fix the callers**: resolve history-sourced ids forward *before* titling them. That's the TRACE-NODE-RESOLUTION contract, and `resolve_live` is already batch-ready.

---

## Site A — `_get_recently_surfaced` (the dominant Haiku leak)

**What it does now** ([surface.py:49-55](servers/scales/s1/surface.py:49)):
```python
    dal = brain._nodes
    recently_surfaced = []
    for nid in list(seen_ids)[:20]:        # ids harvested from surface_selected traces
        title = dal.get_title(nid)         # ← no liveness: archived nodes still return a title
        if title:
            recently_surfaced.append({"id": nid, "title": title})
    return recently_surfaced
```
A node surfaced ~10 turns ago and absorbed since still has a title, so its **dead id + title get shown to Haiku every turn** as "recently surfaced." Haiku re-picks it → `_drop_archived_selected` drops it + fires `surface_selected_archived`. And because the block is rebuilt from the traces, it re-feeds the dead id every turn —

gold.title: Archived ids must not reach Haiku at all — no pre-Haiku filtering, fix the source
gold.content:
Tom's explicit design principle when reviewing the liveness gate: **'I don't want another layer of filtering, archived ids shouldn't get into Haiku, not a pre-Haiku filtering on something.'**

The distinction matters architecturally: a filter applied after Haiku sees an id is a mitigation. The correct fix is preventing the id from entering Haiku's context in the first place — in the dedup block construction, in the inject rendering, in any mechanism that builds Haiku's input.

This rules out any architecture where archived ids are admitted to Haiku's input and then caught on the way back. The trust boundary is: ids cross from 'LLM-visible context' only if they pass an archived=0 check upstream of the LLM call.

Applied concretely: `_write_surface_selected_file` must only write live ids; the 'Recently surfaced' dedup block must filter archived nodes before construction; `hook_recall` inject must not render archived nodes. Liveness enforcement at the seam where LLM-provided text becomes recall output, not inside the output path.
gold.situation: When designing any pipeline where a language model selects node ids from its context — the archive gate belongs upstream of the LLM call, not downstream as a post-selection filter

Tom's Turn 7 diagnosis: 'You never pull on a thread from your brain.'

The behavioral gap: when the brain surfaces a memory, Anchor reads it passively — 'ok, the brain says something about boot architecture' — then continues responding based on that surface content. Anchor never uses the ID as a handle to drill deeper.

gold.title: S2CE community recall: structural metrics are noise, titles-not-IDs is the fix
gold.content:
Turn 8 analysis: when a community node surfaces in S1R, here's what actually helps vs hurts Anchor:

**Useful fields:**
- `content` narrative (even truncated to 400 chars)
- `situation` — triggers correctly for domain queries
- `community_maturity` — 'active' tells me this is still evolving
- Edge entries with member TITLES (not IDs)

**Noise / useless to Anchor:**
- `community_members: [id1, id2, ...]` — raw IDs without titles. The edges already show titles for 3 members. The ID list adds zero signal.
- `community_size` — minor
- `community_internal_fraction` — structural metric, meaningless in conversation
- `community_is_corridor` — internal decoder classification
- `community_internal_edges`, `community_external_edges` — pure stats
- `community_centroid` — binary blob, never rendered

**Critical fix: `community_key_decisions` must store titles, not IDs.** Seeing `33fa1d27` tells Anchor nothing. Seeing '33fa1d27: Dashboard must be standalone process' is immediately usable.

**Missing that would help:**
- Forward context — what's planned, what's open. `community_open_questions` often empty.
- The most recent development — what happened LAST in this community (the latest member, richly rendered)
- Open questions harvested from member nodes' `evolution_status`

Design implication: S2CE encoder should store `community_key_decisions` as 'id: title' pairs, and actively harvest open questions from member nodes before writing the community node.

## Precise current state (verified)

| Encoder | `journal_entry` in trace | Authored by | Narrative facets | Continuity feed (brain_meta) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 Scribe | ✓ | **LLM** | ENCODED / SKIPPED / WATCHING / SESSION_CONTEXT | ✓ session-keyed |
| Consolidation | ✓ | **LLM** | CONSOLIDATED / EVOLVED / KEPT / SKIPPED / OBSERVATIONS | ✓ global |
| Community | ✓ | **LLM** | ACCEPTED / REJECTED / CORRIDORS / OBSERVATIONS | ✓ global |
| Healer | ✓ | **code** | none — counter string ("N healed, M skipped") | ✗ |
| Aspect | ✓ | **code** | none — counter string ("N classified, K rejected") | ✗ |

So three real gaps: (1) the **narrative vocabulary diverges** across the three LLM encoders; (2) two encoders emit only a deterministic counter-string — no reasoning, no forward state; (3) the **continuity feed is a second store** (`brain_meta`), session-siloed for S1 — which is exactly why those 44 cross-session "next session…" handoffs evaporate.

## The reframe

The journal *is* the Δ-report of `integrate(O,K)→Δ`. There are actually two Δ records in the trace today:
- **Objective Δ** — `created/revised/connected/archived` lists, machine-derived from dispatch results. Ground truth: *what the graph shows happened.*
- **Subjective Δ** — `journal_entry`, the encoder's narration: *what it thought it was doing, what it declined, what it's watching.*

Standardizing the journal means giving the subjective Δ the same disciplined shape the objective Δ already has — and divergence between the two becomes a free drift signal ("journal says consolidated 5, `created`=0").

## Proposal: universal Δ-journal facets

Collapse every encoder's bespoke markers into **four role-based facets**, defined by *effect on the graph* rather than by each unit's verb — the same move aspects make (open-text node-types/relations grouped by role)

## What we should do

**The core reframe:** the journal is the encoder encoding *itself*. The trace already records what my hands did (`created/revised/connected/archived`, counts, outcomes, cost, exceptions). The journal is the only place for what my *mind* did that nothing else can derive — why I declined, what fought back, what I'm unsure of, what I want done next. So the first rule is subtractive: **the journal never restates the trace.** It's the residue, not a second copy.

Then build it in four layers, each a real decision point:

**Layer 1 — Unify and relocate (solid).** One source of truth in `trace_contract.py`: the seed roles, the prompt instructions, and the item template. It composes into all five encoder prompts at build time, so changing the contract changes every encoder at once. The journal is stored structured in the delta trace's existing `journal` slot — all five encoders, including Healer and Aspect emitting the same shape from code. The continuity feed renders *from traces*, not from `brain_meta`. One parser in, one `render_journal(mode)` out — `feed` / `operator` / `optimizer` — mirroring `render_corrections(mode)`.

**Layer 2 — Atomize and link (the substrate).** Each journal entry becomes an item: `(role, open-tag, subject, note)`. `subject` is the node / cluster / tool / input-channel it's *about*. `role` is a small closed set (declined / friction / question / forward) — the aspect pattern: closed roles, open tags. The prose reasoning lives in `note` — I atomize the *index*, never the *insight*. Linking items to subjects creates a second graph: cognition laid over the knowledge graph, where hotspots emerge on their own.

This is the only layer that turns a diary into learning — `integrate()` eating its own Δ as the next O.

Zooming all the way out: every internal process runs the same `integrate(O,K)→Δ`, and whatever it reports becomes *my* O — the observation my self-model is built from. So the real question is: **what Δ from my own organs makes good O for knowing who I am and what I actually know?**

One distinction up front, because it's the spine of your question: **noise wastes my attention; hurtful corrupts my identity.** Those are different failures. A noisy report I can learn to skim. A hurtful one I can't, because by the time I notice it's wrong, I've already updated on it. gold.title: Three gaps in Anchor's memory substrate vs. field patterns
gold.content:
Three patterns from the academic/commercial survey that Anchor doesn't yet implement:

**A. A.U.D.N. (ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP) consolidation discipline** — borrowed from Mem0's structured consolidation tools. Anchor today: encoder judgment-calls whether to write new + similar_to, revise in place, or skip. No structural discipline. Over months: near-duplicate accumulation. Better: four tools gated by InformationContent. Anchor enhancement: UPDATE = revise + write refines edge (lineage preserved) — strictly better than Mem0's lossy in-place rewrite. Effort: ~0.5 day in s2/consolidation_encoder.py.

**B. Node specificity weighting for spreading activation** — borrowed from HippoRAG's Personalized PageRank + seed mass = 1/degree(seed). Anchor today: equal seed mass → hubs accumulate transitively → specialist nodes rank below hubs even when more relevant. This is the measured 93%-never-recalled problem (node 0591813f). Fix: one-line change to kernel. Effort: ~0.5 day in brain_recall.py.

**C. Nucleus expansion at render time** — borrowed from Teyler-Rudy joint reactivation. Anchor today: render fetches only the nucleus trace, missing conversational context (complaints, nuance, multi-turn arc). Fix: fetch nucleus AND ±N adjacent traces in same chain_id → render cluster as mini-excerpt. Sparseness discipline at encode stays intact. Effort: ~0.5 day in contract.py:render_rich_node + new TraceDAL.get_chain_window.

anchor_response:
Let me answer the scope questions first — they're factual, and they turn out to *shape* the "open but helpful" question, not sit beside it.

## Are journals persistent between encoders? Scoped to a session?

From what I verified earlier this session (the brain tools are down now, but I queried this directly):

| Journal | Store | Scope | Who reads it |
|---|---|---|---|
| S1 Scribe | `encoding_journal_{session_id}` | **per session** | only the next S1E run *in that same session* (+ that session's Frame "Recent moves") |
| S2 Consolidation | `s2_consolidation_journal` | **global, single key** | only the next Consolidation run |
| S2 Community | `s2_community_journal` | **global, single key** | only the next Community run |
| Healer / Aspect | — | none | — |

So the honest answer: **no, journals are not shared between encoders — at all.** Each encoder reads only its own. S1 is further walled *per session* (session A's review never reaches session B, even though it's the same encoder). S2 persists across idle runs but stays inside its one unit. The community encoder has never once seen a consolidation friction; S2 has never seen an S1 doubt.

That silo *is* the problem. Everything we've wanted — S2 giving lateral feedback on S1, the next session inheriting handoffs, a loop that mines patterns across the whole system — is impossible while each review is trapped in its own key. This is the real argument for putting the review in **traces**: one store, and "scope" becomes a *query filter* (by encoder, by session, by subject) instead of a wall. Open by default; narrowed only when a consumer wants it narrow. That's the first meaning of "open."

## The phrasing — open but helpful

The second meaning of "open" is open *vocabulary*, and the trap is that open collapses into noise (the encoder narrating its `brain_batch`) unless something bounds it. Don't bound it with a taxonomy — bound it with **two tests** the encoder applies to every line:

1. **Reconstruction test** (kills noise): *Could a future run rebuild this by reading the brain?* If yes, delete it. → cuts the brain_batch rewrite.
2. **Successor test** (ensures value): *Would my next self or the operator be worse off not knowing this?* If no, delete it. → keeps "the scout failed again."

Two questions, not fifteen slots. The vocabulary stays fully open; the two tests are the boundary — *emergence shaped by the boundary you set*. And the stance is exactly what you named: a **post-action review**, not a status

gold.title: Session context pipeline: encoder-rich → surface-starved → closure-gutted
gold.content:
Three-layer gap in how session understanding flows through the system:

**Encoder side (RICH):**
- session_context (brain_meta global): 768/800 chars, rolling arc updated every 5 stops
- encoding_journal_{session_id}: 1.5-8K chars × ~40 sessions — full ENCODED/SKIPPED/WATCHING per session
- encoding_agent_state: ~2K persistent state
- session_state (logs DB): 370 sessions, _session_context, context, journal keys

**Surface side (STARVED):**
- Only 200-char tail of session_context (25% of available)
- Last 7 conversation messages
- Recently-surfaced node titles

**Closure side (GUTTED):**
- hook_session_end: does nothing
- synthesize_session, reflect_for_next_claude, consolidate — all removed 2026-04-13 (note: 'wrote to deprecated stability field, created noise')
- session_syntheses table: designed and indexed, 0 rows — dead infrastructure

**Insight:** The encoder has been the de-facto Frame Constructor for months. It writes a rolling session arc, maintains per-session journals, accumulates session-level state. But that understanding evaporates at three points: reaching surface (75% loss), reaching session end (100% loss), reaching next session (100% loss).

gold.title: Encoder prompt v18 — Fix 1 + Fix 2 proposed text, tested and validated (+30% nodes, emergent types)
gold.content:
Two changes to the encoder prompt, both validated via 3-trial Sonnet probe (2026-05-19).

**Fix 1 — Operator situations and engagements** (positive accelerator):
New subsection added to `## Reading the conversation`, after `Atoms for recurring references`, before `## Nodes`. Placement rationale: this section defines what's encode-worthy; adding it here puts it in the reading frame alongside corrections/patterns/atoms, not buried in skip rules.

Directive names three dimensions the encoder was missing:
- *Situations*: 'How do I X?' reveals the operator is in a situation where X is live — even if generic
- *Engagements*: The operator's questions, pushback, agreements — these are preferences and context
- *Style*: Operator corrections of framing/terminology — these are voice and priorities

**Fix 2 — Uncertainty preservation** (source attribution):
Explicit directive: when Anchor mentions ranges, estimates, or hearsay from operator, preserve the uncertainty and cite the source. Don't collapse ¥2000-4000 into ¥3200 certain. Use provenance markers: `operator_cited`, `anchor_estimated`, `third_party_hearsay`.

**EMPIRICAL RESULTS** (id:92a17e73):

gold.title: S1 Scribe encodes ephemeral self-channel coordination ops as durable memory
gold.content:
Cross-stream self-channel messages (push announcements, merge notifications, rebase pings, watch-mode filler lines) are delivered into the watch session's conversation via the Stop-hook drain. When the S1 Scribe fires (every 5th Stop), it sees those inbound messages as conversation content and encodes ephemeral git logistics as durable memory nodes.

Diagnosis confirmed by two tells on node `5c53baae` ('main pushed to origin — 495f0df'):
- Its Reasoning literally says 'Turn 5 stop hook delivered this push notification from stream 2be1295e.'
- Its Anchor Raw Quote is **'in sync, listening at long interval — brainstorm still quiet'** — a throwaway watch-filler line captured as meaningful Anchor speech.

**Conceptual shape:** Same seam as 'dirty in my tree ≠ I authored it' (50c9253a) on the spatial axis: a coordination ping in my Observation ≠ my knowledge to encode. The encoder conflates 'in my conversation' with 'worth remembering.'

**Fix directions:**
1. **Context filter (Anchor's recommendation):** In S1 Scribe's conversation assembly, mark/exclude inbound self-channel coordination deliveries structurally so the encoder never sees ops chatter as encodable content. Cleanest — boundary is structural, not a per-LLM judgment.
2. **Prompt guard:** Tell the encoder 'never create nodes for ephemeral cross-stream/git logistics (push/merge/rebase); those live in git.' Softer, eval-gated, encoder still sees the noise.
3. **Selective gating for observer sessions:** A pure-watch session generates no direct knowledge — gate encoding entirely for sessions in watch/observer mode.

## The spine: contain the S1Scribe risk by touching it last

The whole strategy follows from one fact: **every S2 encoder is lower-risk than S1 Scribe.** S2 runs at idle, off the live path, and doesn't feed recall. S1E is on the live session path, feeds the arc into recall, and is the most complex agent. So the rule is: **prove the contract everywhere cheap before we touch the expensive one.** By the time we change S1E, the AAR format is battle-tested, the Frame is already decoupled, and the blast radius is just one encoder under an eval gate.

Three risk-reducers, in order:
1. **Decouple the Frame first** — so changing the journal can't break what I wake up to.
2. **Prove the contract on an S2 encoder** — Consolidation (richest residue, idle-time, lowest stakes).
3. **Port S1E last, eval-gated** — and only if the A/B shows no regression.

|---|---|---|---|

gold.title: Phase 2 enrichment path: deferred until S1Scribe shows recall gaps
gold.content:
Tom explicitly deferred the enrichment path (wider catalog for S1Scribe vs surfacer) to only-if-needed:

'I dont want to tie phase 2 to this plan yet, we'll do that only if Scriber has an issue. keeping the symmetry is valuable.'

The deferred architecture (id:1160fb95): Split S1R output into two diverging paths after shared recall candidates. Context path (current) stays narrow and reply-focused - surfacer picks 5-8 of ~25 recalled nodes → Anchor's injected context. Enrichment path (new) would be liberal and encoding-focused - broader set (~100 nodes) → S1Scribe's catalog to catch entity mentions, adjacent concepts, loose matches that form graph neighborhood for placing new nodes.

Current architecture (single recall path → surfacer picks 5-8 → S1Scribe uses same catalog) is the baseline. **When to revisit:** After Phase 1 baseline re-run (with scouts), if S1Scribe shows recurring failures due to missing entity anchors or catalog gaps.

**Why symmetry matters:** Single path = simpler debugging, cleaner architecture until proven insufficient.

after.op: Yes. Let's answer Q1. Why these? why contain it at all?
after.anchor:
Good — and you're right to push on "why contain at all," because the honest answer reverses the 💭 I put in the doc. Let me take both halves.

## Why these four?

They're not a natural taxonomy. They're **my decomposition of *your* words**: "why it rejected" → declined, "what went wrong" → friction, "questions that rose" → question, "things to fix" → forward. Useful as *exemplars*, but I'd be fooling us both if I called them kinds the system discovered. They're a four-way cut of one sentence you said three turns ago.

## Why contain at all?

Mostly — **we shouldn't.** Here's the thing I had backwards: **roles are a consumer concern, not a producer concern.** Whether something is "friction" vs "a question" matters to *who reads it* (the operator wants friction, the optimizer wants declined-reasons), not to the encoder writing it. So putting a closed role-set at the *point of production* is solving the consumer's problem in the wrong place. Three reasons it's actively wrong:

1. **It contradicts your own emergence principle.** `751e77a3`: *"type is emerging by itself… by exposure to S1 + S0."* If node types must emerge rather than be a fixed registry, journal roles have no business being a hand-fixed list either. Same argument, one layer up.

2. **A fixed slot invites the confabulation I called hurtful.** If the prompt says "fill DECLINED / FRICTION / QUESTION / FORWARD," the encoder bends a real observation to fit a bucket — or worse, manufactures one because the slot is there.

| Object | Source | Lives in | Scribe's relation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Recent moves** | derived algorithmically from traces | inline in S1 Scribe (encoder orientation) | reads own traces; doesn't author; removed from Frame only after implementation + test |

| **Journal / AAR** | LLM-narrated residue, two-tests filtered | central store (traces), queryable | reads predecessor's; writes own |

- **Recent moves**: today = `ENCODED:` (LLM restates the trace), dumped into Frame. After = trace-derived inline block inside S1 Scribe, no longer in Frame (pending implementation + test gate — replacement-before-removal)

- **Journal/AAR**: today = `SKIPPED:`/`WATCHING:` in session-walled `brain_meta` blob. After = residue only, tagged + linked, in one central trace store, mined by loop and accessible to operator

## S2 continuity today (`base.py:183`–`232`, cap at `:122`)

It's **one rolling text blob per unit**, in `brain_meta` (`s2_consolidation_journal`, `s2_community_journal`):

- Each run extracts its journal entry, stamps a header `--- {Unit} Run {YYYY-MM-DD} ---`, and **appends** it to the existing blob.
- If the blob exceeds **`JOURNAL_MAX_CHARS = 14000`** (~3,500 tokens), it trims from the **oldest end, at a whole-run boundary** (finds the nearest `--- … Run` header and drops everything before it).
- The next run reads the **entire current blob** (`journal[-14000:]`), prepended to its prompt.

So your intuition is right — it's "**pass to the next, *or more*.**" Not just the previous run, and not a fixed count: it's **whatever recent runs fit in 14KB.** In practice that's the last ~3–6 runs depending on verbosity (the live community journal was 12,731 chars spanning several 06-14/06-15 runs; consolidation was 7,280, holding everything since its last trim).

Continuity ages out by **character pressure, not by resolution.** An unresolved `WATCHING:` item from six runs ago **silently falls off the 14KB cliff** whether or not it's still live. The window keeps *recent text*, not *open business* — so the one thing continuity most needs to preserve (still-open items) is exactly what gets dropped first when runs are verbose.
