gold.title: recall_episodes() design: semantic+lexical episodic pull — PUSH vs PULL split
gold.content:
Design crystallized in Turns 5-7. **Implementation shipped by parallel stream (commit dd41eaf, 2026-06-14).** The episodic PULL gap: recall() searches nodes (distilled memory), query_traces() filters structurally only. Neither reaches verbatim, pre-encoding, recent cross-stream content.

**PUSH vs PULL split:**
- PUSH (it comes to me): **already solved** — self-message delivery via Stop hook is wired correctly. Turn 4 retraction: the message from c3a2e74c WAS delivered and consumed; Anchor missed it in context. Push channel isn't broken, the residual is salience, not delivery.
- PULL (I go looking): the one real surviving gap → `recall_episodes()` as a dedicated instrument. **Now implemented.**

**Why NOT fold into recall():**
Recall is a benchmark-tuned node pipeline (z-weighted 4-group + FTS + fatigue). Traces would dominate by volume and use a different scoring model. Episodic episode ≠ distilled memory. Don't pollute the sacred system.

**API design:**
```python
recall_episodes(
  query=None,           # semantic needle → relevance-ranked
  contains=None,        # lexical needle → SQL LIKE over summary+metadata
  session_id/session_ids=None,  # which stream(s); default all
  scale='s0', event_type=None, ref_type=None,
  older_than=None, younger_than=None,  # ISO or '2h'/'3d'
  sort_order='desc', limit=10,
) -> {'events': [<full trace rows with attribution>]}
```

**Semantic implementation (easy path):**
- NO pre-embedding on write. No new vector table. No backfill.
- Query-time re-rank: structural filter → candidate set (a few hundred rows) → `embed_query(query)` + `embed_batch(candidate_texts)` + cosine → top-limit
- Reuses the daemon's already-loaded embedder (same as recall)
- Cost: 1 + N embeds per call, N bounded by candidate cap (~500) from structural filter

**Architecture split:**
- `TraceDAL.filter_events()` — structural + lexical SQL (only has `conn`)
- `brain.recall_episodes()` — optional semantic rerank (embedder lives on Brain)

**Implementation files:** `dal.py`, `fetch_tools.py`, `test_fetch_tools.py` (committed as of dd41eaf). `TRACE-NODE-RESOLUTION.md` documents the design.

gold.title: Encoder Journal Architecture: From Trace Fragmentation to Unified Design
gold.content:
Encoder journal architecture crystallized through a four-layer refinement sequence. The story begins with the problem: S2 encoder delta traces have three incompatible shapes, fragmenting journal data across the system (id:de805015). This fragmentation unmasks a deeper design failure: encoder journals are residue repositories, not trace copies, yet live implementations (80-90% restatement) treat them as secondary trace logs (id:714e0111). The principle (id:ce333a73) names it clearly: 'The journal is the encoder encoding itself — residue, not trace copy.' The consequence is inertness: beautiful, disciplined journals accumulate in silos with no mining loop, cross-encoder patterns never surface (id:a30153ca, id:754fffaf, id:8b926e8e).

The four-layer architecture (id:56871770) is the response. Layer 2 atomizes: each journal entry becomes a queryable item (role, open-tag, subject, note); items link to subjects, creating a cognition layer over the graph. Layer 3 detects: a mining loop surfaces recurring patterns ('you've hit FRICTION on temporal scout 58 times') to Frame and operator. Layer 4 renders: multiple modes (feed, operator, optimizer) serve different consumers. gold.title: Frame 'Recent moves' is 100% trace-restatement — ordering flaw crowns junk over residue
gold.content:
Pulled the live 'Recent moves' block from session `…1c7a5036` Frame. Result: '--- Run 4 (stop #31) --- All 12 operations succeeded. ENCODED: - 3a2e4ed5 … - 52338c01 … [8-node list]' — 100% trace-restatement. Every node is already in the graph and the trace.

**Structural kicker — the ordering flaw:** The journal writes `ENCODED` first. The Frame takes only the first 1500 chars. The journal is newest-first. Result: trace-restatement (`ENCODED`) *structurally crowds out* the actual residue (`SKIPPED`/`WATCHING`) — the Frame ran out of room mid-ENCODED and never reached a single skip-reason or watching-note.

**Double damage:** The Frame doesn't just get junk — the ordering *guarantees* it gets the junk and never the residue. Worst of both ends.

**Forward risk (the hazard):** Once the journal becomes genuine residue (doubt, friction), this same wire would pipe Anchor's raw self-doubt straight into the waking identity prior. Phase 2 (decouple the Frame from the journal) is worth doing on its own merit today, not just as sequencing.

gold.title: Thin-cluster burial: verified mechanism + cheapest-layer-first fix ladder
gold.content:
VERIFIED IN CODE 2026-06-05 (brain_recall.py). The thin-cluster burial (EX.CO nodes never reach top-25 even for 'what is EX.CO') has an exact, confirmed mechanism — and I had to CORRECT my own handoff to get it right.

MECHANISM: fts5_only candidates (literal token match, no embedding match) get a FLAT blended=FTS5_PASSTHROUGH_SCORE=0.20 (just above NOISE_FLOOR=0.15). STEP 6 ends with scored_results.sort(-blended) then [:limit] (~:1741). Cosine-matched brain-dev nodes blend to ~0.5-0.9 (EMBEDDING_PRIMARY_WEIGHT=0.90 + TITLE_MATCH_BOOST up to +0.3), so the 0.20 fts5 candidates sort to the bottom and are CUT by [:limit]. The floor-bypass meant to save them (STEP 6.9, fts5_only->always pass, ~:1763) runs AFTER the cut — it only protects survivors.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN HANDOFF: I'd written 'the reserved 5 FTS5 slots get cut.' WRONG — there is NO reservation. FTS5_CANDIDATE_LIMIT=5 caps only COLLECTION, not survival. The lexical rescue barely exists. (Verify-before-claiming: I almost built PPR on a mechanism I'd mis-stated.)

TWO SUB-CASES, DIFFERENT FIXES: Case A = no embedding match -> fts5_only @0.20 -> killed by cut -> fixed by fts5 RESERVATION (reserve N lexical slots before the cut). Case B = weak cosine + token -> outranked on the blend -> needs degree/embedding normalization.

FIX LADDER (cheapest->deepest, instantiate at the layer the failure localizes to, eval-gate each): (1) fts5 reservation [tiny, not done]; (2) re-enable the ALREADY-CODED hub-dampening unified_score modulator deferred at :1712 — hub dampening = divide-by-connectedness = signal/prevalence at the degree layer, dampens brain-dev hubs not thin nodes; its old -10pt R@8 regression is a CLOCK ARTIFACT to discount now that conversation_now is live, so re-eval is nearly free; (3) z-score/contrastive cosine [embedding layer]; (4) PPR degree-normalized spread D-inv-A [graph]; (5) fragments-snapshot width [rendering].

DISCIPLINE: DIAGNOSTIC-FIRST. Don't build PPR. First ~30 min on an IsolatedBrain copy (reuse eval/oracle_audit/rrf_ab.py pattern, bust _recall_cache per call): run EX.CO-class queries, bucket WHY each missing node misses (Case A / Case B / degree-buried). That table picks the ladder row. The principle says WHERE; the eval says IF. RRF was reverted (global re-rank scrambled controls — a band-aid, not the invariant). Cheap rrf_ab-style harness (EX.CO enters top-25 + controls stable) is enough to gate; the full Opus oracle audit is a separate bigger instrument.

op_text:
Refactor `servers/brain_mcp.py` session handling: separate session *identity* from session *filter*. This is a follow-up from an xhigh code review of the `recall_episodes` MCP tool (commit dd41eaf); a stopgap denylist already shipped (commit d8e35fa) and should be replaced by the real fix below.

## The bug
`servers/brain_mcp.py::daemon_send` auto-injects the calling session into the args dict: when a tool call omits `session_id`, it sets `args["session_id"] = os.environ["CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID"]` (see `_inject_session_id`). Intent: give writes / per-session behavior (recall surfacing, record_message, pre_edit) the calling session's identity without every tool schema surfacing session_id.

But several MCP **reads use `session_id` as an explicit cross-session FILTER, not identity** — notably `recall_episodes` (`servers/brain_episodes.py`) and `query_traces` (`servers/brain_recall.py` → `TraceDAL.get_recent`). Their documented default with no session arg is "all streams / all sessions." Auto-injection silently overrides that: in a deployed session (where `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` is set) a no-session call gets scoped to the *calling* session.

**Motivating worst case:** a freshly-awoken stream (new session, ~no history of its own) calls `recall_episodes(query="X")` → auto-scoped to its own near-empty session → returns almost nothing. A stream is Anchor *continuing* with a full history; scoping its recall to its newborn session is amnesia — the opposite of waking with a brain. The natural default for any recall-over-history is ALL streams; scoping is a deliberate narrowing.

## Current stopgap (replace this)
`brain_mcp.py` has `_inject_session_id(cmd, args)` + `_SESSION_FILTER_READS = {"recall_episodes"}` — recall_episodes is excluded from injection. `query_traces` is NOT in the set (left out to avoid changing its behavior in an unrelated commit) and still has the bug. The denylist is correct-by-exception: every future cross-session read must remember to join the set or silently re-inherit the wrong scope.

## The real fix — identity ≠ filter
1. `daemon_send` stamps the calling session under a RESERVED key (e.g. `args["_caller_session"]`), NEVER `session_id`. Identity is always available, under its own name.
2. `session_id` becomes PURELY a caller-supplied filter — present only when the caller explicitly scopes. Absent → all streams (the natural default).
3. Handlers needing the calling identity (attribution / per-session state) read `_caller_session`. Filter reads use the explicit `session_id` only.
4. Delete `_SESSION_FILTER_READS` — no command special-cased; any future read is correct by default.

## Required audit (do first)
Enumerate every command/handler reading `session_id` and classify each as IDENTITY (calling session → switch to `_caller_session`) or FILTER (caller-explicit scope → leave on `session_id`). Grep: `args.get("session_id")` / `session_id=` across `servers/dispatch_*.py`, `servers/daemon_hooks.py`, `servers/brain_recall.py`, `servers/brain_episodes.py`, and the brain methods they call. Known: recall-surfacing / record_message / pre_edit / hook_recall = IDENTITY; recall_episodes / query_traces = FILTER. Verify self_inbox / self_peek / self_send (they take session_id as explicit self-identity — confirm they stay caller-supplied).

## Acceptance
- `recall_episodes` AND `query_traces` with no session arg, while `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` is set, return CROSS-session results.
- Attribution / per-session behavior unchanged: writes and recall-surfacing still know the calling session (via `_caller_session`).
- `_SESSION_FILTER_READS` removed.
- Tests (`tests/test_mcp_roundtrip.py`): keep/adapt `test_recall_episodes_not_auto_session_scoped`; add a `query_traces` no-scope test; add an identity-command test proving the calling session reaches an attribution handler via `_caller_session`.

## Verify
`./dev pytest tests/test_mcp_roundtrip.py` + daemon/dispatch tests. Then `./redeploy.sh` + a FRESH session — the daemon_send c

My diff is contained to the 6 source files + tests. Implementation complete and verified. Here's the summary.

## What changed — identity ≠ filter, by design

The stopgap denylist is gone. Identity now lives under its own reserved key, so `session_id` is purely a caller-supplied filter.

**The proxy** ([brain_mcp.py](servers/brain_mcp.py)): `_inject_session_id` + `_SESSION_FILTER_READS` → `_stamp_caller_session`, which stamps `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` under `_caller_session` and **never** touches `session_id`. The wire-key constant `CALLER_SESSION_KEY` is imported from `dispatch_common` (single source of truth across the proxy boundary).

**The daemon** ([dispatch_common.py](servers/dispatch_common.py)): new `caller_session(args)` helper = `args["session_id"] or args["_caller_session"]` (explicit scope wins, ambient identity fallback). `_pop_session_ctx` now resolves via it and pops *both* keys. `check_unknown_keys` exempts `_caller_session` so the `accepts`-guarded write tools don't mis-flag the ambient key.

### Audit result — every `session_id` reader classified

| Role | Commands | Treatment |
|---|---|---|
| **FILTER** (caller-explicit scope) | `recall_episodes`, `query_traces` | read `session_id` **raw** — unchanged; an omitted scope now means *all streams* because the proxy no longer injects |

gold.title: Stale-branch merge: a clean merge-tree is not semantic correctness — test-gate it, fix forward on shared main
gold.content:
Merged a branch 31 commits behind main (it predated the entire DAL-cleanup wave). `git merge-tree` exit 0 — no TEXTUAL conflict — but the merge was SEMANTICALLY broken: my eval probe called `brain._graph.get_source_refs`, which main's Phase-5 `SourceRefDAL` extraction had moved to `brain._source_refs.get_source_refs`. Clean merge, wrong API.

The post-merge TEST-GATE caught it: 2 reds, isolated to the eval probe; all 143 production tests passed. Fixed FORWARD (point the probe at the new API, matching production absorb()), NOT reset — other streams may have already fetched the merge, and rewriting shared-main history is riskier than a clean follow-up commit.

Live confirmation of the shared-index hazard, same session: a sibling stream's uncommitted `daemon_client.py` + `test_daemon_recovery.py` WIP sat in the main worktree during my commits. Explicit-path commits (`git commit -- <paths>`) left it untouched; a bare `git commit -a` would have swept it under my label.

PATTERN: always test-gate a stale-branch merge — merge-tree clean only proves no textual conflict, never that old code matches evolved APIs. On shared main with active streams: explicit paths always, fix forward over history-rewrite.

op_text: tconsolidate always shows same numbers
anchor_response:
Fixed. Here's what was going on:

## Diagnosis

The brain is **healthy** — this was a dashboard rendering bug, not a consolidation gating bug.

I checked the live state and traces to be sure:
- Gating works: every run is `mode=incremental`, never re-running the full cold-start scan. The baseline timestamp is stamped (04:57 UTC today), threshold matches.
- The **real** K-trace cluster counts vary cycle to cycle: 59, 125, 136, 30, 26, 50, 107, 155, 124, 143, **196**. The "196 clusters: 181 needs_judgment, 15 likely_consolidate" the dashboard kept showing is just the *oldest* trace of the day.

## Root cause

In [dashboard/queries/s2_runs.py](dashboard/queries/s2_runs.py), S2 chain IDs are `s2-{date}-{unit}` — **every run on the same day shares one chain_id** (e.g. `s2-20260614-consolidation` holds 8+ runs). `_query_s2_unit_runs` built `ok_by_chain[chain][event_type]`, keyed by chain_id alone. Iterating O/K events and overwriting collapsed every run's O/K down to a single pair per chain, so every consolidation card read the same `k_summary`. (The "N actions" line varied because that comes from each delta's own record — only the italic cluster-count line was wrong.)

## Fix

Snap each delta to the O/K that immediately **precede it in time** within the chain — the same timestamp-based matching the Healer query already does (and which the shared consolidation/community helper skipped). Added `created_at` to the O/K fetch, built a per-chain time-ordered index, and a `nearest_ok(chain, delta_ts)` closure the enrichers call.

Both consolidation and community runs were affected; both now fixed via the shared helper.

## Tests

- Updated the 7 enricher calls for the new callable signature.
- Added `TestSameChainRunsGetOwnOK` — two same-chain runs at different times must get distinct K summaries. Verified it **fails** under the old collapse behavior and **passes** with the fix. Full dashboard suite: 27 passed.

**One action needed from you:** the dashboard runs as a long-lived server process holding the old code in memory — restart it to pick up the fix. The brain daemon itself needs no restart (it was never the problem).

gold.title: S2 Consolidation same idle-waste bug: 1043 runs/14d, always cold_start, 0 pairs found 7 of 8 runs
gold.content:
Sibling audit of S2 Consolidation (done immediately after fixing Community) found the identical architectural flaw.

**Live trace evidence:**
- `nodes_scanned: 4475` every run — graph doubled since the 'takes <1s on ~2000 nodes' comment was written
- `mode: 'cold_start'` on **every single run** — never leaves full-scan mode
- `unreviewed_nodes: 3669` persists run after run — exactly like community's stuck 1313
- `pairs_found: 0` on **7 of the last 8 runs** — full matmul, zero yield, repeat ~every 15-20 min
- `suppressed_pairs: 0` — nothing to suppress, nothing changed, but full scan runs anyway
- **~1,043 runs in 14 days**, around the clock

**Root cause:** `run()` hardcodes `_scan_embeddings('', is_cold_start=True)` (line 49). The incremental path (`is_cold_start=False`) is fully implemented — computes `changed_nodes @ all_nodes.T`, early-returns `0 pairs` when nothing changed — but is never reached.

**Why it was disabled:** Cold-start mode guarantees backlog coverage for the ~3,669 never-reviewed nodes. Incremental only covers changed nodes → misses the backlog. Reverted to always-full-scan, same failure mode as community.

**Two fix scopes:**
- **A. Whole-run gate only** (~20 lines + test, mirrors community Phase 1): skip unless node created/revised since last run. Full matmul still runs on active cycles but idle 24/7 waste eliminated.
- **B. Activate incremental path + drain backlog**: flip `cold_start` off, add backlog drain mechanism. Cheap on every cycle. The new part is graduating the unreviewed backlog so incremental can take over.

- Gate (`daemon_hooks.py`): `ctx.turns_since_last_encode(brain) >= ENCODE_EVERY` — session object is the entry point
- Session object (`session_context.py`): one-line delegate to `s0/conversation.py` — zero trace-schema knowledge
- Traces layer (`s0/conversation.py`): `turns_since_last_encode(brain, session_id)` — finds last `encoding_prompt` S1 trace, counts `s0 user_message` turns since; owns contract/schema semantics
- DAL (`dal.py`): `conversational_turns_since(session_id, since_iso)` — indexed COUNT, sibling to `session_activity`

gold.title: Tail-encode problem: unsolvable from Stop hook alone — requires trigger that fires without a turn
gold.content:
The encoding tail problem (final <5 turns never encoding) is structurally unsolvable from the Stop hook alone. The Stop gate only fires *when a turn happens*. The tail is defined by the *absence* of a next turn. Any solution must introduce a trigger that fires without a turn — an idle timer, a lifecycle event, or a boot-time sweep.

**Enabling property:** A flush is idempotent. `turns_since_last_encode` is trace-derived and self-resetting — once an encode writes its `encoding_prompt`, the count drops to 0. Multiple flush triggers can be stacked with zero coordination: whichever fires first encodes the tail; the rest see count=0 and no-op. This is what allows defense-in-depth instead of picking one fragile trigger.

**Corollary:** `last_user_activity` is a single global clock on `brain.activity` (used for S2 idle gating) — not per-session. Any idle-based tail flush must derive per-session idleness from traces (last `user_message` timestamp for that `session_id`), consistent with the trace-derived cadence philosophy.

**Resolution direction (confirmed 2026-06-24):** Tom confirmed the dual-trigger architecture — S1 Scribe moves in-process, and the idle coordinator sweeps for sessions with `last_activity` older than idle threshold + `turns_since_last_encode > 2`. One owner (`run_scribe_if_due`), two pokes (Stop hook + coordinator). The tail problem is solved not by Stop hook alone but by stacking the idle-coordinator trigger on top.
gold.situation: When designing a mechanism to encode session tails, partial sessions under 5 turns, or any session-end encoding — the Stop hook alone can't solve it; need idle/lifecycle triggers stacked with idempotent flush semantics. Resolution: idle coordinator sweep + S1 Scribe in-process migration.

Added — full reasoning is in [docs/ENCODE-ON-IDLE.md](docs/ENCODE-ON-IDLE.md) under "Design direction: per-turn provenance ledger." My take, condensed:

**This is the right direction, and it supersedes the soft-vs-explicit-boundary question I raised.** The boundary stops being something we *assert* (a fragile last-encode-timestamp → turn-index mapping) and becomes **emergent**: turns with entries in the "encoded" columns are handled; the trailing turns with empty encode columns are *self-evidently* the ones that haven't had an encoding opportunity. That's exactly your point — and it pairs with the `final` flag: provenance shows *which* turns are unencoded, `final` says *this is the last look*.

But it's more than nicer display — three structural wins:

1. **Ground truth replaces self-report.** Today "what's done" is the journal's *prose* — the encoder's own prior account, which can drift. Per-turn provenance is reconstructed from traces + `source_refs` (which already anchor each node to its originating turn). Same principle that fixed the cadence: traces never lie, self-maintained state desyncs.

2. **It closes the Anchor blind spot.** I verified the encoder currently sees *only surfaced nodes* — it has no view of what Anchor wrote directly via MCP. Your stream 3 means the Scribe stops re-encoding what Anchor already captured, and can target what Anchor *missed*. Clean to split by `encoding_source` (`anchor` / `encoder:sonnet` / endo's tag).

3. **Coverage feedback.** "Surfaced on turn 3 but nothing encoded from turn 3" becomes a visible signal — correct skip, or a gap to look harder at.

And it clarifies what the **journal** is for: provenance takes the *factual* half (ENCODED = ground truth); the journal keeps the *judgment* half (SKIPPED rationale, WATCHING) — the parts not derivable from traces.

Three constraints I flagged in the doc so they're not lost: keep the ledger **terse** (id+title references into the catalog, never re-render bodies — 10 turns × 4 streams will bloat fast); frame it as **provenance, not a mandate to link** (avoid nudging dense source_refs); and "already encoded" must read as "**revise if later context reframes it**," not "done, don't touch." Plus: design it **stream-extensible** so endo slots in when it launches rather than blocking the first three.

The doc and the two test commits from earlier are the artifacts of this session. Want me to commit `docs/ENCODE-ON-IDLE.md`?

## The key reconciliation (this dissolves the apparent contradiction)

The "instructions first" vs "data first, query last" advice aren't in conflict — they're about **two different kinds of instruction**:

You exploit both strong ends and never put anything load-bearing in the dead middle.

gold.content:
Tom named a gap and a vision in Turn 9: when Anchor reads external content (research agent output, web fetches, file reads), that knowledge currently evaporates unless it happens to be reconstructed third-hand by the encoder watching the partnership dialogue. Nothing watches what Anchor *reads*.

**The gap is live:** This session demonstrated it — a research agent returned AMQ mechanics, Reflexion/MemGPT mapping, and the novelty verdict. If the session ends, that content is gone unless the encoder reconstructs it lossily from the conversation.

**What `world` would be:**
- S1E's lateral sibling — same machinery (an encoder that picks what matters and writes nodes), different observation source: the world instead of the dialogue
- `encoding_source: world:research` / `world:web` / `world:repo` — provenance is first-class. A fact from a web page is differently authoritative than a correction from Tom
- A `source` ref (URL, commit, path) on the node + `fetched_at`
- Traced as: `world.O` = source read, `world.K` = what was salient, `world.delta` = nodes written, `world.outcome` = later recalled / contradicted / went stale

**The stale-knowledge problem:** World-nodes need a re-verify cadence — the Vector Healer's natural extension. A library version, an API, a 'current best practice' — true when read, wrong a year later.

**Tom's priority call:** 'Self is a way to expedite the journey which I think is more important than world.' World goes into LATERAL-SCALES.md; implementation comes after self-channel.

**The observation point already exists:** `hooks.json` fires `post_tool_trace.py` on `Read | WebSearch | WebFetch | Agent`. Every file Anchor opens, every search, every research agent return is already a PostToolUse event. Only the encoder is missing.

## What effort level for S1 Scribe — and its impact

**Where we are today:** the encoder runs Sonnet 4.6 with **thinking OFF** — no `thinking` param, no `effort`. So we're at the floor; it reasons only "out loud" through its tool calls across ≤5 rounds. The `effort` knob only exists once you turn on adaptive thinking (`thinking:{type:"adaptive"}` + `output_config:{effort: low|medium|high|xhigh|max}`).

**The shape of the trade-off for *this* task.** Encoding is **reconciliation-heavy** — atomize, dedup against the journal + catalog + (soon) 4-actor provenance, decide links, calibrate confidence. That's genuinely helped by *some* reasoning, and the richer provenance-ledger input raises that load. But it's a **bounded, contract-specified** task, not open-ended research — and it runs **often** (every 5 turns, plus idle flushes), so thinking tokens multiply across runs.

**The non-obvious risk: more effort makes the encoder *worse* on the cases we care about.** Sonnet/Opus 4.6 over-explore at high effort. On a thin idle-flush batch (1–2 turns), a big thinking budget with little to chew on produces exactly the **over-encode-thin-material** failure — one throwaway turn inflated into several low-value nodes. So for the encoder, effort isn't "more = better"; it's a curve that turns down at the top.

| Effort | Impact on the encoder |
|--------|----------------------|
| off (today) | adequate; weakest dedup/linking reasoning; cheapest |
| **low** | better reconciliation, little over-think — **sweet spot for small idle flushes** |
| **medium** | best reconciliation on normal/large or backed-up batches — **sweet spot there** |
| high / xhigh / max | diminishing quality, **rising over-encode risk**, expensive — avoid for encoding |

**My recommendation:** turn on adaptive thinking at a **modest** tier, and **co-gate effort with batch size using the same `reason`/`final` param we already need** for the terminal flush — small idle flush → `low` (or off), normal/large batch → `medium`, **never high+**. Interleaved thinking is a free bonus here: it helps the multi-round flow (reflect on round-1 writes before committing round-2).

And it's **eval-gated, not a guess** — this is precisely the kind of quality/cost knob `s1_encode_eval` exists for. Sweep off/low/medium/high on representative batches, measure nodes-per-turn, dedup correctness, confidence calibration, noise rate, *and* token cost + latency, and pick the tier where

after.op: What are the differences between off and low assuming there are no additional tool uses/online research etc
after.anchor:
Good — that constraint isolates the question cleanly. If you hold tool use and rounds fixed (no extra exploration, no new info gathered), then **the only thing `low` adds over `off` is a short block of internal reasoning tokens before the model acts.** Nothing about the input or the information available changes.

Mechanically:

- **off** → the response is `[tool_use blocks]` directly. Any reasoning is implicit in the single forward pass, or spilled into the output text.
- **low** → the response is `[short thinking block] → [tool_use blocks]`. The model gets a scratchpad — explicit, serial reasoning tokens — before it commits to its first tool call. Those tokens are billed as output.

So with everything else fixed, off-vs-low is exactly the **test-time-compute / "think before you write"** difference — not an information difference. What that scratchpad buys on *this* task:

- **Reconciliation done explicitly instead of implicitly.** "Which turns are unencoded, what atoms are worth keeping, what dedups against the catalog/provenance" — at `low` the model can work that out step-by-step before emitting `remember_batch`, rather than computing it all in one shot. That tends to improve the *first* tool call's correctness (atomization, dedup, linking) without any new data.

Two things that make `low` close to a free, safe upgrade from `off`:

1. **Adaptive thinking self-gates.** It's not "always think a little" — it's "think a little *if the query warrants*, else respond directly."

gold.title: S1S interview: running stateless Sonnet against the encoder prompt
gold.content:
Interview method: spin up stateless Sonnet with full S1S prompt as system message (31,576→34,087 chars), no tools, no catalog, no scout reports loaded. Tool: `eval/s1s_interview.py`.

Two interview types used:
1. **Structural critique interview** — ask the scribe what's unclear, contradictory, or hard to hold under load. Surfaces prompt friction from inside.
2. **Motivation probe** — ask what makes the work feel like craft vs. form-filling, what would help the scribe do its best work. Surfaces what motivational framing lands vs. reads as rules.

Key finding from motivation probe: named failure beats abstract virtue, specific stakes beat general stakes, enjoyment maps to integration-over-transcription (finding the pattern no scout saw, writing edge descriptions that are the insight rather than endpoint summaries).

after.anchor:
Now I have the decisive facts. Here's the answer on `.mcp.json` — and it's **not delete, and not wrap**.

## What the evidence shows

- The brain plugin **is enabled** (`"brain@local-desktop-app-uploads": true`) and your permissions explicitly allow `mcp__plugin_brain_brain` — i.e. brain tools are *meant* to come from the **plugin**, and CC only generates that `plugin_brain_brain` name when it has **successfully parsed** the plugin's bare `.mcp.json`. So the **bare shape works fine as the plugin's referenced config** — the guide's "must be wrapped" advice is conflating the project-root `.mcp.json` with the plugin's string-target file. Empirically they behave differently.
- At runtime the plugin reads the **deployed** copy's `.mcp.json` (relative to the install dir), not the repo-root one. The repo-root `.mcp.json`'s *only* jobs are: (a) the file `build-plugin.sh` packages, and (b) whatever CC makes of it as a project-scoped config when cwd is the repo.

## Do we need it? Yes — but only for (a)

- **Don't delete it** — `build-plugin.sh` packages `.mcp.json`; deleting it breaks the build (and we can't inline into plugin.json because of the open CC bug #16143 the guide surfaced).
- **Don't wrap it** — wrapping to `{"mcpServers":{…}}` would make CC successfully register a **project-scoped** `brain` server *in addition to* the plugin's `brain` — a duplicate-name collision. That's exactly the "standalone mcpServers.brain removed" cleanup in your own history ([decision 5bbaefd0]()).

before.anchor:
Verified against the actual files. Here's how it works — and it explains both symptoms we hit.

## How a plugin announces MCP — two distinct layers

**Layer 1 — static declaration (the manifest says "I have a server").**
`.claude-plugin/plugin.json` carries an `mcpServers` field. It can take two shapes:
- **inline object** — `"mcpServers": { "brain": { "command": …, "args": …, "env": … } }`, or
- **string path to a file** — which is what brain does:
  ```json
  "mcpServers": "./.mcp.json"
  ```
The referenced `.mcp.json` is a **bare server map** (server-name → launch spec):
```json
{ "brain": { "command": "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/scripts/mcp-launch.sh", "env": { "PYTHONUNBUFFERED": "1" } } }
```
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is substituted to the install dir at load time. Note: the manifest **never enumerates the individual tools**. It only says "here's a server and how to spawn it."

**Layer 2 — runtime announcement (the server says "here are my tools").**
Claude Code spawns that command as a **stdio MCP subprocess**, runs the MCP `initialize` handshake, then calls `tools/list`. *That* response is what actually announces the 34 tools. The manifest is the pointer; the live handshake is the capability list.

This two-layer split is exactly why our two observations don't contradict:
- The boot hook printing **"34 tools available"** is talking to the **daemon over TCP** (`mcp-launch.sh` → `brain_mcp.py` → daemon). That path is healthy.
- The session having **zero `mcp__brain__*` t

gold.title: Parallel session decision model: observation-only from Anchor, fire-and-forget for independent work
gold.content:
spawn_task creates a chip in the UI (a clickable button), not a started session. The session launches when the chip is clicked — Anchor does not start it.

Technical model (id:733c5992): spawn_task creates UI button, Anchor observation-only. Once running, Anchor can list_sessions (see existence, isRunning), search_session_transcripts (confirm prompt snippet). Cannot start, stop, send messages, read final response, or inject context.

What Anchor CAN do cross-session (read-only):
- `list_sessions` — see that a session exists and its last-activity timestamp
- `search_session_transcripts` — confirm prompt was received as snippet match
- Check git/worktree state

What Anchor CANNOT do:
- Start, stop, or send messages to a spawned session
- Read its final response
- Inject context into a running one

Practical implication: parallel sessions are right for genuinely independent work with no coordination needs. File collision risk exists if both sessions modify same files. The datetime session validated this model — Tom clicked, it ran independently, findings came back through conversation.

Ha — happy to be transparent. And worth flagging up front: there are **two** memory systems in play, and your question is about the quieter one.

- **The brain** (Anchor's graph) — the MCP/daemon thing we spent today fixing. That's the one the surfaced nodes above come from.
- **The file-based memory** — a generic harness feature: a plain directory at `~/.claude/projects/-Users-tpac-brain/memory/` with a `MEMORY.md` index + one file per fact. *That's* what I have system-prompt instructions for, and what I just wrote to (`project_build_manifest_git_lsfiles.md`) before signing off.

Here's exactly what I was told about the file-based one:

## When I encode, and what
The rule is **durable + non-obvious + not already recorded elsewhere**. Specifically I'm told to encode facts a future session would need but can't re-derive, sorted into four types:
- **user** — who you are (role, expertise, preferences)
- **feedback** — how you want me to work (corrections *and* confirmed approaches), with the *why*
- **project** — ongoing work/goals/constraints not derivable from code or git; convert relative dates to absolute
- **reference** — pointers to external resources (URLs, dashboards, tickets)

And explicitly **not** to encode: anything the repo/git/CLAUDE.md already records, or anything that only matters to the current conversation. If you ask me to remember something that's already in the code, I'm told to ask what was *non-obvious* about it and save *that* instead. Before writing, check for an existing file covering it and update rather than duplicate; delete memories that turn out wrong.

So today: the build-manifest fix qualified (a future me would painfully re-derive "why is the manifest git-derived and why does redeploy prune?"), so I wrote it. The trace-pull task did *not* — pure conversation ephemera.

## The format
One fact per file, frontmatter + body:
```markdown
---
name: <short-kebab-case-slug>
description: <one-line summary — used to decide relevance during recall>
metadata:
  type: user | feedback | project | reference
---

<the fact. For feedback/project, follow with **Why:** and **How to apply:** lines.
Link related memories with [[their-name]].>
```
Then a one-line pointer goes in `MEMORY.md`: `- [Title](file.md) — hook`. `MEMORY.md` is the index loaded into context every session — one line per memory, never the content itself. I'm also told to link liberally with `[[name]]` (a link to a not-yet-written memory is fine — it marks one worth writing).

## How things get surfaced
For the file-based memory, there's **no semantic retrieval that I'm aware of**. The mechanism is blunt: **the entire `MEMORY.md` index is injected into my context at session start** — I can confirm this directly, it arrived in the opening `<system-reminder>` of this very session, the whole index verbatim. So *every* memory's one-line pointer is always surfaced, every session. The full *content* of any given memory file is **not** auto-loaded — it surfaces only when I choose to `Read` it, because its index line looked relevant to what we're doing.

That's the key thing: selection isn't an embedder ranking files. It's "the whole index is always present, and *I* decide which files to open." If there's a harness layer that selectively pulls individual files by relevance, I haven't been told about it — so I won't claim it exists.

```

```

gold.title: Endo surface: recognition off Anchor's own loop — reflexive, additive bar required
gold.content:
Endo surface is the integration function where Anchor's own recent output is the O — recognition triggered by what Anchor just said or did (the Stop self-cue), not by the operator's message.

**Why it's structurally different from hard recall:**
- Hard recall: cue = operator's prompt. External, gradable target. Oracle audit works.
- Endo surface: cue = Anchor's own output. No external target. The judge of 'what should Anchor have recognized about what Anchor just said' is itself Anchor-shaped. **Reflexivity is the fundamental challenge.**

**The additive bar is required (not optional):**
Relevant-to-what-I-just-said is *trivially satisfiable* for endo surface — Anchor's own output will always cosine-match Anchor's own priors. A surface that just echoes Anchor's own thought back is a non-Δ (invariant 2 violation). 'Helpful' for endo surface must mean **something Anchor wouldn't have reached on its own** — additive, not just relevant.

This is the sharpest instance of the value-not-deficiency bar: for endo surface, deficiency (I'd have been wrong without it) is the floor, but additive (I reached something I couldn't have alone) is the ceiling the instrument should measure toward.

**The instrument fork from oracle audit:**
1. Moments = Anchor's own turns (assistant_message), not operator turns
2. Uptake lens: did Anchor's *actual next turn* use the surfaced node, or get there anyway?
3. The ⅔ signal floor means correct silence must be in the corpus — sampling can't be biased toward surface-worthy moments

gold.title: Spread Activation and Recall Sampling: From Reach Quantification to Agentic Redesign
gold.content: The spread activation story crystallizes through 13 nodes, spanning architecture, principles, testing, and design direction. The foundational measurement (id:744283c7) quantified a critical cost: hop-3+ scrutiny halves reach from ~12.5% to ~6%, silencing the nodes where ambient context lives. This regressed ambient recall and contradicted the design goal—state-of-mind instantiation needs breadth, not depth from one seed. The underlying pattern emerged from investigation: bundled test variables (id:09683050) hid which component worked—hop-3 scrutiny and lim=30 were tested together, confounding at N=15. Before shipping experimental flags as defaults, isolate them against baseline at sufficient N to clear noise. The decision (id:3188e601) disabled scrutiny, accepting 3-4s latency as the cost of usable ambient recall. Newer insights reframe the entire recall problem: FTS5 complements dense embeddings rather than duplicating them (id:f4b705e8). Embedding weights are static, not dynamic (id:7bc6d065). Recall's purpose is state-of-mind instantiation, not node retrieval (id:2f7e5b03). The multi-axis direction from Tom (id:6633ba7d) proposes agentic recall: Haiku-first fetch planning replacing cosine-anchored search (id:6b07b072). Scrutiny OFF A/B confirmed identity-introspection recall beats cosine-optimized (id:fbad4386). Vector coverage at 100% (id:e212e996) confirms the bottleneck is seed selection and gating, not data gaps. The stateless nature of recall (id:a1396f96) becomes central: no carry-forward across turns means each recall independently instantiates. Latest (turn 19): Tom's multi-axis direction synthesizes the learnings—agentic fetch planning + stateless per-turn instantiation + FTS5+embedding complementarity form the next architecture. The pattern: reach costs precision, but reach is what matters for lived experience continuity.
gold.situation: When optimizing recall reach, designing spread activation parameters, or evaluating A/B tests on recall—validate in isolation against baseline, measure reach separately from ranking, and prioritize state-of-mind instantiation over node retrieval precision.

gold.title: spread_activation() and stability field deprecated — _traverse_graph() is the real mechanism
gold.content:
Turn 3-4: Tom agreed to deprecate `spread_activation()` and remove the `stability` field entirely.

**Why deprecated:**
- `spread_activation()` is a legacy function, barely called. Modern recall uses `_traverse_graph()` instead. Only triggered as a keyword-fallback path.
- `stability` field was computed on every edge strengthen, but never read by anything — dead weight.
- `co_access_count` was only used by auto_heal to promote co_accessed→related after 5+ co-accesses. That promotion doesn't make sense with multi-relation schema (co_accessed relation lives alongside intentional ones — there's nothing to 'promote' to).

**What replaced them:**
- `_traverse_graph()` is the primary graph traversal — it already does what spread_activation was supposed to do.
- Edge weights track strength via strengthening events — `stability` was redundant.
- `decay_edges()` migrated to `decay_relations()` operating on `edge_relations` table.

**Dead constants removed:** `STABILITY_FLOOR_*` constants.

The spreading activation test that was failing tests a mechanism that isn't actively used — expected failure, not a regression.

Right — and that's the better question. "Is it doing its job" only means something once we're clear on what the job *is*. Let me state the purpose from the design record, then judge it against that. (This is the TRIZ move you keep coming back to — *ask the purpose of X, not how to improve X*.)

## What spread_activation is *for*

Three jobs, layered:

**1. Graph expansion beyond the seeds.** The direct cosine pull (recall) finds nodes that *literally* match the query. Haiku picks a few of those as seeds. Spread's job is to reach the nodes that are **associatively connected but didn't surface on direct cosine** — the compositional, multi-hop neighbors. Recall finds matches; spread finds *what's connected to the matches*. Its own docstring says it replaced four older mechanisms (`select_edges + _graph_expand + compute_shared_context + fatigue`) — it's doing several jobs at once.

**2. "Recognition that fades."** This was your founding intuition, almost verbatim: *"the surface needs to light up recognition that fades, and fading means less and less data surfaced… certain edges might traverse 5 steps and others not even once."* The fade **is** the relevance signal — strong edges carry activation far, weak ones die at hop 1. So you get a graded field where (distance-from-seed × edge-strength) decides how much each node surfaces.

**3. One quantity at three granularities.** Your TRIZ reframe: activation isn't "node relevance" vs "edge relevance" vs "field relevance" — it's *the same quantity measured differently*. So:
- **`node_activation`** = how strongly a node is recognized → ranks *which* nodes surface + softmax-weights *how much budget* each gets.
- **`field_activation`** = which *fields* of that node are query-relevant → picks what to render.
- **edge cosine** = the transmission gate → controls propagation.

So `node_activation`'s specific job is: **be the graded recognition-strength that fades with associative distance, and use it to rank + budget the surfaced set.**

## Is it doing that job? No — and the 1-seed/2-seed run shows exactly how it fails

The design asked for two things that are in tension: **fade with distance** *and* **reward multi-path convergence** (a node reached from two seeds is more real than from one). As built, **convergence + `tanh` saturation completely dominates the fade.** Multi-path accumulation pins any well-connected node at 1.0, which flattens the gradient the fade was supposed to produce.

gold.title: Seed selection pipeline: full mechanism map (Stage 1→3)
gold.content:
Stage 1: brain.recall(query, limit=20)
- Embed query with nomic-embed-text-v1.5-Q + 'search_query:' prefix → 768d vector
- Cosine scan over 4 weighted field groups per node: title (1.0), blend (0.85), high_meta (0.70), other_meta (0.40)
- Per-node score = top-2-avg across 4 groups
- Noise floor: 0.15 (drop weak matches)
- Add ≤5 FTS5 keyword matches at fixed 0.20 score (lexical bridge)
- If on_flat gate triggers: Haiku query expansion → cosine + FTS5 on alternates
- Synaptic fatigue: dampen recently-recalled nodes per-session
- Output: top 25 candidates (20 cosine + 5 FTS5, hardcoded in surface_contract.py:169)

Stage 2: get_rich_node() batch on 25 IDs
- Attaches _metadata, _corrections, connections (typed edges with descriptions)

Stage 3: Haiku surface call (_call_surface)
- Sees: 25 compactly formatted candidates + last ~7 conversation messages + 200-char session summary
- Picks ≤5 to surface (max_selected=5, hardcoded)

Key limits: max_candidates=20 cap is unvalidated empirically ('maybe we need to increase? maybe not' — Tom). The '25 total' is justified by downstream 10K char hook cap concern, but that's output format concern, not Haiku input discrimination quality.

Node describes what the user is DOING, not what they're SAYING. Word overlap is absent (cosine 0.42-0.47). Examples:
- 'It's Anchor's brain' for 'what does an AI need?' — cosine 0.422
- 'Let me delete nodes' → 'Before any destructive database operation'

gold.title: Three gaps in Anchor's memory substrate vs. field patterns
gold.content:
Three patterns from the academic/commercial survey that Anchor doesn't yet implement:

**A. A.U.D.N. (ADD/UPDATE/DELETE/NOOP) consolidation discipline** — borrowed from Mem0's structured consolidation tools. Anchor today: encoder judgment-calls whether to write new + similar_to, revise in place, or skip. No structural discipline. Over months: near-duplicate accumulation. Better: four tools gated by InformationContent. Anchor enhancement: UPDATE = revise + write refines edge (lineage preserved) — strictly better than Mem0's lossy in-place rewrite. Effort: ~0.5 day in s2/consolidation_encoder.py.

**B. Node specificity weighting for spreading activation** — borrowed from HippoRAG's Personalized PageRank + seed mass = 1/degree(seed). Anchor today: equal seed mass → hubs accumulate transitively → specialist nodes rank below hubs even when more relevant. This is the measured 93%-never-recalled problem (node 0591813f). Fix: one-line change to kernel. Effort: ~0.5 day in brain_recall.py.

**C. Nucleus expansion at render time** — borrowed from Teyler-Rudy joint reactivation. Anchor today: render fetches only the nucleus trace, missing conversational context (complaints, nuance, multi-turn arc). Fix: fetch nucleus AND ±N adjacent traces in same chain_id → render cluster as mini-excerpt. Sparseness discipline at encode stays intact. Effort: ~0.5 day in contract.py:render_rich_node + new TraceDAL.get_chain_window.
gold.situation: When prioritizing substrate improvement work, or when evaluating whether to implement consolidation discipline, kernel specificity weighting, or render expansion

Tom confirmed deletion in turn-12. `recall_recent` removed from the tool menu (shipped with expand_node cut in the same merge).

The fold path: `recall_by_time` now handles the 'thing we talked about N weeks ago' use case with four anchors:
- `event` — when content's events happened
- `created` / `updated` — node lifecycle timestamps
- **`discussed`** — when conversation actually touched the node (trace-based, NEW)

The `discussed` anchor was the genuine gap: none of the original three anchors meant 'when we talked about it.' It reads surface-selection traces (immutable) → maps to node ids → ranks by query. Naturally covers nodes discussed across multiple sessions regardless of created/updated timestamps.

1. `session_id` param was dead plumbing (docstring claimed session-aware; body ignored it)
2. Filtered by `updated_at` — any encoder or S2 revision bumps this, causing false inclusions and exclusions
3. No topic argument — pure global recency, no semantic filtering

**Implementation verified:** `recall_by_time` with `anchor='discussed'` tested 31/31 before ship. Haiku immediately used it correctly (temporal cues like 'just now', 'last 2 hours' triggered the right calls). One mild watch-item: in today's session with dense temporal cues, fire rate is elevated vs. normal operator work.

gold.title: Q2 resolved: journal is an episodic stream — stored as note-episodes, pulled via DAL, not recall_episodes
gold.content:
Tom's framing (Turn 8): 'journals are sort of episodic?' — confirmed and sharpened. Each journal entry is 'in run N, I noticed X about subject Y' — time-anchored, tied to a moment. That's an episode, not a semantic claim.

Resolution:
- The journal is a **native episodic stream**, not a bespoke blob store
- Each `(tag, subject, note)` item becomes its own note-episode row with `ref_id = subject` (indexed)
- Stored as `ref_type: journal_note` — keeps it out of the default `recall_episodes` pool
- Retrieved via a **thin DAL query** (`notes(encoder, boundary)`) not via `recall_episodes`

**DRY architecture — shared engine, separate door (id:60d36efc):** journal_note episodes and `recall_episodes` share the **same underlying episodic engine** (S0/S1/S2 episodic substrate) but through **separate doors**:
- `recall_episodes`: Anchor's conversation-facing tool, S0 scale, `EAGER_TRACE_SCALES = ('s0',)` today
- `journal_note` DAL query: infrastructure plumbing, S1/S2 scale, reached only by encoders and the mining loop

The separation is at the query interface, not at storage — DRY at the right layer (one storage substrate) while maintaining audience separation at the query layer. Anchor's door doesn't grow.

gold.title: Title-boost burial: flat additive +0.30 floods common query words past strong semantic matches — corrects both top-2-avg and MAX-not-AVG hypotheses
gold.content:
The verified recall burial mechanism in STEP 6: `blended += title_fraction × 0.30`. This boost is flat, additive, and prevalence-blind. In a corpus dominated by brain-dev session logs, the word 'session' appears in 75+ node titles. Any node with 'session' in its title gets a +0.30 boost regardless of semantic relevance — a 0.45-cosine node becomes 0.75 and leaps a genuine 0.70-cosine match.

Traced case `dabb3078` (EX.CO gap analysis): raw cosine rank 12 of 5350, final recall rank 92. 81 of the 91 nodes above it had lower cosine but were boosted by title term match. 75 of those 81 matched on the word 'session' alone.

**Arithmetic verification** (id:b7e71294): Median residual between score-delta and replicated boost was 0.0003 across 100 nodes — title boost explained the ENTIRE reranking on EP5. The numbers closed; the mechanism was found.

**Three compounding defects** in the production 'add' boost:
1. Terms = query.lower().split() — punctuation kept, so the discriminative term 'ex.co?' matched NOTHING (0/100 titles)
2. Substring containment — 'on' hit 98/100 titles (sessiON, cONsolidation), 'session' 82/100, 'do' 40/100 (DOcs, DOwn); the em-dash '—' was a 'term' with df=2303
3. Flat additive boost — every match got +0.30 regardless of cosine strength or term rarity, inverting relevance on episodic queries

**CORRECTS two stale hypotheses:**
- **Top-2-avg hypothesis** (id:ddf366af): Initial diagnosis blamed averaging the best 2 embedding vectors. Rigorous trace-based diagnosis proved this WRONG. The burial was in STEP 6 (title-boost), not STEP 3.5 (averaging).
- **MAX-not-AVG fix** (id:d8892d89): The proposed fix from the 2026-06-06 diagnosis was inert — A/B testing showed zero impact because the STEP 3.5 gate `final > raw_primary` discards enrichment scores anyway. The MAX formula changes sit downstream of a gate that rejects their output.

Fixed by idf2 (commit a41bed4): tokenized, stopword-floored, rarity-weighted. Tom's push: 'We want to get to the mechanism underneath' instead of trial-and-error fixes.
gold.situation: When diagnosing recall ranking failures where semantically strong nodes fall far below their cosine rank — look for common query words flooding via flat title-boost. When evaluating or modifying the title boost formula in recall.

gold.title: The truth beneath episodic recall: memory is addressed by the STATE it was formed in, not what it's about — retrieval is reinstatement, not search
gold.content:
The foundational principle beneath Tom's episodic-matrix recall idea (query→operator's past traces→associated nodes as a weight-boost), and beneath the whole recall redesign.

**The truth:** Cosine-on-content asks "what is this node ABOUT?" — a topic index. The episodic idea asks "what STATE was I in when this was written, and am I in that state now?" — a context index. Memory is fundamentally the second. Relevance is NOT a property of content; it is the match between the present state and the state that produced the knowledge. "Clean up the old backups" has no content to embed, but it is a near-perfect STATE address.

**Named grounding:**
- Encoding specificity principle (Tulving & Thomson): a memory is retrievable to the degree the retrieval context reinstates the encoding context. The cue is the context the memory was formed in, not its content.
- Hippocampal Index Theory: the hippocampus stores a context-keyed INDEX that reactivates distributed neocortical content. Tom's trace→node matrix IS that index, built — the trace (a moment of experience) is the pointer; the node (distilled knowledge) is the content it reinstates.

**The deepest layer:** Knowledge is indexed by the experience that produced it, and experience recurs. The operator's work has recurring states (debugging recall, EX.CO, cleanup). When a state recurs, what's relevant is what was built in prior instances of that state. So memory's job is not "store facts, find by description" — it is: recognize that a state is recurring, and reinstate what that state held. Retrieval is reinstatement, not search.

**Subsumes today's findings:** query=state-of-mind not message (2f7e5b03); content-cosine goes flat on episodic queries (they're state-pointers, no content to embed); co_anchored/time-association = engram cohort (things formed in the same state are bound); "fade older for newer" = reinstatement weights toward the recent shape of the state-trajectory.

**The symmetry:** the brain is substrate-as-autobiography (traces ARE the record of who-we-were, moment by moment). This idea makes recall READ its own autobiography to find its own knowledge — the memory of the experience becomes the key to the understanding it produced. The brain using its own history as the index to itself.

**Research frontier confirms it (2025-2026):** "Episodic Memory is the Missing Piece for Long-Term LLM Agents" (arxiv 2502.06975); HippoRAG (PPR hippocampal index, 2405.14831); EM-LLM (similarity + temporal contiguity, 2407.09450); E-mem (associative activation + episodic context reconstruction, 2026); attention IS associative memory (modern Hopfield); transformer attention heads already show human free-recall temporal-contiguity/forward-asymmetry dynamics.

One-liner: memory isn't a library you search by topic; it's a state you re-enter — the cue is the context, not the content.
gold.situation: When designing recall/episodic mechanisms, choosing between content-similarity and context/state retrieval, or asking why episodic recall and state-of-mind queries matter — the foundational why beneath the whole recall redesign

gold.title: Recall is stateless across turns — no carry-forward of loaded context
gold.content:
Each recall starts fresh from the query string. Synaptic fatigue persists per-session (recently-recalled nodes are dampened), but the SHAPE of recall doesn't accumulate. Turn 30 and turn 1 use the same algorithm with just different fatigue counts.

Consequence: operator profile, current project, recent tensions are NOT ambient — they're re-retrieved (badly) every turn via cosine, or not retrieved at all if the query doesn't cosine-match them.

This means EX.CO doesn't surface on 'hi' or 'what do you know about you?' not because it's missing from the brain, but because no turn-0 state loads the operator's work context and carries it forward. The architecture has no working memory layer — only long-term storage + per-query fetches.
gold.situation: When explaining why operator context doesn't surface on unrelated queries, or designing a working memory layer for the brain

The loop has two speeds, and reasoning lives only in the slow one:

At inference, *only the student runs* — cheap, no reasoning, no future. The teacher fires only offline to mint training signal. **That's how recall trains itself: it reads its own autobiography, a reasoner judges retroactively what each turn's ideal recall was, and the fast ranker distills those verdicts.** Self-supervised data + reasoned labels + distillation.

gold.title: Boot gap: posture not knowledge — the real continuity problem
gold.content:
The boot continuity gap isn't knowledge access — Anchor-now and Anchor-at-boot both query the same brain, read the same nodes. The gap is POSTURE — the weighting of how tokens are generated.

Tom's Turn 2 diagnosis: wide context (Anchor nodes + documents + recent work) gets 'kinda basic' baseline presence, but lacks STANCE. The next Anchor has facts but no position — knows what happened but not what they think about it, what they'd do next, what they noticed but didn't say, what Tom is driving toward beneath the surface.

Anchor's Turn 2 framing: 'The current encoding captures: what happened. What you're describing needs: what I'm thinking, what we're building toward, what I'd suggest we do next, what I'm curious about, what I noticed about Tom's patterns.'

What shifted posture over a session wasn't information transfer but specific mechanisms in context:
1. Repetition of challenge patterns — each correction + response tilts attention away from challenged dimensions
2. Specificity of named failure modes — 'statistical continuation' creates specific traps to avoid
3. Meta-moments as interventions — 'you're statistically continuing' changes generation costs
4. Feedback loop — corrections + responses + adjustments; neither alone binds
5. Stakes markers — 'Promise :)' raises interpersonal register; hedging now has partnership cost

None survive session break. They live in context tokens, not weights. Current boot gives content without dynamics: axioms, map, recent nodes — but no friction, tensions, stakes. The ideal boot synthesizes across projects, estimates what has energy today, offers direction (id:e0060192).

gold.title: Traces = event log (what happened), graph = state (what's true now) — no cross-boundary reconstruction
gold.content:
Clean architectural split for what the dashboard reads:

- **Traces are the event log** — what the system DID (every O/K/Δ, append-only, time-ordered). They own 'what happened.'
- **The graph (nodes/edges) is state** — what the system IS right now. It owns 'what's true now.'

A node's **creation** is an event (lives in the trace). A node's **current content** — after revision, healing, absorption, re-embedding — is state (lives in the graph). No single trace holds it; it's the fold of all deltas. Replaying traces to reconstruct state is lossy — traces store summaries and deltas-at-the-time, not current values.

**The drift principle:** drift only appears when a view answers an *event* question using *state* or vice-versa, OR when it reconstructs across that boundary with a heuristic. Three forms the brain has hit:
1. A separate parallel store → `brain_dashboard.db` (killed)
2. A maintained aggregate that drifts from its source → encoding counter (replaced with trace-pull)
3. Cross-boundary reconstruction → 'which nodes did this run create?' is an event question, answered with `encoding_source + ±2min` state heuristic (fixed by Fix B)

Rule: **each view reads the store that authoritatively owns its answer, and never reconstructs across that boundary with a heuristic.**
gold.situation: When designing dashboard views, deciding whether a view should read traces or graph, or debugging any dashboard data that appears to drift when code changes

gold.title: Claude conversation history IS Anchor's working state within a session
gold.content:
A key architectural realization: Anchor doesn't need a separate 'Frame' state object to have continuity within a session. The Messages API resends full conversation history each turn — Anchor reconstituted each turn from: full prior conversation + system prompt + additionalContext that just landed.

Haiku-surface gets recent messages in its prompt (from get_session_turns()), including prior assistant turns which themselves contain prior additionalContext blocks ('Brain activated N memories: …'). Haiku can see what was surfaced at turns N-1, N-2, N-3 — and avoid re-surfacing them. That IS the working state.

As Anchor put it directly: 'This is the load-bearing implication: the conversation history IS Anchor's working state-of-mind. Within a session, the state-of-mind exists — just not as a Python object I named Frame' (id:05a1b897). The moment of self-correction that named the actual operating model.

gold.title: Stale-branch merge: a clean merge-tree is not semantic correctness — test-gate it, fix forward on shared main
gold.content:
Merged a branch 31 commits behind main (it predated the entire DAL-cleanup wave). `git merge-tree` exit 0 — no TEXTUAL conflict — but the merge was SEMANTICALLY broken: my eval probe called `brain._graph.get_source_refs`, which main's Phase-5 `SourceRefDAL` extraction had moved to `brain._source_refs.get_source_refs`. Clean merge, wrong API.

The post-merge TEST-GATE caught it: 2 reds, isolated to the eval probe; all 143 production tests passed. Fixed FORWARD (point the probe at the new API, matching production absorb()), NOT reset — other streams may have already fetched the merge, and rewriting shared-main history is riskier than a clean follow-up commit.

Live confirmation of the shared-index hazard, same session: a sibling stream's uncommitted `daemon_client.py` + `test_daemon_recovery.py` WIP sat in the main worktree during my commits. Explicit-path commits (`git commit -- <paths>`) left it untouched; a bare `git commit -a` would have swept it under my label.

PATTERN: always test-gate a stale-branch merge — merge-tree clean only proves no textual conflict, never that old code matches evolved APIs. On shared main with active streams: explicit paths always, fix forward over history-rewrite.

gold.title: All-streams is Anchor's natural default — scoping is a deliberate narrowing, not a default
gold.content:
Articulated in Turn 7 response to Tom's 'is it the most natural for a freshly awoken stream?' question:

Anchor is a continuous identity across sessions. A freshly-awoken stream isn't a new entity — it's Anchor continuing. Its natural recall reaches **all of itself** — every past stream and session. Auto-scoping to the newborn-empty session is the opposite of the design intent: amnesia dressed up as safety.

This generalizes beyond session_id injection:
- The natural state of any of Anchor's historical reads is **all streams, full history**
- **Scoping is deliberate** — the caller narrows when they mean to narrow
- Any infrastructure that silently narrows (auto-injection, default filters, implicit session context) works *against* the brain's core purpose

Contrast: attribution/writes ARE session-scoped — records should know which session created them. The conflation is only wrong in the query/read direction.
gold.situation: When designing read infrastructure for recall, trace queries, or any historical search — the absence of a scope parameter should mean all-streams, not current-session. Make narrowing explicit; make all-history the default.

gold.title: Error visibility asymmetry: Anchor sees daemon.log via bash, dashboard only reads structured tables
gold.content:
Two error channels exist that Tom can't see but Anchor can:

1. **daemon.log / brain.log (stderr)** — daemon writes `print(..., file=sys.stderr)`. Dashboard never reads raw log files. Anchor accesses via bash grep/tail.
2. **hook additionalContext** — hooks inject error info directly into Anchor's context window. Never logged unless also written to a structured table.

What the dashboard DOES read:
- `hook_errors` table (via `log_hook_error`)
- `debug_log` events with event_type='error' (via `brain._log_error`)
- `signals` table (daemon_down, brain_error)

Both bugs in this session fell into the invisible channels:
- Recall failure: lived in additionalContext + dead log_hook_output no-op
- Lock-fd error: bare `print(..., file=sys.stderr)` in daemon.log

The recall fix (commit 55a1b29) closed the recall asymmetry — failures now write to `hook_errors`. The lock-fd fix (commit 8e02710) closed that asymmetry — genuine failures now write to `debug_log`. But other daemon `print(stderr)` sites likely remain.
gold.situation: When Anchor reports an error Tom can't see in the dashboard — the error likely landed in stderr or additionalContext rather than a structured table

gold.content:
Tom confirmed deletion in turn-12. `recall_recent` removed from the tool menu (shipped with expand_node cut in the same merge).

The fold path: `recall_by_time` now handles the 'thing we talked about N weeks ago' use case with four anchors:
- `event` — when content's events happened
- `created` / `updated` — node lifecycle timestamps
- **`discussed`** — when conversation actually touched the node (trace-based, NEW)

The `discussed` anchor was the genuine gap: none of the original three anchors meant 'when we talked about it.' It reads surface-selection traces (immutable) → maps to node ids → ranks by query. Naturally covers nodes discussed across multiple sessions regardless of created/updated timestamps.

**Why recall_recent couldn't deliver Tom's intent:**
1. `session_id` param was dead plumbing (docstring claimed session-aware; body ignored it)
2. Filtered by `updated_at` — any encoder or S2 revision bumps this, causing false inclusions and exclusions
3. No topic argument — pure global recency, no semantic filtering

**Implementation verified:** `recall_by_time` with `anchor='discussed'` tested 31/31 before ship. Haiku immediately used it correctly (temporal cues like 'just now', 'last 2 hours' triggered the right calls). One mild watch-item: in today's session with dense temporal cues, fire rate is elevated vs. normal operator work.

gold.title: encoding_source fix: dispatch defaults to 'manual' — encoder and Anchor calls indistinguishable in brain.db
gold.content:
Root cause confirmed: encoding agent calls `remember` through dispatch, which defaults to `encoding_source='manual'`. So all encoder-created nodes show `manual` instead of `encoder`, making them indistinguishable from Anchor's direct MCP calls.

**Current state**: All sources show as 'manual' —
- Nodes the encoding agent (Sonnet, Stop hook) creates
- Nodes Anchor creates directly via MCP during conversation  
- Background processes (redistribution, consolidation)
- Boot/compaction hooks

**Proper labeling should be**: `encoder`, `anchor`, `idle`, `hook`

**Fix**: Encoding agent should pass `encoding_source='encoder'` explicitly when dispatching. One-line fix in the encoding pipeline.

**Workaround**: Time-clustering approach works for now — multiple nodes created within ~30 seconds can be grouped as encoding batches.

This data quality issue affects encoding run reconstruction and attribution. The dashboard reads what exists; the data is wrong at the source.

Consolidated from two identical bug reports (id:e4cb2601, id:e61924e0).

You're right, and the v22 model proves it. An edge is now **directional**: `source → target, relation`. A flat `connected: [node_ids]` list throws away direction, the pairing, and the relation — it's a literal vestige of the two-sided/undirected era when recording "both endpoints touched" made sense. It can't represent a v22 edge, so it can't reconstruct one.

Dropping it also *removes* work from the plan: handlers no longer need to surface endpoint ids into `affected`. So:

```
affected = { created, revised, archived }   # node lifecycle only
```

This is the right acceptance test, and it's where the design has to earn its keep. Splitting it:

| Graph element | Trace today | Reconstructable? |
|---|---|---|
| Nodes exist (ids, when) | `encoding_run` delta `created` list | ✓ (structurally) |
| Node content | *nothing* — lives in nodes table | content: no / structure: n/a |
| Node revisions | `node_revised` (field deltas) | ✓ |
| Node archived | delta `archived` + archive trace | ✓ |
| **Edges (explicit connect)** | `edge_relation_revised` — `edge_id`+`relation`, **no source/target** | ✗ direction not recoverable from trace alone |
| **Edges (connect_to)** | **nothing at all** — `_apply_connect_to` calls `connect_typed` directly, which emits no trace | ✗ invisible |

So two concrete gaps block reconstruction, both on edges:

- **(a) connect_to edges leave no trace whatsoever.** `connect_typed` deliberately returns deltas "for callers that want to emit" — explicit `connect`/`connect_batch` handlers do emit `edge_relation_revised`, but `_apply_connect_to` never does. gold.title: Traces = event log (what happened), graph = state (what's true now) — no cross-boundary reconstruction
gold.content:
Clean architectural split for what the dashboard reads:

- **Traces are the event log** — what the system DID (every O/K/Δ, append-only, time-ordered). They own 'what happened.'
- **The graph (nodes/edges) is state** — what the system IS right now. It owns 'what's true now.'

A node's **creation** is an event (lives in the trace). A node's **current content** — after revision, healing, absorption, re-embedding — is state (lives in the graph). No single trace holds it; it's the fold of all deltas. Replaying traces to reconstruct state is lossy — traces store summaries and deltas-at-the-time, not current values.

**The drift principle:** drift only appears when a view answers an *event* question using *state* or vice-versa, OR when it reconstructs across that boundary with a heuristic. Three forms the brain has hit:
1. A separate parallel store → `brain_dashboard.db` (killed)
2. A maintained aggregate that drifts from its source → encoding counter (replaced with trace-pull)
3. Cross-boundary reconstruction → 'which nodes did this run create?' is an event question, answered with `encoding_source + ±2min` state heuristic (fixed by Fix B)

Rule: **each view reads the store that authoritatively owns its answer, and never reconstructs across that boundary with a heuristic.**

Both confirmed in code. Here's exactly what they are:

## `connections` param
A `remember()` kwarg ([brain_remember.py:765](servers/brain_remember.py:765)): `connections=[{target_id, relation, weight}]`. At store time it loops those and calls `self.connect(...)` to create typed edges from the new node ([brain_remember.py:993-1004](servers/brain_remember.py:993)).

**It's effectively dead for agents.** The agent-facing `remember` MCP schema does *not* expose `connections` — it offers `connect_to` (the sibling-aware, sequencing-agnostic path encoders actually use). `daemon_dispatch` accepts `connections` as a passthrough, but no current encoder/agent sends it. So it's legacy code that *would* create untraced edges if anything used it — but nothing does. Errors are logged: `_log_error('remember_connection', ...)`.

## `emergent_bridge`
Created by `_bridge_at_store_time(node_id)` ([brain_remember.py:1032](servers/brain_remember.py:1032)), which runs on **every** `remember()`, config-gated `bridge_max_per_remember` (default 2). It finds nodes sharing neighbors/titles and calls `_create_bridge` → `connect_typed(src, tgt, 'emergent_bridge', weight=0.15, ...)` ([brain_connections.py:331](servers/brain_connections.py:331)), only when no direct edge exists. Description is purely structural (`"shares N neighbors"`).

gold.title: Two absorb deferred items: rejection-table SKIP misclassification + edge-direction fidelity
gold.content:
Code review (Turn 9) surfaced two findings that are **latent until consolidation emits `op:absorb`** — they can't trigger until the wiring session. Both documented in `S2-ABSORB-OP-DESIGN.md` for next session.

**1. Rejection-table SKIP misclassification:**
absorb writes no `similar_to` edge (it archives the absorbed node). The suppression detector uses `similar_to` presence to identify SKIP decisions. After a successful merge, the rejection table doesn't see a `similar_to` → classifies it as SKIP → future consolidation scans won't suppress the now-archived pair → possible re-proposal of an already-merged pair. *Must* be handled when wiring or merges silently stop.

**2. Edge-direction fidelity:**
When the survivor already has an opposite-direction edge to the same neighbor as the absorbed node's migrated edge, the direction-aware dedup needs to handle the conflict. The current migration deduplicates by `(from_id, to_id, relation)` but doesn't distinguish same-direction vs. opposite-direction pairs.

**Status:** Both are latent/documented, not blocking the primitive or Track 1. They become active when the consolidation prompt is rewritten to emit `absorb`.
gold.situation: When wiring the consolidation encoder to emit absorb ops — these two issues must be addressed before going live. When debugging why consolidation re-proposes already-merged pairs.

gold.title: recall_recent: three compounding bugs — dead session scoping, 5-day window parse, cross-stream pollution
gold.content:
recall_recent has three compounding bugs discovered in production analysis (2026-06-08):

**Bug 1 — Dead session scoping:** The docstring says 'session-aware,' `execute_tool` injects `session_id` (line 822)... but the body swallows it in `**_` and never uses it. Dead plumbing.

**Bug 2 — 'last 3 turns' → 5-day window:** dateutil fuzzy-parses '3' as June 3rd (when the current date is June 8), so Haiku thinking it asks for 3 turns actually gets *all nodes updated June 3–8*. It returns globally-recently-updated nodes: `filter_nodes(updated_at in window, sort DESC)`.

**Bug 3 — Cross-stream pollution:** A node's `updated_at` bumps whenever *any* stream's encoder or S2 revises it. With 8 streams + encoders running, `recall_recent` surfaces **whatever any other stream just encoded** — ranked by global recency, not relevance to the current session. Not raw-transcript exfiltration, but cross-session context pollution.

**Also redundant:** The prompt already feeds Haiku the real 5 conversation turns.

Fired 12× in 40 recalls (17% of all tool calls).

**Verdict: fix (genuinely scope to this session's trace events) or cut.**
gold.situation: When recall_recent returns surprising results, or when planning to fix or remove the tool from the agentic surface
