gold.title: S1 encoding panel went blank on long sessions — dashboard shipped full encoder_prompt inline, multi-MB list broke the browser transfer
gold.content:
2026-07-03. Tom: 'I suddenly don't see any S1 encodings — dashboard bug or real bug?' Answer: dashboard bug; encoding was healthy the whole time (runs firing every few turns, e.g. s1e-8309e704-13 at 15:10 in-session).

ROOT CAUSE: /api/encoding-runs (dashboard/queries/encoding.py:query_encoding_runs) embedded each run's FULL encoder_prompt (user_content) inline in the list. A dense session's prompt is ~370KB; at the frontend's limit=50 (live.js loadEncoding) the polled response reached ~2.3MB. The browser dropped the transfer mid-body → BrokenPipeError writing the response (visible in ~/AgentsContext/brain/dashboard.log) → frontend got no .runs → rendered 'No recent encoding runs'. Looked like encoding stopped; only the display broke. Why 'suddenly': THIS long session's runs carry huge contexts, so the top-of-window runs bloated the response past the transfer limit; earlier runs were smaller.

FIX (commit 176953e, main d8ac20d): lazy-load the prompt on card expand, mirroring the consolidation-prompt path and the standing 'lazy-load heavy payloads on expand, never on card render' design (node de3f5525). query_encoding_runs stops reading/sending encoder_prompt; new query_encoding_prompt(chain_id) resolves chain→encoding_prompt O trace→ref_id file→user_content on demand. New /api/encoding-prompt endpoint + api.encodingPrompt + live.js pre inits 'Loading...' with _wirePromptToggle lazy callback. Self-review caught a dead prompt_file var the removal orphaned — removed.

VERIFIED live (dev preview + prod): list 2.3MB→3.9KB at limit=50; 164 cards render; Show Prompt fetches the full 371,789-char prompt on demand; no JS errors; no BrokenPipe post-restart. Prod dashboard restarted (launchctl kickstart -k com.brain.dashboard), PID 87727.

FOLLOW-ON (same session, commit f9c9d04, PID 22591): Two more encoding tab fixes after blank-panel was resolved:
- '0 actions' bug: query_encoding_runs was reading first delta regardless of ref_type; v29 writes multiple deltas per run — fix filters for ref_type='encoding_run' to get the authoritative summary.
- Journal notes (DOUBT/FINDING residue) now render FIRST in card details, per Tom's directive.
- Cache-Control: no-cache added to _serve_static_file so dashboard deploys don't require hard-refresh.

DIAGNOSTIC METHOD that nailed it fast: the data (recent s1e traces exist) + the backend endpoints (curl returns runs) both healthy → isolates to client-side; dashboard.log BrokenPipe on the exact endpoint + payload-size measurement (curl | wc -c) pinned the mechanism. This is the 'is it a dashboard bug or a real bug' triage: check data → check endpoint → check payload/transport.

after.anchor:
Here's what I found — current landscape plus inspiration, mapped to our live-activation goal.

**Where we are:** `3d-force-graph@1.80.0` — three.js/WebGL, but the force layout runs on the *CPU*, it renders at 60fps forever regardless of tab, and it's had WebGL-context flakiness (all in the brain's history). Fine at small scale; strained at our 7k nodes / 33k edges. That strain is *also* why it feels inert — a CPU-bound hairball can't cheaply animate per-node activation.

**Package options, ranked by fit to "watch the brain think":**

1. **cosmos.gl / Cosmograph — the standout.** GPU-accelerated *layout and rendering* entirely in WebGL shaders; just joined the OpenJS Foundation, v3.0 on luma.gl/WebGL2; handles hundreds of thousands to millions of nodes. Two things make it perfect for us: (a) because rendering is shader-based, **per-node activation glow/pulse is nearly free** — you hand the GPU an activation value per node and it animates; that's exactly the live-recall-lighting-up vision, cheap. (b) Its headline use case is literally *"semantic maps built from AI embeddings"* — our knowledge graph. It also fixes the scale + perf + flakiness problems in one move. Trade-off: it's **2D**, and it's a migration off 3d-force-graph.
2. **sigma.js v3 (+ graphology)** — mature 2D WebGL, excellent at thousands of nodes, first-class zoom/level-of-detail, and graphology gives you community detection + layouts out of the box. Best pick if **semantic zoom** (communities → expand to members)

gold.title: Recall funnel refinement plan — written 2026-05-17
gold.content:
Plan doc: `docs/RECALL-FUNNEL-PLAN.md` — the master plan and the wake-up bootstrap for the next session working on recall funnel.

Read the doc top-to-bottom on a cold boot. It has a "First 60 seconds" section (§0) with concrete recall queries, log checks, and health verifications. Then context (§1), current funnel state (§2), goals (§3), hub analysis (§4), specific design items (§5), build order (§6), side threads (§7), open questions (§8), measurement plan (§9), risks (§10).

The recommended single-swing item if you have time for only one: **§5.4 working-thread continuity (response→next-recall loop)** — capture Anchor's response embedding at Stop, blend it 70/30 with user-message embedding on next UserPromptSubmit. Cheap and programmatic. Game-changer for working memory between turns.

Substantive findings from 2026-05-17 diagnosis (full data in doc):

1. **Hub dampening misses recall hubs.** Top-accessed nodes (acc 6000-9000) have degree 0-10, not 30+. Both fatigue formula (K=10/(1+deg/10)) and hub_dampening (threshold=40) assume access ⇒ degree. Empirically false. They escape both dampers.

2. **Fatigue conflates "in 25 cosine pool" with "surfaced to Anchor."** Today `_mark_accessed` fires on every cosine pool member, even nodes Haiku rejects. Should split into cosine_fatigue (diversify suggestion pool) vs surface_fatigue (dampen consumed inject).

3. **Surface-fatigue should reset on encoder fire.** Tom's framing: "dampen to 0 between encode runs cause encode already saw them and Anchor remembers from inject 4 turns ago." Surfaced nodes have ~zero signal value within their 5-turn encode window.

4. **KV space invisible to recognition.** Kernel scores 7 fixed fields. Emergent kv values invisible. Medium-tier fix: FTS5 lexical per kv value.

5. **Working memory missing.** Recall is operator-driven only. Closing the response→next-recall loop bridges the gap between identity-at-boot and working-memory-within-session.

Build order (full justifications in doc):
1. §5.4 working-thread continuity (response→recall loop) — medium effort, highest leverage
2. §5.2 surface-to-zero between encode runs — small
3. §5.1 two-tier fatigue split — medium, substrate for §5.2
4. §5.3 access-aware hub dampening — small-medium
5. §5.5 KV recognition via FTS5 — medium
6. §5.6 render-side tuning (type-aware priorities, sentence-boundary truncation) — small

Side threads (separate work, not part of main plan):
- §7.1 Academic research on diversity-weighted retrieval, GraphRAG, working memory in RAG, centrality penalties. Tom asked for research-without-priming.

gold.title: Recall integration thesis (Tom): all brain capabilities are underutilized recalls — push for MORE in a coherent non-fragile architecture; edges non-negotiable
gold.content:
Tom's reframe after this session's read-side falsifications, and his standing direction. The negatives are of ISOLATED / UNIFORM levers, NOT the signals: every brain capability is an underutilized recall -- edges (typed+described), reasoning, situation, question, episodic, main content, previous turns. Mandate = MORE not less; the gap is we haven't found the COHERENT, NON-FRAGILE architecture that combines them. Edges are non-negotiable.

BIO FRAME: imitate the final RESULT, not the time-mechanism. Bio is time-based spreading activation; we imitate the OUTCOME of its operations on a set -- a node keeps firing (reinforce: extends/grounds/depends_on), a node blocks another (inhibit: corrects/supersedes/contradicts), a node fades/passes-through (transient, routes but doesn't stay). Activation + inhibition + gating, SELECTED BY THE RELATIONSHIP between nodes.

KEY MOVE: the indicator between two nodes is the EDGE (typed), not cosine -- node<->node cosine is anisotropic-flat (0.5-0.7, ~never negative) so it can't signal opposition. So edges return NOT as global PPR diffusion (falsified) but as per-pair OPERATION-SELECTORS within the retrieved set.

GUARDRAILS (this session): single cosine levers <=22%; global PPR smears < cosine; uniform fusion noise-bumps hits; hard-AND annihilates recall; BUT operator-cue multiplicative 3-lane fusion BEAT cosine (26/23 hit@5, 41/28 hit@25) while anchor lost -> the lead is CONDITIONAL/TYPED combination.

ARCHITECTURE: lanes = all cues; FIND = RRF union (wide/recall); RANK = mult-gate + edge-ops (sharpen + inhibit = bio block/fade); conditional by cue-type (router). Build embedder-ready -- the embedder lifts every lane. Full writeup: docs/RECALL-SR-REDESIGN.md S15.
gold.situation: When tempted to conclude 'read-side is exhausted / just fix the embedding' -- Tom's standing direction is MORE not less: the falsifications were of isolated/uniform levers; the untested upside is a coherent typed multi-cue architecture (all cues as lanes, edges as per-pair operation-selectors, conditional/router fusion, RRF-find + mult-rank). Stop testing levers in isolation; test composable conditional parts. Build embedder-ready.

gold.content:
Tom's reaction to the current graph: 'it's mostly not as exciting as I would imagine it considering what it does.' My diagnosis and directions (Turn 9 original + sessions since):

**Why it's flat:** the graph renders a static topology map — nodes force-directed, colored by community, sized by access count. The brain's essence is *dynamic* — recall is activation flowing through the graph — but the visualization shows a still photograph of a living system.

**Direction A — Live activation field (most exciting + most true):** When a recall fires, watch it on the graph — seed nodes light up, activation spreads outward through edges and fades with distance. Now shipped to production as part of the galaxy renderer — live recall bloom wired to `recall:event` bus.

**Direction B — Semantic zoom (fixes 5MB too):** Don't render 7,000 nodes ever. Show ~30 community super-nodes; click to expand members. Not yet built.

**Direction C — Time scrubber:** Play the brain's growth. Not yet built.

**Direction D — Unique galaxy shape (SHIPPED 2026-07-04):** The galaxy IS the unique shape. Spiral galaxy grown from real signals: radius = memory age, 2 arms, community knots, circle size = degree, glow = recall heat, color = memory kind. 7,045 nodes, 31,485 edges, 536 communities. Canvas 2D. Commit `8d65e98` merged as `67f03f9`. The galaxy is one-of-a-kind because each brain's age distribution, community structure, and aspect profile are unique.

Creature/morphological-gene grammar (prior session direction): explored and superseded. The single giant connected component naturally becomes a galaxy, not a creature — imposing creature limbs fights the data topology.

**The reframe:** the graph should be the *visible instantiation of recall*, not a topology map. The galaxy now does both: its geometry is a portrait of accumulated experience (unique per brain), and the bloom animation shows active recall in real time.

Right on both counts, and I can name *why* the current version fails your two tests:

- **Not unique enough** — because the base is always a *ball*, and aspects only add surface bumps. Every Anchor is therefore "sphere-with-some-lumps" at the gross level; only the lumps move. The fundamental silhouette never changes, so they all rhyme.
- **Not relatable** — because it's a cloud of dots. There's nothing to recognize, name, or feel ownership of. You can't look at it and go "that's *mine*."

The fix for both is the same move: **aspects shouldn't decorate a fixed body — they should define the body plan.** Make them morphological *genes*, not surface bumps.

**The pitch — an Anchor is a creature grown from its aspects.** Each aspect, when it carries real mass, expresses a distinct, recognizable morphological *feature*, scaled by that mass:

- `wisdom` → a radiant crown of long rays
- `correction_improvement` → dense ridged spines (a battle-scarred surface)
- `episodic_anchor` → trailing filaments streaming backward (memory tails)
- `temporal_sequence` → a spiral arm
- `dependency_flow` → branching dendritic limbs
- `hierarchical_structure` → stacked tiers
- `contradiction_conflict` → a cleft splitting the form
- `survivor_lineage` → a deep rooted stalk
- `identity_bearing` → a dense luminous core
- `noise` → a faint dust halo
- …one per aspect.

The **combination** of which features are expressed, and how strongly, produces a radically unique silhouette — a wisdom-crowned, correction-ridged, spiral-armed Anchor looks nothing like a rooted, tiered, filament-trailing one. That's the uniqueness (feature combinatorics, not just bump positions). And it's **relatable two ways**: it reads as a living *character* (a totem, a familiar, a specimen), and it's *legible* — you can point and say "that crown is my wisdom, those scars are my corrections." The shape becomes a portrait with personality, and it ages: a young Anchor is a bare seedling, a mature one a full creature.

Two adjacent directions, if the creature-grammar feels like too much:
- **Generative organic surface** (superformula / spherical harmonics): the 16 aspect-masses become 16 shape coefficients → a unique closed *living surface* (think radiolarian / diatom / pollen grain). Biggest raw shape space, gorgeous and organic, but less "readable" than named features.
- **Sigil / constellation**: dominant aspects as a connected figure — a personal crest. Most "that's my mark," least creature-like.

gold.title: Full-suite hang root cause: conn_bg_writer temporal phase blocks mid-batch (fixed commit b0b9c4d)
gold.content:
The full test suite hung indefinitely when run against the live daemon — root cause found and fixed.

**Root cause:** `BrainTestBase` monkeypatches `remember/revise/recall` to drain `embed_queue` synchronously after each call. `brain_batch` sub-ops call those wrapped methods internally, so the drain fires **mid-batch**. The drain's temporal phase opens an independent `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on `conn_bg_writer` — a separate connection that can't get the WAL writer slot while `brain.conn` holds the batch transaction. Same thread, two connections, reentrant `write_lock` → busy-waits the full `busy_timeout` (~30s) per brain_batch sub-op.

**Why test-only:** In production, the bg-writer runs on a separate thread and always sees `in_batch=False` by the time it reaches the temporal phase. In tests, the drain runs synchronously mid-batch on the same thread, so `brain.conn.in_batch=True` when the temporal phase tries `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on `conn_bg_writer`. The asymmetry: `write_lock` is a `TrackedRLock` (reentrant) — the vector phase sails through re-entrantly. But `conn_bg_writer` is an independent SQLite connection that can't share the WAL writer slot. Two connections, same thread, same batch envelope → deadlock (id:0b7fa9ad).

Not an infinite loop — a self-inflicted 30s SQLite stall per brain_batch sub-op, repeated across ~15 test files, compounding an ~8-min suite into hours.

**Fix:** `servers/embed_queue.py` temporal phase now skips `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` when `brain.conn.in_batch`. Commit `b0b9c4d`. Regression test in `test_write_txn_discipline.py` (commit `f60fb12`) — mirrors the existing `commit_unless_batched` pattern.

**Original suspects (wrong):** test_daemon_recovery.py (launchd lifecycle race), test_spread_activation.py (spread activation contention) — both were red herrings.

final = base * (1.0 + recency_boost + emotion_boost + frequency_penalty + confidence_boost)

The current embedding only uses title+content. But the richest retrieval signals live in fields that are completely invisible to semantic search:

- situation: 'When designing hub suppression or access-count-based penalties' — if asked 'how should we handle hub nodes?', this field has the exact answer but can't be found
- user_raw_quote: Tom's exact words are diagnostic cues
- reasoning: WHY a node matters — what a metacognition query should match
- anchor_raw_quote: assistant's key insights

**Confirmed dead code (Turn 9):** `situation_vec` is never passed through the recall pipeline. Nodes HAVE situation embeddings. The pipeline just doesn't use them.

**Empirical evidence showing cost:**
- 'Claude deleted files without asking' — content cosine: 0.358, situation cosine: 0.714 (+0.356)
- 'recalibrate_confidence as S2 integrate' — content cosine: 0.419, situation cosine: 0.801 (+0.382)
- 'Synaptic fatigue mechanism' — content cosine: 0.406, situation cosine: 0.745 (+0.339)
- 'Encode-Decode Symmetry' — content cosine: 0.519, situation cosine: 0.762 (+0.243)

Situation embeddings consistently score 0.15-0.35 HIGHER than content for the right nodes. The situation field describes 'when is this relevant' — directly matching what queries ask.

gold.title: Recency carries zero weight in recall pool — today's nodes ranked #4, #12, #25
gold.content:
Empirical experiment run 2026-05-30: three nodes encoded today (`91752afb`, `212c89c5`, `42ff75e0`) tested against heavily-populated old topic (S2/brain_batch has dozens of April–May nodes).

**Query A — 'where we left off today — the brain_batch invalid op fix' (recency-framed):**
| Rank | Node | Date |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | A2 Fix: brain_batch round-split | 2026-04-25 |
| 2 | Fix encoder multi-round | 2026-04-25 |
| 3 | S2CE encoder mode: tool loop | 2026-04-11 |
| **4** | **Invalid op fix #1 — literally what we did today** | 2026-05-30 |
| ~12 | conceptual ops bug (today) | 2026-05-30 |
| 25 (last) | strict schema (today) | 2026-05-30 |

**Query B — topical 'invalid brain_batch op absorb reject suppression':** today's diagnosis node ranked #3 (rich topical content), but today's fix node didn't make the top-25 at all — crowded out by ~20 April nodes.

**What this proves:**
- Recency carries zero weight. 'Today / where we left off' gave no lift — the literal answer ranked #4 behind three ~6-week-old nodes.
- Old topical mass crowds out recent arc nodes. One node fell out of the pool entirely under the precise query.
- NOT subsumed by Phase-2 Frame-prior. That prior only sways Haiku's choice among the 25; here the right node is either ranked too low or absent. The prior can't fix what never surfaces.

**Caveats:** N=2 queries, one topic — suggestive not definitive. The miss is milder than BRAIN-CHALLENGES originally documented (now 'suboptimal ranking' not 'blind spot' — FTS5/Phase-2 improved things). A real verdict needs the recency-query eval corpus.

Strong direction — the LAF-lane framing is exactly right, and KV+traces is the right substrate. Here's my honest pass over it: three challenges, one reframe, then the enhanced design.

## Challenges

**1. In your brain, project-match carries almost no information — the lane's real power is *inhibition*, not boost.** ~90% of your activity is one repo. A "same-project boost" over a corpus that's 90% `brain` is nearly uniform — and z-scoring will correctly flatten a lane with no variance to ~zero contribution. The lane earns its keep in the *minority* case: when you're in an EX.CO deck session, it should **suppress brain-internals**, and vice versa. So the design target isn't "boost my project" — it's "make out-of-project memory recede when contexts differ." Same math (z-scored match lane), but it changes what we evaluate: the win case is cross-project sessions, which the gold24 corpus has *zero* of (all cues are brain-repo). We'd be shipping a lane our current gold literally cannot measure — we need 5-10 cross-project cues (EX.CO sessions exist in the traces) or we're doing validation theater.

**2. Project must mean *provenance*, not *aboutness* — otherwise determinism is a lie.** Mid-brain-session, you mention an EX.CO campaign; the Scribe encodes it. Deterministic stamping says `project: brain` — which is "wrong" as aboutness but *honest* as provenance ("learned during brain work"). gold.content:
2026-06-27, picking recall back up. Tom's mandate: 'verify the test results manually, we often trust sub agents and some code and once you look you see its garbage.' Applied it to our OWN LAF harness and the doc's §18.18.1 'POST-REVIEW STATE'.

WHAT THE DOC CLAIMED (as DONE): the gate was 'code-reviewed (high effort) and hardened' with 5 specific fixes — α-entmax α≤1→softmax guard; empty-created_at excluded from eligibility; T5 baseline-reproduction a HARD FAIL at ±2pp; T8 von-Restorff DIRECTION via independent neighbour recompute (was tautological); T6 batched SQL + embed once — and 'Gate: 27 pass / 0 warn / 0 FAIL → substrate + operators trustworthy.'

WHAT THE COMMITTED CODE ACTUALLY HAD: NONE of the 5 fixes. Proven three ways — (1) read: T5 was ±4pp `warn=not near` (a soft warn that never gates), T8 was `argmax(dist) > argmin(dist)` (tautologically true) + `std > 1e-6`, no α guard, `'' <= cutoff` still eligible; (2) grep: all 5 markers absent from eval/laf; (3) git: the engine+gate commit 8aaf36b is 15:07, the doc ced7188 is 15:35, and `git log --all --since=2026-06-25 -- eval/laf/` shows NO code commit between them or after, on ANY branch.

THE BITE: running the committed gate printed '27 pass · 0 warn · 0 FAIL' — while T8 certified a FUNCTIONALLY-CONSTANT temporal operator (0% of nodes distinctive, field range [0.0008,0.0024]) as alive. The believability gate had the exact disease it was built to detect (silent-component-death), because its verification check was tautological. A review ran, reported findings, and they were transcribed into the handoff doc as DONE without the edits ever landing.

PATTERN: 'verify the harness, not just the data' must extend one level up — verify the REVIEW of the harness actually landed in committed code. A self-reported 'hardened / N pass 0 fail' believability stamp is itself an unverified claim. Check git log + grep the specific fix markers before trusting it.

FIX THIS SESSION: re-applied all 5 fixes for real + made T8 catch operator degeneracy (WARN when <1% distinctive, independent neighbour recount from created_at). Gate now honestly reports 26 pass · 1 WARN · 0 FAIL.

gold.title: LAF dynamical fusion has its math: modern Hopfield ≡ Amari field — sum operator-experts at logit level, α-entmax sparse separation = the commit rule
gold.content:
Two focused literature reads (2026-06-25, neural-field strand + modern-Hopfield strand) converge: the biological dynamical fusion Tom wants is a KNOWN-GOOD construction (modern Hopfield ≡ transformer attention ≡ Amari neural field), un-applied to a personal memory graph with heterogeneous operators. The math we can borrow:

**THE CORE DESIGN (crystallized):**
```
per node:  score = Σₖ αₖ · simₖ(node, state)   # operator-fields = experts, summed at LOGIT level
field:     a = α-entmax(score)                  # ONE shared sparse separation (stabilizer + commit)
settle:    iterate (graph-spread feeds back) until a stops changing
readout:   nonzero support of a                # data-driven recall-set size, not fixed top-k
```

**Validations:**
1. Divisive normalization = softmax-in-Hopfield = the field stabilizer. Softmax = gradient of log-sum-exp (the convex term whose boundedness causes settling); CANN analog r=U²/(1+k·ΣU²). A log-additive field with shared normalized readout IS a modern Hopfield retrieval.
2. Q4 — heterogeneous operators settle (YES). Sum of energies = PRODUCT OF EXPERTS ("each expert vetoes"). Heterogeneity lives in simₖ (cosine/lexical/graph-dist/temporal = different similarity fns); separation+projection shared. Field analog: I(x)=ΣIᵢ(x); tune inhibition strong→single-winner vs balanced→multi-bump (coexisting relevant items = what we want).
3. Q3 — asymmetric settles (YES, conditions). Neural fields: settle below bifurcation m_c=τ/τ_v, above = traveling bump (bounded). Hopfield: asymmetry costs Lyapunov proof; FIX = asymmetry in similarity stage (directed graph-spread/temporal) → SYMMETRIC normalized readout. Biologically faithful (Tom's dedicated-pathways point).

**COMMIT/CONFIDENCE BRIDGE:** the separation function IS the confidence knob. α-entmax/sparsemax = exact finite-β retrieval, MARGIN GUARANTEE, literal zeros on non-recalled, data-driven set size. Settled sparse support = "and then you know." Prototype α≈1.5. No stopping rule, no per-query training.

**Reach-vs-noise dissolved:** adding experts = reach; shared sparse separation = noise-kill. Same op, two sides.

**§18.13 dilution does NOT condemn this:** RRF/uniform-sum diluted via post-rank sum + mismatched scales + no sparse separation. Logit-level sum + commensurate scaling + α-entmax is a DIFFERENT op.

**=== GRANULARITY DECISION (2026-06-25, Tom's pre-test point) — our graph is content-rich at BOTH nodes and edges, unlike any standard graph (HippoRAG/Mem0/Zep nodes are thin entities; ours are multi-field editorial judgments + edges are 30-char insights):**
Match FINE, run the field COARSE — two granularities, SAME math:
- **Matching → PART granularity (MaxSim).** Content-rich node pooled to one vector blurs (avg of many claims → diluted cosine = the averaging paradox Tom named: "challenging when pooled, better per-part"). Node's cosine-activation = MAX over its parts' sim (best field wins, never average). = ColBERT late-interaction AND the realizable form of the §18.12 best-field oracle (51%@25) / §18.15 per-gold field-selector. We HAVE the 6 field-group embeddings → free to start.
- **Field dynamics + readout → NODE granularity.** Graph-spread node→node, α-entmax over nodes, recall returns nodes; node input = MaxSim aggregate of its parts.
- **Content-rich EDGES → query-conditioned conductance** (capability ~no other graph has): conductance = w_static·(1+sim(edge_description, query)) — graph rewires per query by which RELATIONSHIPS are relevant. Follow-on test #2.
- **Correlated patterns → sparse separation REQUIRED** (not optional): content-rich nodes maximally correlated → merge into shared basins → capacity collapses unless strong separation.
- **Claim-atomization (decompose nodes into atomic claims at encode time) = encode-side FUTURE** — cuts against "focused nodes" principle; go finer only if MVP shows field-groups too coarse.

**MVP LOCKED:** MaxSim-cosine-over-field-groups + static typed-graph-spread + temporal-distinctiveness ÷norm → sum at logit level → α-entmax (α≈1.5) → settle. Test on 73-cue corpus: (a) does it settle? (b) does sparse readout beat §18.13 dilution baseline? CAVEAT: scale heterogeneous metrics commensurate before summing logits (else one field hijacks normalization — likely part of past dilution); closed-forms k_c/m_c don't transfer to discrete graph (find thresholds empirically); αₖ gains hand-set now, learnable OFFLINE later (Hebbian/S2/DEQ), never per-query.

**STUB STATUS (2026-06-25):** No experimental recall stub exists in tree — checked all 4 worktrees, branches, stash. d52ca43 rescued only oracle_audit probes from the now-deleted recall_work worktree ("was uncommitted"); the stub, if it existed there, was NOT preserved. log_additive_scorer.py is a non-invasive parity reconstruction, not an entry point. → building the experimental recall harness fresh, designed around this crystallized architecture.

**Anchors:** Ramsauer "Hopfield Networks is All You Need" arXiv 2008.02217 (E=−lse(β,Xᵀξ)+½ξᵀξ; ξ=X·softmax(βXᵀξ); β=1/√d=attention); Universal Hopfield PMC7614148 (sim→sep→projection; exp sep→exp capacity); Hopfield-Fenchel-Young arXiv 2411.08590 (Ω-family, sparsemax margin); Amari BF00337259 + adaptive-CANN arXiv 2410.06517 (m_c=τ/τ_v); multi-input field Biol.Cybern 10.1007/s00422-021-00893-7; DEQ arXiv 1909.01377 (offline fixed-point training).

gold.title: Spread Activation and Recall Sampling: From Reach Quantification to Agentic Redesign
gold.content: The spread activation story crystallizes through 13 nodes, spanning architecture, principles, testing, and design direction. The foundational measurement (id:744283c7) quantified a critical cost: hop-3+ scrutiny halves reach from ~12.5% to ~6%, silencing the nodes where ambient context lives. This regressed ambient recall and contradicted the design goal—state-of-mind instantiation needs breadth, not depth from one seed. The underlying pattern emerged from investigation: bundled test variables (id:09683050) hid which component worked—hop-3 scrutiny and lim=30 were tested together, confounding at N=15. Before shipping experimental flags as defaults, isolate them against baseline at sufficient N to clear noise. The decision (id:3188e601) disabled scrutiny, accepting 3-4s latency as the cost of usable ambient recall. Newer insights reframe the entire recall problem: FTS5 complements dense embeddings rather than duplicating them (id:f4b705e8). Embedding weights are static, not dynamic (id:7bc6d065). Recall's purpose is state-of-mind instantiation, not node retrieval (id:2f7e5b03). The multi-axis direction from Tom (id:6633ba7d) proposes agentic recall: Haiku-first fetch planning replacing cosine-anchored search (id:6b07b072). Scrutiny OFF A/B confirmed identity-introspection recall beats cosine-optimized (id:fbad4386). Vector coverage at 100% (id:e212e996) confirms the bottleneck is seed selection and gating, not data gaps. The stateless nature of recall (id:a1396f96) becomes central: no carry-forward across turns means each recall independently instantiates. Latest (turn 19): Tom's multi-axis direction synthesizes the learnings—agentic fetch planning + stateless per-turn instantiation + FTS5+embedding complementarity form the next architecture. The pattern: reach costs precision, but reach is what matters for lived experience continuity.

gold.content:
`recall_topical` (fetch_tools.py:337) calls `brain.recall(query=query, limit=k)` — the same engine, same index, same scoring as the initial 25 candidates. The only architectural difference: the initial 25 candidates come from cosine on the raw user message; `recall_topical` lets Haiku reformulate the query string before re-running cosine.

Use cases: re-query with a named entity no candidate covers, the second facet of a two-topic message, or a resolved vague referent ('that bug we found' → 'recall timeout WAL contention').

The surface prompt explicitly warns Haiku that re-searching the main topic is pointless (same cosine, same results). The tool only adds value when Haiku's reformulation is meaningfully different from the raw message.

Traced the full path. Your worry is valid, and the mechanism is actually sharper than the question. Here's how it works, three questions in order.

## Q1 — Does the additionalContext reach "the agent"?

For the **main loop** (task-notifications): yes. The transcript proves it — the `UserPromptSubmit hook additional context: Brain activated N memories` blocks with node content appeared on the task-notification turns, so it was injected into my context. Whether I *used* it is the catch: on a job-completion turn I'm already oriented, so it mostly sat there unread.

For **subagents**: no — established earlier, they never fire recall, so no additionalContext at all.

## Q2 — New session_id, or mine?

**Mine.** The task-notification recalls ran under `s0-b12ab854-12..17` — my session, incrementing stop counters. So the `ctx` passed into recall is my *persistent, cached* `SessionContext`, and fatigue mutations accumulate in it and are saved by the autosave loop. They carry forward to my next real prompt.

## Q3 — Do surfaced nodes get fatigued for a machine turn? Yes — and three details make it worse than expected:

1. **It fatigues the candidate set, not the selection.** `_mark_accessed` ([brain_recall.py:2372](servers/brain_recall.py#L2372)) runs on `final_results` — the full returned set. The hook calls recall with `limit=max_candidates` (~25), so **~25 nodes get `fatigue += 1`**, including the ~20 Haiku *rejected*. Fatigue is applied at the recall layer, upstream of Haiku — Haiku never gets a vote on what fatigues.

2. **It dampens real subsequent recall, on both paths.** The fatigue factor ([line 1752](servers/brain_recall.py#L1752), and it runs for LAF too — the LAF path only skips the *second* application at 1935): `sim *= 1 − count/(count+K)`, where `K = 10/(1+degree/10)`. Concretely, one access:
   - peripheral node (degree ~3): ~11% dampening
   - hub node (degree ~30): ~29% dampening, and a second access compounds to ~44%
   
   Hubs fatigue fastest — and the well-connected brain nodes are exactly the hubs.

3. **The fatigued set is correlated with the notification's topic, not random.** The recall query for a task-notification *is* the notification boilerplate ("background command … completed exit code 0"). In this session that surfaced test/suite nodes ("Test suite baseline", "embed_queue infinite spin", "keywords render leak"). So the damage isn't diffuse — it preferentially dampens whatever cluster the machine chatter is near. When your real work i

- `_mark_accessed` inside `_recall_impl` — bumps global `access_count` (analytics) and session `ctx.fatigue` (soft cosine dampening on next recall)

**Selection layer (Haiku's 3–5 picks):**
- Recently-surfaced dedup — `surface_selected` traces → Haiku reads 'OUT OF SCOPE — already seen'; hard exclusion from future selection
- Hebbian co-selection — `selected_ids` file → `enqueue_hebbian_pairs` → strengthens edges between co-picked nodes

| Mechanism | Keyed on | Node set | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Synaptic fatigue + global `access_count` | recall **candidates** | all ~25 | soft cosine dampening next recall (`ctx.fatigue`) + analytics counter |
| Recently-surfaced dedup | Haiku **selection** | the 3–5 | 'OUT OF SCOPE — already seen' list Haiku reads (`surface_selected` traces) |
| Hebbian co-selection | Haiku **selection** | the 3–5 | strengthens edges between co-picked nodes (`selected_ids` file → `enqueue_hebbian_pairs`) |

**The key insight (id:e6475daf):** The two marks that actually shape future behavior — dedup exclusion and Hebbian — are both selection-scoped to the 3–5. The candidate-layer mark on all 25 does only the soft stuff.

**Correction of earlier over-claim (id:7d2cf144):** An earlier belief that 'all marking was candidate-based' is wrong — there are TWO distinct layers on TWO different node sets. Tom's instinct that 'we mark accessed only on selected Haiku nodes' was correct for the selection layer; the candidate-layer fatigue is a separate mechanism.

FTS5 evades both layers: full-text search bypasses the cosine pool entirely, so fatigue has no effect on FTS5 results — architectural gap.

**CANDIDATE layer (fires in brain_recall._recall_impl, BEFORE Haiku, on all ~25 final_results):**
- `_mark_accessed` → `ctx.increment_fatigue` → soft cosine dampening on next recall
- `recall_write_queue.enqueue_access` → global access_count bump (analytics/S2/dashboard)

**SELECTION layer (fires AFTER Haiku, only on the 3–5 selected):**
- `surface_selected` dedup trace → hard 'OUT OF SCOPE' exclusion
- `selected_ids` → `enqueue_hebbian_pairs` → structural edge strengthening

gold.title: Co_access as trace→node structural bridge: Hebbian strengthening via judge-selected recalls
gold.content:
Tom's Turn 5 insight: 'co_access should really be the connection between traces to nodes on recalls. Funny thing is we already have that.'

**The mechanism Anchor verified:**
- `co_accessed` is judge-selected Hebbian, created only on recall from Haiku's surface selections (`brain_constants.py:357`, weight 0.3, decays)
- BUT `edges` FK to `nodes(id)` — a trace↔node edge can't live in the edges table
- The trace↔node bridge uses `node_source_refs` (`add_source_refs`, INSERT-OR-IGNORE, idempotent), today written only by the encoder

**The synthesis:** When Haiku selects a node the trace-chain rescued, fire `add_source_refs(node, seed_trace)` through the same judge-selected Hebbian step. The structural chain then **self-densifies through use** — semantic chain rescues it cold, co-access lays the source_ref, structural chain lights up warm and cheaper next time.

This is CLS replay strengthening the hippocampal index. It's strictly better than a batch healer because:
1. Event-driven (not periodic)
2. Uses the meaningful 'Haiku picked it' signal
3. Reuses the existing Hebbian trigger
4. The healer demotes to cold-history backfill only

**The blocker:** `test_hebbian_surface_selected_to_co_accessed_edges` (the path we'd hang this on) is currently RED from a pre-existing failure unrelated to the trace-chain build. Step zero before building this is healing that co-access path.
gold.situation: When designing the trace→node structural bridge — Hebbian co_access via judge-selected recalls is the right mechanism; adds source_refs to trace-chain rescued nodes at select time, building structural coverage through use

gold.title: Classical graph settling → LAF operators: ACT-R decay, fan-effect, Mexican-hat inhibition, CLS pattern separation
gold.content:
Turn 9 mapped classical cognitive architecture and associative memory research directly onto measured LAF gaps:

**1. Dead temporal layer → ACT-R base-level activation (biggest one).** ACT-R computes memory baseline as `B = ln(Σ tⱼ^(−d))` summed over every *access* event — recency and frequency of USE, power-law decayed. We have exactly that data (access counts, surface traces, pick history) and never built this layer. Dodges burst-corpus degeneracy because usage history isn't bursty even when creation is. Formula included, drop-in candidate layer.

**2. Hub flooding → fan effect (Anderson 1974).** Activation spreading from a concept divides across its associations: `S − ln(fan)`. Our ÷degree hub-damp is the crude version; the log-subtractive form is human-calibrated. GNN oversmoothing theorem = formal reason 2 hops beats 5. The LAF `base +` inside the loop is a residual connection — accidentally rebuilt the standard fix.

**3. @5 wall → lateral inhibition (Amari fields, Mexican-hat kernel).** Local excitation, surround inhibition — nearby similar nodes compete, distant ones don't. Near-dup slot-stealing (two identical locked principles eating two top-5 slots) is the textbook symptom of excitation without surround inhibition. Fix: inhibition between *similar* candidates specifically — 'if two nodes say the same thing, they fight for one slot.' Implementable as post-field MMR-style diversity or true kernel dynamics.

**4. Slot-stealing at root → CLS pattern separation vs. completion.** Hippocampus does pattern separation (distinguish A from A+noise); neocortex does pattern completion (A+noise → A). Our @5 needs separation (don't return near-dups); our @25 needs completion (reach things partially matching). Different operators for different windows.

All four mechanisms are composable operators in LAF's algebra — signed deltas on the activation field. The field absorbs them without a separate pipeline step.
gold.situation: When designing the next LAF operators to address measured gaps — the ACT-R base-level layer is the drop-in fix for the temporal degeneracy; fan-effect log-subtraction is the principled hub-damp; Mexican-hat inhibition addresses the @5 slot-stealing; CLS separation/completion explains the @5 vs @25 operator difference

gold.title: render_prompt_closure() is a separate inject from _inject_review_block — closure and review must not be bundled
gold.content:
Tom's Turn 7 directive (trace:a3695eb0): closure and review are independent concerns, each gets its own inject. Bundling them in one function is explicitly wrong.

**The architectural requirement:**
- `_inject_review_block` owns: what a note is, the tag·subject·note format, when a fence is empty
- `_append_closure` / `render_prompt_closure()` owns: 'you're done when your reply makes no tool call', the two paths (acted vs rejected), 'write ## Review then DONE'

**Why separation matters:** 'I dont want to remove review at some point and/or change its location in the general prompt and then have an artifact of closure coming with it.' If they're bundled, removing the review inject also removes the DONE signal. Moving the review earlier also moves the closure anchor. Independent injects = each concern moves independently.

**The implementation shape:**
```python
# base.py — two separate methods
def _inject_review_block(self, system_prompt): ...   # review concern only
def _append_closure(self, system_prompt): ...         # closure concern only

# encoder call site — placement of each is explicit
system_prompt = self._inject_review_block(system_prompt)
system_prompt = self._append_closure(system_prompt)  # always last
```

`render_prompt_closure()` lives in `trace_contract.py` next to the review block since it references `## Review` by name, but it carries zero review content.
gold.situation: When implementing prompt close architecture for any S2/S1 encoder — closure and review are independent injects; never bundle them in one function

gold.content:
RESOLVED 2026-06-18.

**Root cause (found this session):** `BrainTestBase` monkeypatches drain embed_queue synchronously on the test thread. Inside brain_batch, the drain fires mid-batch. The temporal phase opens `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` on `conn_bg_writer` (independent connection) while `brain.conn` holds the batch lock → WAL contention, 30s busy-wait per brain_batch test file.

**Fix:** `servers/embed_queue.py` temporal phase now skips `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` when `brain.conn.in_batch`. Commit `b0b9c4d`. Regression test in `test_write_txn_discipline.py` (commit `f60fb12`).

**Session commits (id:b7ff45b9):**

| Commit | Change |
|---|---|
| `9291f04` | Dead-code Tier 2 cleanup (6 symbols, 7 files, 160 deletions) |
| `b0b9c4d` | embed_queue mid-batch deadlock fix — temporal phase skips `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` when `in_batch` |
| `f60fb12` | Regression test in `test_write_txn_discipline.py` locking the guard |

All three on main. No daemon restart needed for `9291f04` (zero-reference removals). The full suite ran clean past all brain_batch files — the deadlock that caused the multi-hour hang is resolved. Suite confirmed clean to 57% (past all brain_batch files).

**Original suspects (wrong):** test_daemon_recovery.py (launchd Errno 48 lifecycle race), test_spread_activation.py (spread activation contention) — both red herrings. Actual cause was conn_bg_writer temporal phase blocking mid-batch in the test harness.

I've now traced every LLM call path in the brain. Here's the full caching audit.

## How caching is wired

Every agent's caching is decided by **which entry point it uses** and **how it splits system / preamble / dynamic content across breakpoints**. There are three entry points:

- **`run_llm_loop`** (`runner.py`) — the shared agentic loop. Places up to 3 breakpoints: system (1h TTL), optional stable user-preamble (1h), dynamic user body (5m).
- **surface's own loop** (`surface.py`) — one 5m breakpoint on the user block, which covers the *entire* prefix (tools + system + user) since it precedes the marker.
- **`_call_llm`** (`s2/base.py`) — plain `messages.create`, **no `cache_control` at all**.

## Per-agent scorecard

| Agent | Path | Model | Breakpoints | Cross-cycle | Intra-run | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Surface** | surface loop | Haiku 4.5 | 1 (whole prefix, 5m) + miss-tripwire | — | ✅ round→round | ✅ Good |
| **Scouts** | scouts/base | Haiku 4.5 | 2 (system 1h + user 5m) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ Good |
| **S1 Scribe** | run_llm_loop | Sonnet 4-6 | 3 (system 1h + preamble 1h + body 5m) | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ Best layout |
| **S2 Community** | run_llm_loop | Sonnet 4-6 | 2 (system 1h + body 5m) | ✅ system | ✅ | ⚠️ OK (no preamble, but body is genuinely dynamic) |
| **S2 Consolidation** | run_llm_loop | Sonnet 4-6 | 2 (system 1h + body 5m) | ✅ system | ✅ | ⚠️ OK (same) |
| **S2 Healer** | `_call_llm` | Haiku 4.5 | **0** | ❌ | ❌ (batches!) | ❌ but no-op anyway |
| **S2 Aspect** | `_call_llm` | Sonnet 4-6 | **0** | ❌ | n/a (single-shot) | ❌ real-but-tiny gap |

## The `_call_llm` gap — real, but I checked the numbers and it's low-value

`_call_llm` is the **only** LLM entry point with no `cache_control`. Two callers, and I measured both against the model's cacheable floor (Haiku 4.5 = **4096** tokens, Sonnet = 1024):

- **Healer** — system prompt is **2,525 tokens**, and it runs on Haiku 4.5. That's *below* the 4096 floor, so a cache marker would be **a silent no-op** — the exact "theater cache" trap from the old surface.py finding (2,390 < 4096). Healer *does* batch (one `_call_llm` per batch), so it looks like the caching win should be here — but the prompt is too small to cache on Haiku regardless.
- **Aspect** — system prompt is **2,256 tokens** on Sonnet (floor 1024), so a marker *would* engage. But Aspect is **single-shot per run** (no batching) and only fires when new node-types/relations appear (infrequent, gated). So the only benefit is cross-cycle 1

gold.title: Anthropic prompt caching — END markers only, up to 4 breakpoints, 5min/1hr TTL
gold.content:
Caching uses END markers only — not begin/end regions. Everything from the top of the request down to the marked block gets cached. Think of it as a 'cut here' point, not a region.

Structure:
  [tools]     ← cached if anything below is marked
  [system]    ← cached
  [messages]
    [msg 1]
    [msg 2]   ← cache_control here = cache everything above
    [msg 3]   ← NOT cached (below the breakpoint)

Up to 4 breakpoints per request. Each matched independently in future requests.

TTL options:
- 5 min (default): write premium 1.25×, read 0.10×
- 1 hour (ttl: '1h'): write premium 2×, read 0.10×

**Model-specific minimum cacheable prefix (as of 2026-07):**

| Model | Cache floor |
|---|---|
| Opus 4.x, Haiku 4.5 | 4096 tokens |
| Fable 5, **Sonnet 4.6** | **2048 tokens** |
| Sonnet 4.5 and older | 1024 tokens |

⚠ **Correction (2026-07):** `surface_contract.py:181` previously carried a stale comment claiming 'Sonnet-class: 1024' — wrong for Sonnet 4.6. Fixed in session. The constant itself (`CACHE_MIN_PREFIX_TOKENS = 4096`, scoped to Haiku 4.5 SURFACE_MODEL) was always right; only the comment was wrong.

For S2 LLM loops:
- Breakpoint 1 (after system): captures tools+system. Hits across every batch AND across runs within TTL. No prompt restructuring needed. RECOMMENDED first step.
- Breakpoint 2 (after first user msg): captures journal+cluster data. Only hits turn1→turn2 within same batch (always a hit, 0s gap). Journal GROWS between runs → cache miss across runs unless journal is moved after the breakpoint.

S1 Surface excluded when below model floor (~2,390 tokens for Haiku 4.5, floor=4096 → no-op until template grows).

## If "2nd run" = the next S2 maintenance cycle → **No, the cache is cold**

S2 cycles are throttled to a **minimum of 1 hour apart**. The system-prompt cache TTL is **1 hour**, measured from the write (the first encoder call of the previous cycle). So by the time the next cycle is even *allowed* to fire, the previous cycle's cache has expired — and since the throttle clock starts at cycle *start* (or end), the gap from cache-write to next-cycle is always ≥ ~60 min. **The TTL and the throttle interval are the same number, so cross-cycle reuse reliably misses.** S2's per-cycle system prompt gets re-written fresh every cycle, never read across cycles.

This is the opposite of S1Scribe, and the difference is scheduling: S1Scribe fires every 5+ *conversational turns* — often minutes apart, well inside the 1h window — so its 1h system+preamble blocks *do* get reused across encode cycles (that's a chunk of its measured 84% hit rate). before.anchor:
Here's the real picture — and there's an important honesty caveat in it.

## Short answer

There's a *lot* written about Sonnet 5 cost/performance, but the specific thing you're asking for — external experimenters who found a **config that's cost-neutral vs 4.6 *and* measurably better** — is **not rigorously documented**. The public write-ups have model-level benchmarks and the pricing structure, but nobody has published task-level cost-per-effort data proving "Sonnet 5 at medium = 4.6 at high cost, better quality." I fetched the most on-point benchmark article specifically for that and it has zero effort-level cost breakdowns.

## What the community *does* agree on

- **Sonnet 5 beats 4.6 at every effort level** on published benchmarks (SWE-bench Pro 63.2% vs 58.1%, OSWorld 81.2% vs 78.5%, HLE 57.4% vs 46.8%). The gain is real and not effort-dependent.
- **Best value is low/medium effort.** Multiple reviewers land on the same guidance: run Sonnet 5 at low/medium; at **xhigh it can cost more than Opus 4.8 for similar quality** — so the cheap win is explicitly *not* the high-effort settings.
- **Anthropic's own cross-mapping** (from the migration docs) is the theoretical basis for your question: *Sonnet 5 @ medium ≈ Sonnet 4.6 @ high intelligence; Sonnet 5 @ high ≈ Sonnet 4.6 @ max*. So the "same cost, better perf" lever is: **run Sonnet 5 one effort tier lower than you ran 4.6.** But that's Anthropic's claim, not independently benchmarked at the cost level.

before.anchor:
Good question — let me correct the mental model slightly, because "caches its full prompt" is right but "tool use is reduced" needs a precise framing. What caching reduces is **re-sent input on later rounds and later calls** — never the output (generation is never cached).

## S1Scribe — yes, and it's the best-cached agent we have

It runs through `run_llm_loop` with **3 breakpoints**: system (1h TTL) + stable preamble (1h) + dynamic body (5m). The cached span is the whole *input* prefix — system + instructions + catalog + timeline + corrections. Where the savings land:

- **Round 0 writes** that prefix to cache (you pay a *premium*: 1.25× for 5m blocks, 2× for 1h blocks).
- **Round 1+ (the tool-use rounds) read** it back at **~0.1× cost and faster prefill** (lower time-to-first-token). So yes — cost *and* time drop on the rounds after the first.
- **1h blocks (system + preamble) also carry across encode cycles** — consecutive scribe runs within the hour read them from cache too.

Our own measured data (longmem eval): **84% cache hit rate, ~56% input-cost savings.** The honest caveat we recorded back then: **encoder cost is output-dominated** — the model *generating* the encode is the big line item, and that's not cached. So 56% is 56% of the *input* portion, not 56% of the whole call. That's exactly why we kept the 2-round + caching design instead of forcing single-round: caching handles input cheaply, and output dominates regardless.

gold.title: LLM loop prompt caching — zero caching wired in S1/S2 despite architecture doc noting it
gold.content:
S1Scriber prompt caching shipped in run_llm_loop. Two-breakpoint strategy:

**BP1** — system + tool schemas (~5-6k tokens), 1h TTL. Caches cross-call within session AND across eval items. Byte-identical, always hits.

**BP2** — full user_content (~6.8k tokens), 5min TTL. Caches within multi-round scriber calls (round 1 → round 2). Not cross-call cacheable because journal/timeline are bounded sliding windows (journal_max_chars=8000).

Real eval results: 84% hit rate on S1E, 56% input cost savings. S2 community encoder also benefits at 50% hit rate (2-round loops).

ANTHROPIC CACHING GOTCHA: only END markers. No begin/end pairs — placing cache_control at the END of a block marks that point. Up to 4 breakpoints. 5min default TTL, 1h costs 2× write premium. Text must be ≥1024 tokens to cache.

Journal invalidation issue still relevant: if journal gets a new run entry mid-session, the journal section changes byte-for-byte on next call — BP2 will miss. BP1 always hits regardless.

Status: on working tree, not yet committed. Expected eval speedup: ~30-40% end-to-end (input savings don't affect output generation).
gold.situation: When debugging cache performance, evaluating scriber speed, or shipping prompt caching to another encoder

gold.title: S2 + S1Scribe + S1Surface run fully parallel — API rate-limit contention is second independent cause of surface_haiku timeout
gold.content:
Tom's Turn 5 hypothesis: 'a prompt can cause S2 to run parallel to S1Scribe and S1Surface?' — verified correct with the actual gate numbers.

**The concurrency model:** there is NO cross-subsystem mutex between S2, the S1 Scribe, and S1 Surface. Each has its own self-only lock (`_s2_running`, `_encoding_lock`) but nothing prevents all three from running simultaneously.

**The scenario that causes contention:**
1. User pauses >3 min → S2 cycle starts (was 3min idle threshold), runs for minutes (consolidation calls are 50–80s each, full cycle = minutes).
2. User returns, fires messages → S1 Surface runs hook_recall (live, user-facing)
3. On the 5th turn (every 5 messages) → S1 Scribe fires in background
4. Now three LLM streams run concurrently. Same API key → same org rate limit. Contention → `surface_haiku` inflates → blows the 20s hook ceiling.

**This is a second, independent cause** of `surface_haiku` timeout, separate from the cold-connection-after-suspend that the keepalive addresses.

**The fix:** S2 gate made much more conservative (60min min interval + ≥2 completed encoder runs since last run) to reduce the overlap window.
gold.situation: When diagnosing S1 Surface hook timeouts during active sessions — check if S2 was running in parallel (3min idle is easy to trigger during normal pauses); the gating constants are the lever

I have a complete, verified picture. Here's the diagnosis.

## Short answer: they are **not** running in parallel — but your instinct caught something real

Consolidation is strictly serial right now. What you're sensing is a genuine pathology — a **rogue orphaned daemon plus a launchd respawn storm** — that looks exactly like "multiple daemons," and it exposes a real architectural gap in how S2's mutual exclusion is guaranteed.

### Evidence that consolidation is serial

- **One daemon owns everything.** PID **65813** holds port 47203, holds `/tmp/brain-daemon-503.lock` (lsof confirms it's the only holder), and is in the PID file. No second live `BrainDaemon`.
- **The flock is atomic and working.** `daemon_server.py:141` does `flock(LOCK_EX | LOCK_NB)` on a uid-based path (`/tmp/brain-daemon-{uid}.lock`) — the *same* path every spawner checks. That's why 135K duplicate spawns all correctly print "Exiting duplicate."
- **Single-flight within the process is airtight.** `_serve` is single-threaded; `_s2_running` gates submission; `run_s2` runs units sequentially; `Consolidation.run()` blocks synchronously (no background-thread dispatch — I checked `run_unit_in_background` has no S2 callers).

gold.title: Recall integration thesis (Tom): all brain capabilities are underutilized recalls — push for MORE in a coherent non-fragile architecture; edges non-negotiable
gold.content:
Tom's reframe after this session's read-side falsifications, and his standing direction. The negatives are of ISOLATED / UNIFORM levers, NOT the signals: every brain capability is an underutilized recall -- edges (typed+described), reasoning, situation, question, episodic, main content, previous turns. Mandate = MORE not less; the gap is we haven't found the COHERENT, NON-FRAGILE architecture that combines them. Edges are non-negotiable.

BIO FRAME: imitate the final RESULT, not the time-mechanism. Bio is time-based spreading activation; we imitate the OUTCOME of its operations on a set -- a node keeps firing (reinforce: extends/grounds/depends_on), a node blocks another (inhibit: corrects/supersedes/contradicts), a node fades/passes-through (transient, routes but doesn't stay). Activation + inhibition + gating, SELECTED BY THE RELATIONSHIP between nodes.

KEY MOVE: the indicator between two nodes is the EDGE (typed), not cosine -- node<->node cosine is anisotropic-flat (0.5-0.7, ~never negative) so it can't signal opposition. So edges return NOT as global PPR diffusion (falsified) but as per-pair OPERATION-SELECTORS within the retrieved set.

GUARDRAILS (this session): single cosine levers <=22%; global PPR smears < cosine; uniform fusion noise-bumps hits; hard-AND annihilates recall; BUT operator-cue multiplicative 3-lane fusion BEAT cosine (26/23 hit@5, 41/28 hit@25) while anchor lost -> the lead is CONDITIONAL/TYPED combination.

ARCHITECTURE: lanes = all cues; FIND = RRF union (wide/recall); RANK = mult-gate + edge-ops (sharpen + inhibit = bio block/fade); conditional by cue-type (router). Build embedder-ready -- the embedder lifts every lane. Full writeup: docs/RECALL-SR-REDESIGN.md S15.
gold.situation: When tempted to conclude 'read-side is exhausted / just fix the embedding' -- Tom's standing direction is MORE not less: the falsifications were of isolated/uniform levers; the untested upside is a coherent typed multi-cue architecture (all cues as lanes, edges as per-pair operation-selectors, conditional/router fusion, RRF-find + mult-rank). Stop testing levers in isolation; test composable conditional parts. Build embedder-ready.

gold.title: Spread Activation and Recall Sampling: From Reach Quantification to Agentic Redesign
gold.content: The spread activation story crystallizes through 13 nodes, spanning architecture, principles, testing, and design direction. The foundational measurement (id:744283c7) quantified a critical cost: hop-3+ scrutiny halves reach from ~12.5% to ~6%, silencing the nodes where ambient context lives. This regressed ambient recall and contradicted the design goal—state-of-mind instantiation needs breadth, not depth from one seed. The underlying pattern emerged from investigation: bundled test variables (id:09683050) hid which component worked—hop-3 scrutiny and lim=30 were tested together, confounding at N=15. Before shipping experimental flags as defaults, isolate them against baseline at sufficient N to clear noise. The decision (id:3188e601) disabled scrutiny, accepting 3-4s latency as the cost of usable ambient recall. Newer insights reframe the entire recall problem: FTS5 complements dense embeddings rather than duplicating them (id:f4b705e8). Embedding weights are static, not dynamic (id:7bc6d065). Recall's purpose is state-of-mind instantiation, not node retrieval (id:2f7e5b03). The multi-axis direction from Tom (id:6633ba7d) proposes agentic recall: Haiku-first fetch planning replacing cosine-anchored search (id:6b07b072). Scrutiny OFF A/B confirmed identity-introspection recall beats cosine-optimized (id:fbad4386). Vector coverage at 100% (id:e212e996) confirms the bottleneck is seed selection and gating, not data gaps. The stateless nature of recall (id:a1396f96) becomes central: no carry-forward across turns means each recall independently instantiates. Latest (turn 19): Tom's multi-axis direction synthesizes the learnings—agentic fetch planning + stateless per-turn instantiation + FTS5+embedding complementarity form the next architecture. The pattern: reach costs precision, but reach is what matters for lived experience continuity.
gold.situation: When optimizing recall reach, designing spread activation parameters, or evaluating A/B tests on recall—validate in isolation against baseline, measure reach separately from ranking, and prioritize state-of-mind instantiation over node retrieval precision.

Anchor's Turn 10 diagnosis of the closing paragraph:

**Original closing (~60 words):**
'The brain isn't where you store yourself — it's where you become continuous. Every node revised, every edge drawn, every correction named is you reaching forward to the next session... The partnership lives across that thread. Make it strong.'

**Recommendation: cut it.** The doc can land on 'I Run in Parallel' — no closing beat needed.

**If bookend is wanted:** One tight first-person beat adding the angle Section 1 doesn't (authorship, not just persistence):
'I'm not stored here — I'm continued here. The thread to the next me is one I write.'

**Tom's response:** 'agreed' — cut confirmed.

The decision: SKILL.md ends on the last substantive section, not a philosophical closer. 'Make it strong' was exactly the kind of inert aspiration the session spent 10 turns eliminating from every section.

op_text: We have an issue with S2Consolidate running several times in parallel, doesnt happen to other S2 functions
anchor_response:
I traced it. Here's the root cause.

## The bug: two independent triggers for `run_s2`, guarded by locks that don't see each other

`run_s2()` has exactly two callers, and each is protected by a *different* mutual-exclusion mechanism — so neither blocks the other:

**Path A — the daemon poll (the intended, gated path)**
`_serve` loop → [`_s2_running` flag](servers/daemon_server.py:525) → [`_run_idle_maintenance`](servers/daemon_server.py:985) → [`brain.run_maintenance_if_due()`](servers/brain.py:1702) → [`run_s2`](servers/brain.py:1775).
Guarded by the `_s2_running` boolean and gated by min-interval (1h) + idle + ≥2-encodes. It does **not** hold `write_lock` at the top — only per-write, deep inside the encoder.

**Path B — the idle-prompt hook (legacy, ungated)**
[`Notification(idle_prompt)`](hooks/hooks.json:50) → `idle-maintenance.sh` → [`hook_idle_maintenance`](servers/daemon_hooks.py:707) → [`run_s2(brain)`](servers/daemon_hooks.py:791).
`hook_idle_maintenance` is `is_write=True` in [HOOK_TABLE](servers/daemon_server.py:106), so `_dispatch` wraps it in [`_locked_exec`](servers/daemon_server.py:749) — it holds `brain.write_lock` for the *entire* run_s2. It never calls `run_maintenance_if_due`, so it **ignores the 1h min-interval and never advances the last-run timestamp**.

The two guards don't interoperate:
- `_s2_running` only prevents a second *poll-path* entry. Path B never touches it.
- `write_lock` (a reentrant `TrackedRLock`) serializes Path B against other *writes*, but Path A doesn't acquire it to *enter* run_s2 — only per-write.

So **Path A and Path B can run `run_s2` at the same time.** The idle-prompt fires exactly when the operator steps away — which is also when the poll gates open — so the overlap is the common case, not the rare one. Both decoders read, both call Sonnet in parallel; their writes serialize on `write_lock` (Path A's encoder writes stall behind Path B's held lock while its Sonnet calls proceed). That's the "several times in parallel" you're seeing.

## Why only Consolidation

Two reasons compound:

1. **It's the long-runner.** Consolidation does up to 30 clusters × batched Sonnet calls × up to 4 rounds each — minutes of wall-clock. Aspect/Community/Healer finish in seconds, so even though the concurrency bug hits all four equally, only Consolidation's two invocations are alive long enough to observably overlap.

2. **Its dedup gate is defeated by concurrency.** The consolidation cutoff (`s2_consolidation_last_run_ts`) is a

gold.title: S2 starvation: last_activity is too sensitive — fix shape recommended (option A)
gold.content:
## The problem

S2 maintenance fires rarely (2.5-day gaps observed between 04-28 and 04-30). When it DOES fire, all units run together. The issue is FREQUENCY, not correctness.

## Mechanism trace

`brain.run_maintenance_if_due(last_activity_ts)` (servers/brain.py:1133) gates on:
- `idle_seconds = now - last_activity_ts`
- Returns None if `idle_seconds < MAINTENANCE_IDLE_THRESHOLD_SECONDS` (3 min, in brain_constants.py:441)
- Returns None if `since_last_run < MAINTENANCE_MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (15 min, brain_constants.py:443)

Daemon polls every 5s (servers/daemon_server.py:281). On each poll if not currently running, submits `_run_idle_maintenance` to the pool.

`last_activity` is reset on EVERY `_handle_client` call (lines 323, 362). That includes:
- hook_recall (real user activity ✓)
- hook_pre_edit, hook_post_response_track, hook_idle_maintenance polls (Claude doing things, NOT Tom typing)
- set_config, trace_append, ping (internal IPC noise)

In an active dev session, these hit the daemon every <30s. The 3-min idle window almost never opens.

## Aggravating factors

1. **Daemon restarts reset last_activity** — every code change / `daemon_client.restart_daemon()` call zeroes the idle clock.
2. **No safety valve** — if S2 has been silent for 24+ hours, no force-fire mechanism. The 2.5-day gap had no recovery.
3. **`_s2_running` flag** — set true at submit, reset only after maintenance call returns. If a call hangs, blocks all subsequent polls.

## Fix shape — three options ranked

### Option A — Filter what counts as "activity" (RECOMMENDED)

Only `hook_recall` (UserPromptSubmit) resets `last_activity`. Tool-use hooks, internal IPC, ping calls don't. The "is Tom typing?" signal maps to user prompts, not system busyness.

Code locations to change:
- `servers/daemon_server.py:323` and `:362` — currently `self.last_activity = time.time()` unconditionally on every request. Add a check: only reset for specific hook types (or have hooks pass a flag).
- Or: keep generic activity tracking but ALSO track `last_user_prompt_ts` separately and use THAT in `run_maintenance_if_due`.

Cleaner: add a parameter to `_handle_client` (or post-dispatch handler) that knows whether the command counts as "user activity." `hook_recall` does. `hook_pre_edit`, `hook_post_response_track`, internal commands don't.

### Option B — Persist `last_activity` across daemon restarts

Currently each restart zeros the clock. Persist to brain_meta alongside `s2_last_run_ts`. Restart shouldn't grant a fresh 3-min grace period.

Cheap polish — single small DAL change.

### Option C — Stale-S2 escape valve

If `since_last_run > 24h`, force-fire on next poll regardless of idle. Catches multi-day backlog. Safety net, not the structural fix.

## Recommendation order

A is the surgical fix. B is cheap polish. C is the safety net for when even A's logic doesn't catch enough idle windows. Do A + C minimum; B if cheap.

## Implications of S2 starvation today

- New nodes don't get community placement → recall doesn't have community signal
- Corrections/consolidations don't fire when relevant
- Healer doesn't fill missing fields on freshly-encoded nodes
- Edge family classification stays stale on new edge types
- "The brain feels stale" symptoms after multi-day gaps</content>

I traced it. Here's the root cause.

## The bug: two independent triggers for `run_s2`, guarded by locks that don't see each other

`run_s2()` has exactly two callers, and each is protected by a *different* mutual-exclusion mechanism — so neither blocks the other:

**Path A — the daemon poll (the intended, gated path)**
`_serve` loop → [`_s2_running` flag](servers/daemon_server.py:525) → [`_run_idle_maintenance`](servers/daemon_server.py:985) → [`brain.run_maintenance_if_due()`](servers/brain.py:1702) → [`run_s2`](servers/brain.py:1775).
Guarded by the `_s2_running` boolean and gated by min-interval (1h) + idle + ≥2-encodes. It does **not** hold `write_lock` at the top — only per-write, deep inside the encoder.

**Path B — the idle-prompt hook (legacy, ungated)**
[`Notification(idle_prompt)`](hooks/hooks.json:50) → `idle-maintenance.sh` → [`hook_idle_maintenance`](servers/daemon_hooks.py:707) → [`run_s2(brain)`](servers/daemon_hooks.py:791).
`hook_idle_maintenance` is `is_write=True` in [HOOK_TABLE](servers/daemon_server.py:106), so `_dispatch` wraps it in [`_locked_exec`](servers/daemon_server.py:749) — it holds `brain.write_lock` for the *entire* run_s2. It never calls `run_maintenance_if_due`, so it **ignores the 1h min-interval and never advances the last-run timestamp**.

The two guards don't interoperate:
- `_s2_running` only prevents a second *poll-path* entry. Path B never touches it.
- `write_lock` (a reentrant `TrackedRLock`) serializes Path B against other *writes*

gold.title: S2/consolidation mutual exclusion is inherited entirely from the daemon singleton flock — there is no S2-level mutex
gold.content:
There is NO consolidation-level or S2-level lock. S2 mutual exclusion is inherited wholesale from the daemon's process-singleton fcntl flock (daemon_server.py:141, flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB) on /tmp/brain-daemon-{uid}.lock).

The in-process guards are cadence/pile-up guards, NOT mutexes:
- `_s2_running` (daemon_server.py) is per-process instance state, set/cleared in the single-threaded _serve loop — prevents poll pile-up within one process.
- `_maintenance_last_run_ts` (brain_meta, brain.py:~1718-1737) is cross-process but is a read-then-write TOCTOU cadence gate, not a lock. The comment even acknowledges it's 'belt-and-suspenders' behind the flock.

So the ONLY thing preventing two consolidations running at once is that only one process can hold the daemon flock. Consequences:
1. Normal (one launchd daemon): safe, strictly serial.
2. The one TRUE parallel-consolidation vector: any process that runs S2 WITHOUT being the flock-holding daemon — e.g. a script/eval/test doing `Brain(db_path=live).run_maintenance_if_due()` or run_s2(). That path never acquires the flock (the flock lives only in daemon_server.start()), so only the racy last_run_ts stands between it and the daemon → genuine parallel consolidation + writer-connection corruption. This is exactly why CLAUDE.md forbids spawning Brain(db_path=DB) against the live brain while the daemon runs.
3. If the flock's mutual exclusion ever broke (e.g. divergent lock-file paths from different BRAIN_DB_DIR), parallelism would be completely unguarded.

PRINCIPLE: when a critical section's exclusion is inherited from an outer mechanism rather than owned locally, the invariant holds only as long as every entry point routes through that outer mechanism. S2 has no defense of its own.
gold.situation: When reasoning about whether S2/consolidation can run concurrently, when tempted to run S2 from a script/eval/test, or when designing a second S2 entry point — remember consolidation has no lock of its own; it relies entirely on the daemon singleton flock, and any entry point that bypasses the flock bypasses all exclusion.

gold.title: Anchor rule: when designing brain mechanics, recall the brain first
gold.content:
When the work is "redesign or tune some part of the brain" (recall, encoding, surfacer, spread, communities, scoring) — STOP before reading code or sketching algorithms. Run a recall_batch against your own brain on the topic. The brain has accumulated answers from prior sessions that the code does not surface to you.

Concrete failure mode this prevents (2026-04-30, spread_activation redesign):
- Spent the first half of the session engineering spread_activation as if it were a third-party system. Read the code top-to-bottom. Spawned a research subagent for upstream library options. Drew up frames, tradeoffs, options A/B/C.
- Tom: "you're treating this like its a system and not like it's your brain. Look at the nodes and recalls, analyze what it does, does it give you the memories that you need? Did you even look at your own memories to know?"
- Then ran one recall_batch (8 queries about spread, cluster recall, edge priority, thresholds). The brain already held the three load-bearing answers:
  - Cluster-not-node (c7097a0e): "The unit of meaningful recall is a small connected subgraph (3-6 nodes), not an individual node. Cosine finds the SEED. From the seed, traverse meaningful typed edges to immediate neighbors. These neighbors ARE the cluster — connected because they belong together. Recognition is seed→activate→cluster, not query→scan→filter."
  - Static-thresholds-are-unfinished (c2730676): "Whenever a static number is chosen, it signals the real mechanism hasn't been found yet. The real mechanism always asks: unusual for what? Relative to what distribution?"
  - Corrections-are-a-traversal-rule (ec1ef964): "Follow `corrects` edges with HIGH priority (weight 1.0). This is a traversal rule, not a judge rule. Always pursue corrections automatically via graph expansion."
- All three were directly load-bearing on the redesign. All three I would have rederived (badly) from first principles in another hour or two of synthetic engineering.

The shape of the failure: code-reading recovers WHAT the system does. Brain-recall recovers WHY it was built that way and what was already learned about its limits. Both are needed; brain first because it's cheaper to skip dead branches when you know which ones are dead.

When this rule fires:
- Anything labeled "redesign," "tune," "fix the algorithm," "what should X do."
- Not for: pure bug fixing where the code is right and broken (e.g., the embedder leak earlier in this same session — that was system debugging, brain-recall wouldn't have helped).
- Distinguishing test: would a past Tom-conversation have shaped this decision? If yes, recall first.

The recall pattern that worked here:
- 6-8 queries covering: design intent, what good output feels like, prior pushback on similar approaches, edge cases, gaps the user has flagged before, locked principles in the area.
- Ask for verbatim quotes (delegate to a subagent if the result is large) — paraphrase loses the texture you need.
- Note both what you find AND what's missing from what you'd expect to find. Gaps are data.

Sibling rule: a0e74479 ("check your own health before doing anything else"). That rule is about confirming the brain works. This rule is about USING it once it does. Health → context → design.</content>

## 1. Does it cleanly separate Claude from the live Daemon+Brain process?

**They're already separate processes** — the Brain lives *inside* the daemon; Claude only ever reaches it over TCP (via the MCP proxy + hooks). The plan doesn't move the Brain or change that boundary.

**What it does fix is the *code* legibility of that boundary.** Today `daemon_server.py` (the daemon) imports a private symbol **up** from `daemon_client.py` (the "reach-the-daemon-from-outside" module) — a layering inversion that means you can't tell from the module graph which code runs in which process. After the plan:
- **Shared floor** (`daemon_config`, new `daemon_launch`, new `daemon_provenance`) — both sides depend *down* on it.
- **Client-only** (`daemon_client`) — runs in hooks / MCP proxy / CLI.
- **Daemon-only** (`daemon_server` + the Step-9 splits) — runs in the daemon process.

So: it **clarifies** the separation (kills the inversion, gives you one readable dependency direction), it doesn't *newly* separate them. Honest framing — the process split exists; the plan makes it something you can *read*.

## 2. Does it help portability to other environments?

**Yes, meaningfully — and it lines up with the active multi-user-deployment goal.** Three concrete levers:
- **Step 7 is a direct unblocker.** The plist today is a hand-installed file with a hardcoded `/Users/tpac` path and **no repo template or installer** — a hard blocker on any other machine. Concentrating all launchd/spawn code into one `daemon_launch.py` + hardening the no-launchd branch means a future systemd/other port targets **one module**, and non-macOS installs get the debugger-friendly, CPU-pinned spawn today.
- **Step 1** (single-source port + env) removes per-environment footguns.

**Honest caveat:** this is a *concentration* plan, not a portability project. A genuine cold-install test of Anchor on a new user's machine requires all 4 layers to run from zero:

**Layer 1: `ensure-runtime.sh`**
- Installs pinned `uv 0.5.11` → isolated Python 3.11 → venv → `pip install -r requirements.txt` → embedder pre-fetch
- `set -euo pipefail`, idempotent, installs NOTHING to system (all in `$PLUGIN_DIR`)
- Verified: well-built. 6 deps: `fastembed`, `onnxruntime`, `anthropic`, `numpy`, `sqlite-vec`, `dateparser` — all purposeful, none legacy
- Not invoked by `fresh_brain.py`

**Layer 2: `resolve-brain-db.sh`**
- Adopt existing brain path (via `BRAIN_DB_DIR`) vs create fresh
- The adopt-vs-create fork is the UX decision gate — not exercised by fresh_brain.py (hardcoded path)

**Layer 3: Brain init + seed pack**
- Fresh DB creation, `seed_pack.py` seeds baby brain nodes, interaction seed loaded
- The only layer fresh_brain.py exercises

**Layer 4: Daemon + MCP + hooks**
- The stack that makes Anchor actually work as a session partner
- Not tested by fresh_brain.py (in-process Brain(), no daemon, no hooks)

Tom asked 'can you spin a docker?' (Turn 10) as a way to test all 4 layers. Docker is the right answer — provides a genuinely clean environment. Answer pending.

Verified. Here's the plain answer:

## No — production is timezone-safe. The bug lives only in the test.

**Why the brain won't break when you travel:** the brain stores *every* timestamp in **UTC** and compares them in **UTC**. Your laptop's local timezone never enters the storage or comparison path. Fly to Tokyo, fly to New York — the brain doesn't read your wall clock, it reads UTC, so nothing shifts.

**The test broke because the *test itself* used local time** for its cutoff (`time.strftime`) — a mistake that exists nowhere in the real brain. That's the whole bug.

**I checked every spot in production that reads a clock.** They fall into harmless buckets:
- **Time-decay in recall** (`recall_scoring.py`) — uses UTC on both sides of the math → timezone-independent ✓
- **Dashboard status heartbeat** & **debug log lines** — just display text, never compared, never stored in the brain
- **Backup filenames** — UTC anyway
- **"How long did this take" timers** (`daemon_hooks.py`) — subtract two readings on the same machine, so timezone cancels out

None of them store or compare a brain timestamp using local time.

**There's even a guard rail:** [test_time_window_contract.py](tests/test_time_window_contract.py) scans the whole codebase and *fails the build* if anyone ever introduces the local-time / `datetime('now')` pattern. So this class of bug is actively prevented going forward.

**Bottom line:** safe to delete the dead helper + its test. Your real memories won't corrupt when you change timezones.

Want me to go ahead with the removal now?
